brief.summary: Literature converges on a pure Higgsino thermal relic mass near 1.0-1.1 TeV to saturate Omega h^2 = 0.12, with sub-TeV masses viable only with slepton coannihilation or bino/wino mixing. Direct detection of pure Higgsino is loop-suppressed due to accidental cancellations, leading to purity constraints on gaugino mixing from LZ/Xenon. Recent 2026 preprints propose inelastic Higgsino scattering with delta ~ 350 keV as an interpretation of the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event in 2.84 ton-yr exposure, while a contrasting solar-capture analysis using IceCube non-observation of high-energy neutrinos from the Sun derives delta > 566 keV for ~1.08 TeV Higgsino, excluding the thermal-Higgsino explanation of the LZ event under standard halo and solar model assumptions. The tension hinges on halo high-speed tail (LMC), solar density/capture on heavy elements, elastic cooling in the Sun, and the LZ high-energy sideband joint fit.

directions.goal: Establish the pure-higgsino thermal relic density as a function of mass (about 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV), with and without Sommerfeld enhancement, and find the mass at which Omega h^2 equals the Planck 2018 value of 0.120 +/- 0.001.
directions.rationale: This is the core of the task. The catalog has no inelastic-DM or relic-density compute tool and no coding-task tool, so the Omega h^2(m) curve has to come from published calculations. Each value must be read from text, tables or figures, never estimated.
steps: Confirm the gap: check the tool catalog and list_input_files for any relic-density or inelastic-DM tool or input table. Record the result explicitly.
Download 1411.6930 with download_arxiv_full_text and use read_arxiv_chunk to find the higgsino Omega h^2 versus mass with and without Sommerfeld enhancement, and the quoted thermal mass.

Use get_paper_figures on 1411.6930 to pull the relic-density-versus-mass figure for the higgsino-like case. Record the figure number and read off Omega h^2 at 0.9-1.3 TeV, stating the reading uncertainty.

Use search_arxiv_abstracts for recent independent determinations: 'higgsino relic abundance Sommerfeld 1.1 TeV', 'electroweak dark matter thermal mass higgsino bound state', plus 2021-2026 work. Download one or two and extract their quoted thermal mass and its uncertainty.
Read 1008.2905 for the size of the Sommerfeld effect on non-relativistic relics. Read 1807.06209 for the exact Omega_c h^2 quote.

Build a table: mass versus Omega h^2 (perturbative and Sommerfeld), with the source of each value. Interpolate the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120, using Omega h^2 proportional to m^2 between published points, and state that it is an interpolation.
Use cite to record verbatim quotes for the thermal mass and the Planck value.
success_criteria: A table of Omega h^2 at at least three masses in 0.9-1.3 TeV, each value tied to a paper, figure or table.
The thermal mass with its uncertainty band from at least two independent papers, including any spread between Sommerfeld and non-Sommerfeld results.
An explicit statement that no relic-density compute tool was available and that values come from the literature.

result.summary:
Not finished: only one published pure-higgsino relic-density point was found, so the success criteria (published values at three or more masses, and a thermal mass from two independent papers) are not met.

(1) No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists here, and list_input_files returned no data files (tc-261016_1-w1-d-01-19, finding f-006). Every value below comes from the literature. Nothing was computed.

(2) arXiv:1411.6930, Sec. 3, gives the one published point: a pure higgsino (all sfermions and heavy Higgses decoupled) has Omega h^2 = 0.127 without and 0.126 with Sommerfeld enhancement (off-diagonal rates included). The net Sommerfeld effect is below 1 percent because the neutral channels are enhanced and the charged ones suppressed. The paper's mass for this model appears to be 1172.31 GeV, the mass of its higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006; I inferred this from context, the paper does not state it. For that pMSSM point (dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV) the values are 0.108 without and 0.100 with Sommerfeld, an 8 percent drop. The paper quotes about 5 percent accuracy at best and compares to Planck 2013 (0.1187 +/- 0.0017). Its Fig. 7 (registered as Figure 6, figures_1411.6930/fig07.png) shows only the yield ratio Y/Ypert, not Omega h^2 against mass (finding f-007). A verbatim quote is in references.bib (key arxiv14116930).

(3) hep-ph/0610249 expected the Sommerfeld effect for higgsinos to be roughly 10 percent (versus 50 percent for winos). It was not a full calculation (f-009).

(4) Interpolation, not published values: scaling the 1411.6930 point as Omega h^2 proportional to m^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155 at 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV. Omega h^2 = 0.120 falls at about 1.14 TeV (1144 GeV with Sommerfeld, 1139 GeV without) (f-009, low confidence).

Still to do: the Planck 2018 text was downloaded but not yet read or quoted; 1008.2905 was not read; no independent recent thermal-mass determination was found.

result.summary:
Answer: a thermal pure higgsino at about 1.1 TeV lies about 2 or more orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 limit and below the xenon neutrino floor. Three of the planned inputs were not read: the XENONnT limit, the LZ limit read from its figure at 1 TeV, and a numeric neutrino-fog value. All are recorded as open question q-06.

(1) Prediction. Hisano et al. 1104.0228 work at leading order in electroweak loops. They find the SI cross section of pure SU(2)-multiplet dark matter is O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2, nearly independent of mass above about 1 TeV. An accidental cancellation drives this: twist-2 terms are positive, while the Higgs-exchange, gluon and Z-box scalar terms are negative and of similar size. Their Fig. 5 shows the higgsino (n=2, Y=1/2) at M = 1 TeV against the Higgs mass; the paper predates the measured Higgs mass. Finding f-004.

The newer and more complete calculation is Chen and Hill 1912.07795, which adds O(mW/M) power corrections, QCD corrections to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. Its verbatim result is: 'The upper limit for the pure doublet is less than 10^-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass regime ... lower than the estimated Xenon neutrino floor', with 'the pure Higgsino well below the neutrino floor'. The uncertainty is quoted only as this upper bound; no central value plus or minus an error was read. Citation recorded in references.bib (tc-...-64).

(2) LZ 2024 limit (2410.17036). Verbatim: the strongest SI exclusion is 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 90% CL, and the best median sensitivity is 5.1e-48 cm^2, both at 40 GeV. Finding f-005, citation tc-...-65. No 1 TeV value was read from the text or a figure.

(3) Rescaling. Scaling the 40 GeV limit linearly with mass is my estimate, not a read value. It gives about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, at 1.1 TeV. The ratio of limit to predicted upper bound is then at least about 60, i.e. at least 1.8 orders of magnitude. This extrapolation is likely conservative because the limit curve rises from its minimum. Finding f-008, medium confidence.

Not done:
- The XENONnT 2303.14729 1 TeV limit was not read.
- No limit figure was extracted, so there are no figure numbers for the LZ or XENONnT limits.
- No numeric neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV was obtained; the 'below the neutrino floor' statement rests on Chen and Hill's text.
- Projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD/DARWIN) were not tabulated.

Also noted: 2607.20588 (Bisal et al., 2026) says next-to-leading-order corrections can push the higgsino cross section below the neutrino floor or make it vanish in parts of MSSM parameter space. This is relevant to q-04.

directions.goal: Assess the routes by which a higgsino becomes visible to direct detection: the mass splittings and the inelastic Z-exchange threshold, LZ inelastic constraints (2609.09830), mixing-induced Higgs couplings in the (mu, M1/M2, tan beta) plane (2606.31013), and the (Omega h^2/0.12) rescaling for sub-thermal higgsinos.
directions.rationale: Elastic scattering leaves the pure higgsino invisible, so whether it is visible depends on the splittings set by gaugino masses. This direction goes past the base question and is a robustness check on any 'not excluded' conclusion.
steps: Compute the kinematic threshold by hand and show the arithmetic: delta_max = mu_N v_max^2 / 2 for xenon (A = 131) at m = 1.0 and 1.1 TeV, with v_max = v_esc + v_E (about 544 + 232 km/s).

Download 2609.09830 and read the LZ-excluded delta_m0 range, the expected event counts against delta_m0, and the effect of the one-loop corrections. Use get_paper_figures for the event-count or exclusion figure.

Download 2606.31013 and read the delta_m0 and delta_m+ dependence on M1, M2 and tan beta, the Higgs-coupling expression, and the direct-detection reach in the mass-gaugino plane. Extract the key figure.

Look up the charged-neutral splitting of about 340 MeV in the pure limit, with a source quoted via search_arxiv_abstracts or the papers above. Also look up the tree-level splitting formula, for example delta_m0 approximately m_Z^2 s_W^2 / M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2 / M2. Convert the delta_m0 limit into a lower bound on the gaugino mass that hides the higgsino from inelastic scattering.
State the rescaling of the signal rate by Omega h^2/0.12 for sub-thermal higgsinos, with a sourced example.
Use cite to record verbatim quotes.
success_criteria: A threshold delta_max in keV with the arithmetic shown.
The delta_m0 range excluded by LZ, and the corresponding gaugino-mass scale, sourced from 2609.09830 or 2606.31013.
A sourced description of the mixing region where elastic SI rises above LZ limits.

result.summary: Two of the three success criteria are met; the third is only partly met. (1) The inelastic threshold, worked by hand (f-001): m_Xe = 131 x 0.9315 = 122.0 GeV. The reduced mass mu_A is 108.7 GeV at m = 1.0 TeV and 109.8 GeV at 1.1 TeV. With v_max = 544 + 232 = 776 km/s, (v_max/c)^2 = 6.70e-6, so delta_max = mu_A v_max^2/2 is about 364 keV at 1.0 TeV and 368 keV at 1.1 TeV. The minimum-velocity formula v_min = sqrt(2 delta/mu_A) is Eq. A7 of 2609.09830. (2) Partly met: 2609.09830 does not give an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range (f-002). Its five benchmarks have |mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV, |M1| and M2 of about 5.8-42 TeV, and one-loop on-shell delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. They predict at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, need 9.4-65.5 t-y of exposure to be probed (Table VII, Fig. 6), and are all consistent with LZ. NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV with gaugino masses of O(10) TeV arise only from partial cancellation between the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs; generically the paper quotes O(10-100) MeV. My own estimate, using the formula that is not yet sourced (q-05): same-sign M2 = 2 M1 would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV to bring delta below 364 keV. Inelastic Z-exchange therefore matters only in tuned corners. (3) Mixing region where elastic SI becomes visible (f-003, 2606.31013): Higgs exchange gives f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta). This is suppressed at large gaugino mass and at small tan beta with mu<0. The scan covers 150<|mu|<1000 GeV, 1.6<tan beta<50 and 0.5<M1<10 TeV with M2 = 2 M1. Direct detection is sensitive where mixing produces larger charged-neutral splittings and reaches the thermal mass of about 1 TeV (Figs. 4 and 5 of that paper; the figures were not extracted). The pure-limit radiative charged-neutral splitting is about 356 MeV (Eq. 13 of 2606.31013), rather than the 340 MeV in the brief. (4) Rescaling: 2606.31013 Eq. 38 uses sigma_eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma, computed with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and 2609.09830 states that limits weaken proportionally for sub-thermal fractions. Quotes from both papers are cited in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-higgsino-dd/runs/261016_110437/references.bib. Full texts are at the same run directory as 2609.09830.txt and 2606.31013.txt.

result.summary: One of the three success criteria is met. (1) Met: the Planck 2018 value is quoted verbatim from the abstract on page 1 of arXiv:1807.06209: 'A combined analysis gives dark matter density Ωch2 = 0.120± 0.001' (68% CL). It is at roughly characters 6500-7000 of /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-higgsino-dd/runs/261016_110437/1807.06209.txt (finding f-012, tc-261016_1-w2-d-04-82). It has not yet been added to references.bib with cite(). (2) Not met: a second independent calculation was identified but its number was not read. Bottaro et al., arXiv:2205.04486 ('The last Complex WIMPs standing', 2022), computes thermal masses for complex electroweak n-plets, including the Y=1/2 doublet (the higgsino). Its companion paper, arXiv:2107.09688, describes the method as including Sommerfeld enhancement and bound-state formation at leading order (finding f-013, medium confidence, abstracts only). Its doublet thermal mass was not read, so the spread against the 1411.6930-derived value of about 1.14 TeV (f-009) cannot be stated. For now, only one thermal-mass determination is available, and that one is a rescaled value. (3) Not met: the 1411.6930 mass attribution was not re-read in this direction. The 1172.31 GeV mass behind the pure-higgsino values 0.127/0.126 is still inferred, not stated verbatim (f-007 stays contested). The f-009 rescaling to 0.120 still gives about 1144 GeV (Sommerfeld) and 1139 GeV (perturbative). These numbers are derived, not published, and they depend on the inferred mass. One dead end was recorded: the abstract search for recent thermal-mass papers returned only unrelated LEP notes (x-02). Open question q-08 asks for the 2205.04486 doublet mass and its uncertainty.

Points in the 0.3-5 event band were identified by bracketing with predict_recoil, because the scan file could not be read (x-07).

Event counts from predict_recoil (LZ, 2.84 t-yr):
- delta 340 keV: 10.67 events at 1000 GeV and 17.30 at 1183 GeV
- delta 350 keV: 1.13 at 1000 GeV and 2.90 at 1200 GeV
- delta 360 keV: 0.03 at 1000 GeV and 0.158 at 1183 GeV
- delta 380 keV: 0.00 at both masses

A new 16x16 scan (m_chi 1000-1200 GeV, delta 330-480 keV in 10 keV steps) passes all 256 points and puts 16 in the 0.3-5 band, best fit (1000 GeV, 350 keV). That the 16 are the delta = 350 keV row is inferred from the bracketing, not listed by the tool (f-032). This scan overwrote /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz and constraint_summary.png. The tools return no figure numbers.

Analytic check (f-033, hand-computed): delta_max = v_max*sqrt(2 m_N E_R) - m_N E_R/mu at E_R = 248 keV, with m_N = 122 GeV. At 1000/1100/1183 GeV it gives 358.5/361.3/363.2 keV for 776 km/s, 378/381/383 keV for 800, 419/422/424 keV for 850 and 460/463/465 keV for 900 km/s. It matches the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within about 1 km/s. The tool's 'about 365 keV' edge is the endpoint when E_R is left free, mu v^2/2 = 364-370 keV at 776 km/s, reached near E_R of about 330 keV rather than at 248 keV.

Required v_max (f-034, hand-computed), at 1100 GeV with the event at 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 for 475, 968 for 519, 980 for 529 and 1015 for 557 keV. With E_R left free the minimum is lower: 830 km/s for 422 keV, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 for 557 keV.

What this means for 2609.01590 and the LMC tail:
- The paper's profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s, compared with the tool's 776 km/s. This explains why the tool gives zero events at 400 keV.
- The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need an LMC-boosted tail reaching about 920-980 km/s.
- Clearing the 475 keV IceCube line needs at least about 880-915 km/s.
- Clearing the 557 keV Super-K + IceCube line needs at least about 950-1015 km/s.
The higgsino reading of the event therefore depends entirely on how many particles the halo has above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.

Still open: I could not compare these numbers with the actual v_esc + v_E values of the 2609.01590 halos, because the paper's endpoint sentence has no validated quote (x-04).

Dead end x-07: load_table_data cannot read the binary npz file.

result.summary: Two of the four goals are settled from full texts. The other two, plus the indirect-detection comparison, were not reached. (1) 2609.09830 does not give an on-shell delta_m shift for the 475-557 keV window (f-030). Its benchmark points are tuned to small one-loop on-shell splittings: delta = 36.37, 8.90, 16.39, 10.81 and 10.59 keV for BP1-BP5, at |mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV, all with Omega h^2 < 0.12. Comparing its tree and one-loop masses suggests the shift is of order 0.1 GeV, but that is my reading of their mass table, not a number the paper states. So the paper is not relevant to rescuing the 475-557 keV window. (2) 2610.03692 defines four IceCube treatments, shown at 90% CL in its Fig. 2 (f-031): capture-annihilation equilibrium; SI inelastic cooling only; SI inelastic + SD elastic cooling; and SI inelastic + SD + SI elastic cooling with sigma_SI,el = 4e-50 cm^2. Its inputs: W+W- limits, standard halo with v0 = 220, v_sun = 232 and v_esc = 544 km/s, rho = 0.3 GeV/cm^3, and an LMC tail cut off at v_min = 950 km/s. The solar limits are stated not to change when the LMC is added. The delta values at 1.1 TeV for each treatment appear only in the figure, so they are not quantified. The paper's text calls the 1.1 TeV thermal higgsino only marginally compatible. Blocked items (dead end x-06): the tool budget ran out before narrow re-reads of 2609.01590 and 2609.07807. Findings f-024, f-025 and f-026 therefore remain contested, including whether the 1.69/2 CTAO Omega estimate is from the paper or from the agent. No s-wave <sigma v> versus H.E.S.S. ratio was computed, so the tool's p-wave pass (f-022) is still unreplaced. The full texts are in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-higgsino-dd/runs/261022_110244/ as 2609.01590.txt, 2610.03692.txt and 2609.09830.txt. No cite calls were made.

findings.claim: 2609.09830 does not quote an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range. Its five benchmarks (|mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV; |M1|, M2 about 5.8-42 TeV; tan beta 10.9-26.5) have one-loop on-shell splittings delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. Each predicts at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, and probing them needs 9.4-65.5 tonne-years. All are consistent with the LZ bound. Inelastic events at NLO range from 0.00022 (BP1) to 0.18 (BP4). NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV come from partial cancellation of the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs.

findings.claim: 2606.31013: the SI coupling comes from Higgs exchange, f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta), so it is suppressed at large gaugino mass and at small tan beta with mu<0. The scan covers 150<|mu|<1000 GeV, 1.6<tan beta<50, 0.5<M1<10 TeV with M2=2M1. Rates are rescaled by Omega_H h^2/0.12 (Eq. 38, computed with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0). Direct detection is sensitive mainly where higgsino-gaugino mixing produces sizable charged-neutral splittings, and reaches the thermal mass of about 1 TeV. The radiative charged-neutral splitting tends to about 356 MeV for M >> M_Z (Eq. 13).

findings.claim: Beneke, Hellmann and Ruiz-Femenia (arXiv:1411.6930, Sec. 3) report Omega h^2 = 0.127 (perturbative) and 0.126 (Sommerfeld, with off-diagonal rates) for a pure-higgsino model compared against the higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006 at m_chi = 1172.31 GeV. The net Sommerfeld correction for pure higgsinos is almost zero (below 1 percent) because enhancement in the neutral channels cancels suppression in the chi0 chi+- channels. For the pMSSM higgsino-like point (higgsino fraction 0.98, dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV) they find Omega h^2 = 0.108 (perturbative) and 0.100 (Sommerfeld), an 8 percent reduction. The quoted Sommerfeld accuracy is about 5 percent at best.

findings.claim: Chen and Hill (1912.07795) include the O(mW/M) power corrections, perturbative QCD to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. They find that the pure-higgsino SI cross section has an upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass range, below the estimated xenon neutrino floor. This is about 2 orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 minimum limit of 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 40 GeV. Assuming linear mass scaling of the LZ limit above about 100 GeV (my estimate, not read from the paper), the LZ limit at 1.1 TeV is about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, so the pure higgsino lies at least about 1.8 orders of magnitude below it.

evidence.note: The rescaled 1 TeV LZ limit is a linear extrapolation from the 40 GeV minimum. The rise of the curve near its minimum makes the true value somewhat larger (weaker), so the ratio is conservative. Neither the XENONnT 2303.14729 text nor the neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV was read in this direction.

findings.claim: Hisano et al. (hep-ph/0610249) expect the Sommerfeld effect on the higgsino-like relic abundance to be roughly 10 percent, compared with a 50 percent reduction for the wino. 1411.6930 later found the net pure-higgsino effect is below 1 percent (Omega h^2 = 0.127 perturbative, 0.126 Sommerfeld). Rescaling that single point (taken as m = 1172.31 GeV) with Omega h^2 proportional to m^2 gives the Planck value 0.120 at m of about 1.14 TeV (Sommerfeld: 1144 GeV; perturbative: 1139 GeV). The rescaled values are 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155 at m = 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV. These are m^2 rescalings of one published point, not published values.

findings.claim: Metadata confirms both IDs: arXiv:2606.31013 is 'Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection' by Hamaguchi, Nagata and Osaki (2026), and arXiv:2609.09830 is 'Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter' by Chatterjee, Das, Pasha, Pukhov and Puri (2026). Both abstracts match how the survey uses them. This resolves q-02.

The full text of 2606.31013 supports the f-003 numbers. Eq. 13 reads Delta m+|rad ~ (1/2) alpha2 MZ sin^2 thetaW (1 - 3MZ/(2 pi M_chi+)), with the statement 'For M_chi+ >> MZ, this mass splitting asymptotically approaches Delta m+|rad ~ 356 MeV'. Eq. 33 reads f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 thetaW/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta) and is valid for MZ << M1,2-|mu|; the exact form is Eq. 32. The paper says the coupling is suppressed at large gaugino mass and 'for small tan beta and negative mu, due to an accidental cancellation'. Eq. 38 is sigma_SI/SD,eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma_SI/SD, computed with micrOMEGAs v6.3.0. findings.claim: The 475 keV and 557 keV neutrino lines differ because of how the captured population in the Sun is treated, not because of the halo. 2609.01590 simulates a non-thermal population on extended solar orbits at m_chi = 1.11 TeV with no elastic cooling (elastic blind spot) and 10-year IceCube data, using <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s with Sommerfeld; this gives delta_m >~ 475 keV excluded at 90% CL (466 keV with loose solar/nuclear inputs, about 454 keV with the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty). findings.claim: Inverting the kinematics at m_chi = 1100 GeV gives the v_max (Earth frame) needed to reach a given delta with an event exactly at E_R = 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 km/s for 475 keV, 968 km/s for 519 keV, 980 km/s for 529 keV and 1015 km/s for 557 keV (about +3 km/s at 1000 GeV, about -2 km/s at 1183 GeV). All of these exceed the tool's SHM cutoff of 776 km/s by 55-240 km/s. So the 2609.01590 profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s. The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need about 920-980 km/s of LMC-boosted tail. Covering delta >= 557 keV (above the Super-K + IceCube line) needs at least about 950-1015 km/s, and delta >= 475 keV needs at least about 880-915 km/s. questions.text: The task asks for relic densities from 'inelastic-DM tools', but no such tool, no run_coding_task and no run_pack_kernel is in the catalog. Should the user be told that relic-density values are literature-sourced rather than computed, or is a compute server missing from the connection?
The arXiv IDs 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 are recent. Verify with get_arxiv_metadata that they exist and that their content matches the survey before relying on them.

Published thermal masses differ by about 10-20 percent depending on Sommerfeld treatment, bound-state formation and the treatment of the QCD/electroweak phase transition. Which value should serve as the headline?
Is the SI prediction's interference between the Higgs and gauge (twist-2) contributions stable enough that the conclusion 'below the neutrino fog' is robust?

The tree-level formula delta_m0 ≈ m_Z^2 s_W^2/M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2/M2 has not been sourced yet. Can a quotable reference be found, for example Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, Eq. (9)? Taken at face value with same-sign M2 = 2 M1, delta < 364 keV would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV, so the O(10) keV benchmarks are viable only through sign cancellations and loop corrections.

Still open from d-02: the XENONnT 2303.14729 SI limit at 1 TeV, the actual LZ 2024 limit-curve value at 1 TeV (read from its figure rather than linearly rescaled from 40 GeV), and a numeric xenon neutrino-fog value at 1.1 TeV. None of these were read in this direction.

The XLZD Design Book (arXiv:2410.17137) has been identified but not read: what are its projected SI sensitivity and its xenon neutrino-fog value at about 1 TeV, and how do they compare with the pure-higgsino bound of 1e-48 cm^2?

What thermal mass, with its theory uncertainty, does arXiv:2205.04486 (Bottaro et al. 2022, Sommerfeld plus bound-state formation) give for the Y=1/2 doublet in its thermal-mass table, and how far is it from the 1411.6930-derived value of about 1.14 TeV?

What arXiv paper is Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, and does its Eq. (9) give the tree-level neutral higgsino splitting with explicit sign dependence on mu, M1 and M2? This is needed to re-evaluate the M1 required for delta < 364 keV, given that BP4 and BP5 reach about 10.7 keV with same-sign M1 and M2 of about 12 TeV.
Does compute_relic_density include Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation, or only perturbative freeze-out? This determines how its thermal mass compares with 1411.6930 and 2205.04486.

The hand estimate f-001 gives a kinematic delta_max of about 365 keV for v_max = 776 km/s, yet 2609.01590 fits delta_m of about 500 keV. Which halo assumption (v_esc, LMC tail) does the tool use, and does it reproduce either result?
Do the tool's LZ constraint and the published LZ 2024 curve agree at 1.1 TeV?
Where is the published Ref. [28] tree-level delta_m0 formula (open item d-07)? It is needed to judge how natural delta_m of about 500 keV is.
Do the Fermi-LAT and CMB verdicts from check_all_constraints agree with published TeV-higgsino indirect-detection limits (open item d-08)?

Why does check_all_constraints give N_LZ = 0.00 already at delta = 400 keV for m_chi = 1160 GeV, and why does it use a p-wave, splitting-suppressed sigma_v_today of about 1e-41 cm^3/s instead of the s-wave higgsino WW rate of about 1e-26 cm^3/s? Its indirect and CMB verdicts need an external cross-check against published higgsino limits (q-14).
How large is the 2609.09830 one-loop change to delta_m and to the inelastic cross section (the full text has not been read), and what are the 2610.03692 thermal-mass IceCube variants in numbers?

The LZ 2024 (2410.17036) and XENONnT (2303.14729) SI limits at 1.1 TeV and the XLZD neutrino-fog level remain unread in d-11 (budget exhausted); can a follow-up read them from the text or HEPData instead of extrapolating the 40 GeV limit?
What is the Sommerfeld+bound-state corrected thermal mass spread (1.0 vs 1.1 vs 1.2 TeV) across 1411.6930, 2205.04486 and recent 2026 papers?
Can delta ~300-350 keV inelastic higgsino at 1.1 TeV produce the LZ 248 keV event without violating v_esc+v_E=776 km/s threshold (~364 keV) and neutrino-line bounds 475/557 keV?
How far below LZ 2024/XENONnT and below/above neutrino fog does the pure-higgsino elastic SI cross-section (<1e-48 cm2) sit at 1 TeV, and what gaugino mixing is needed to become visible?

What is the quantitative shift in thermal Higgsino mass when adding Sommerfeld + bound-state formation (2205.04486) vs perturbative 1411.6930/serve-idm.sh, and what uncertainty should be quoted for the 1.0-1.1 TeV target?

Does the LZ 248 keV event survive as inelastic Higgsino scattering when varying halo v_max from 776 km/s (standard) to LMC-boosted ~850 km/s, and at what delta does solar capture/IceCube (delta>566 keV) definitively exclude the thermal mass?
What are the true LZ/XENONnT SI limits at 1 TeV (not 40 GeV extrapolated) and where does the pure-Higgsino loop cross section (<1e-48 cm2) sit relative to the neutrino fog and XLZD reach?

issues.text: Step 1 is not enough: the gap has to show up in the final answer. No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists, list_input_files is empty, and run_test_job only draws random samples. The task asked us to compute relic density with tools, and we cannot. The report must say plainly that every Omega h^2 value is taken from the literature. Do not use run_test_job to produce anything that looks like a computed relic curve.

1411.6930 is a pMSSM scan. It may not give a pure-higgsino Omega h^2(m) curve at 0.9-1.3 TeV with and without Sommerfeld enhancement. Before relying on it, check that such a figure or table exists. If it does not, use the one-parameter thermal mass plus the m^2 scaling, and label every resulting row as derived, not read. Also note that the higgsino Sommerfeld effect is small, only a few percent shift in mass. Bound-state formation (recent 2021-2026 work) can matter as much as Sommerfeld, so the search should target it explicitly.

The budget is tight. Fifteen calls do not cover three or four full-text downloads plus chunk reads, figures and cite. Drop the full read of 1008.2905, which is a method paper and not needed for numbers. Get the Planck Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001 quote with one targeted chunk read of 1807.06209. Limit independent cross-checks to one paper.

Run get_arxiv_metadata on 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 before any download, to confirm they exist and say what the brief claims. The brief cites 2606.31013 for the '~1 TeV' figure but has not read it. If either ID does not resolve, report that and do not attribute numbers to it.

A key literature cross-check is missing. Hill and Solon (for example 1111.0016 and 1409.8290) give the heavy-higgsino SI cross section with a large cancellation-driven uncertainty, possibly near or below the xenon neutrino fog. Because 1104.0228 and 1007.2601 predate refined nucleon matrix elements, the prediction should be quoted as a range across these sources, not a single number. 1004.4090 is a wino paper and can be skipped.

Values read off log-scale limit figures with get_paper_figures need a stated reading uncertainty, for example a factor of about 1.5. Check whether the LZ and XENONnT figures actually extend to 1 TeV. If they do, read the value there and do not rescale. If rescaling is needed, use limit proportional to m for m >> m_Xe and state the reference mass. Also replace the brief's 1e-46 to 1e-45 estimate with read values; the true limit at 1 TeV is likely near the low end of that range.

2510.17473 (ICRC 2025 review) is listed in the brief but not used. Use it as one source for current and projected xenon reach (LZ full exposure, XLZD) and for the neutrino-fog value at TeV masses, instead of searching for a separate fog paper.

The threshold arithmetic is sound. With m_Xe of about 122 GeV, mu is about 109 GeV at 1 TeV and v_max is about 776 km/s, giving delta_max of about 360 keV. State the assumed v_esc and v_E, and note the sensitivity to the halo model. Source the charged-neutral splitting of about 341 MeV to the two-loop result (for example 1410.4549) rather than leaving it generic. Keep the splitting formula approximate, including tan(beta)-dependent and sign terms.

The answer to 'relative to current limits' should mention indirect detection briefly. For example, H.E.S.S. Galactic Center line and continuum limits are weak for TeV higgsinos because the cross section is not strongly Sommerfeld-enhanced. One sourced sentence from a review will do. This keeps the conclusion from resting on direct detection alone without changing scope.
The mixing-induced SI rise in the (mu, M1/M2, tan beta) plane overlaps with the d-02 discussion. Keep it only in d-03, so the two directions do not each download 2606.31013.

contested.reason: None of the three quoted excerpts contains any claimed content. tc-...-35 covers the oblique-parameter chi-square (Eqs. 26-29), tc-...-30 is the title page, and tc-...-33 covers the W/Y parameters (Eqs. 39-40). Missing are the f_q formula, the scan ranges, Eq. 13 (356 MeV), Eq. 38 with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and the statement that direct detection reaches about 1 TeV only with mixing. These may well be in the paper, but the cited evidence does not show them.

The excerpts do not show the Omega h^2 values 0.127, 0.126, 0.108 or 0.100, nor dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV or the 5 percent accuracy. The claim states m_chi = 1172.31 GeV as reported, but the d-01 summary says this mass was inferred from context and is not stated in the paper. The figure is also mislabelled: fig07 is registered as Figure 6.

There are two problems. First, the Chen and Hill verbatim quote (the upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2, below the neutrino floor) is not in any quoted excerpt. The cited tc-...-59 and -58 show only the rate formula and the title, and the citation call tc-...-64 is not listed as evidence. Second, there is an arithmetic error. An upper bound below 1e-48 cm^2 compared with the 2.2e-48 cm^2 minimum is a factor of about 2 or more, not 'about 2 orders of magnitude'. Only the comparison at 1.1 TeV (about 6e-47 cm^2) supports a margin of 1.8 orders or more.

The visible part of Table VII supports only BP1 elastic NLO = 1.028 events, which is consistent with 'at most about 1.03'. The other quantities are not in the shown excerpts: the splitting range 8.9-36.4 keV, the exposures of 9.4-65.5 t-y, the inelastic NLO range, and the BP2 statement. The visible LO numbers for BP2 (inelastic 0.0247, elastic 0.0436) show inelastic below elastic. The 'twice the LO elastic' claim therefore needs the NLO inelastic value quoted explicitly.

issues.text: The core quantity is still unmet. There is no published Omega h^2(m) curve at multiple masses and no second, independent determination of the thermal mass. The m^2 rescaling in f-009 depends on an inferred mass of 1172.31 GeV. If that inference is wrong, every rescaled value and the 1.14 TeV thermal mass shift with it.

The Planck 2018 value of 0.120 +/- 0.001 is used throughout but has never been quoted from 1807.06209.txt, although the file is already downloaded. 1411.6930 normalised to Planck 2013 (0.1187), so the f-009 rescaling should state which target it uses.

The arithmetic checks out: 0.126 x (m/1172.31)^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155, and the thermal masses of 1144 and 1139 GeV are correct. However, the hep-ph/0610249 '10 percent' statement is not visible in the tc-...-68 excerpt.
The excerpt confirms only the 4.2 t-y exposure. The 2.2e-48 / 5.1e-48 cm^2 values at 40 GeV match the published LZ abstract but are not visible in the quoted chunk.

The excerpts support the structure of the cancellation (the Fig. 6 contribution panels), but not the numeric range O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2. This is a 2011 result computed against a scan over the Higgs mass, so it should be quoted at mh = 125 GeV.

The headline answer to 'where the higgsino sits relative to limits' still rests on a linear extrapolation from 40 GeV. None of the following has been read: the LZ or XENONnT limit at 1 TeV, a numeric neutrino-fog value, or projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD). The final answer needs these numbers, each with a stated reading uncertainty.

2606.31013 and 2609.09830 have not been checked with get_arxiv_metadata (q-02). The delta_m0 tree-level formula behind the 1.4e7 GeV estimate is unsourced (q-05). The 356 versus 340 MeV correction to the brief depends on f-003, which is contested.

issues.text: The arithmetic is correct: 2.2e-48 / 1e-48 = 2.2, which is 0.34 decades, and 2.2e-48 x 1100/40 = 6.05e-47, giving a ratio of at least about 60 (about 1.78 decades). The key number is still a linear extrapolation from the 40 GeV minimum, not a read value. The 2.2e-48 input comes from f-005 and is not in this finding's excerpts. The headline 'where does the higgsino sit' ratio therefore still lacks a measured limit at 1 TeV.

The excerpt from tc-...-82 is truncated before the quoted sentence. The retrieved range (chars 5500-10000) does cover the stated location (about 6500-7000), and the value is standard, so it is accepted. It is still not in references.bib; cite() should be called.

None of the Table III, VI or VII numbers appear in the displayed excerpts. Only surrounding prose is shown, although the retrieved ranges (chars 27000-50000) plausibly contain the tables. This was the original reason f-002 was contested, so the trace is only partly verbatim. f-016 is accepted on the strength of the range coverage and the consistent BP3-BP5 prose. The numbers should still be recorded with cite() and table excerpts.

The tree-level estimate that same-sign M2 = 2 M1 needs M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV is misleading for the survey's conclusion. A same-sign tree-level splitting of order m_Z^2 (s_W^2/M1 + c_W^2/M2) at about 12 TeV would be roughly 0.5-0.7 MeV. BP4 and BP5 instead show about 10.6-10.8 keV after on-shell one-loop corrections, a reduction of more than an order of magnitude. Until the formula is sourced, the 1.4e7 GeV figure should be dropped or explicitly labelled tree-level, and the 'tuned corners only' statement should be revised.

issues.text: The steps need about 17 calls: 1 describe, 5 masses, 3 toggles, up to 3 bracketing, 4 sensitivity, 1 constraint check. The budget is 15. Drop the 400 and 600 keV delta_m variations, since a keV-scale neutral splitting has a negligible effect on freeze-out. Keep one delta_m variation as a sanity check and use the 2 freed calls for the charged-splitting variations, which do matter through coannihilation.

If describe_tools shows that compute_relic_density is perturbative only, or omits coannihilation, the crossing will land near 1.0 TeV or lower. It must then not be reported as the higgsino thermal mass. State the result as tool output under those stated assumptions, and compare it with 1411.6930 and 2205.04486 (from d-11) rather than replacing them.

The 1172 GeV value for 1411.6930 is inferred, not stated in the paper. Label it as inferred everywhere. For check_all_constraints, record whether its LZ test is elastic SI, inelastic, or both, and which exposure it assumes. Without this, the LZ verdict cannot be interpreted.

Do not call set_dispatch to polaris or perlmutter. No IRI or Globus authentication has been established, and get_dispatch reports local execution. Size the grid so it runs locally, for example 5 masses by 8 delta_m values, and report the site as returned.

Event counts are unverifiable without LZ signal efficiency and the analysis region of interest near 248 keV, since the standard WIMP search region ends well below that. State the acceptance the tool uses. If the tool has none, report counts as 100 percent acceptance upper bounds and label them that way.

f-001 checks out: mu of about 110 GeV and v of 776 km/s give delta_max of about 368 keV. A standard halo therefore gives zero events at 480-520 keV, and the result rests entirely on halo assumptions. Make the v_esc or high-velocity-tail variation mandatory, not conditional. If the tool has no such knob, record that it cannot test 2609.01590 and stop rather than reporting zero events as a refutation. The 475 and 557 keV lines are literature values, not tool output. Label them as such, and note that the 557 keV line excludes the whole 481-519 keV window.
Annual modulation at 248 keV near the kinematic edge is a low-priority call. Drop it if the budget is tight. Skip the extra check_all_constraints call because d-09 already covers it.
The files from run 261016_110437 may not persist. Run list_files on downloads first, and budget re-downloads if they are missing. Confirm 2205.04486 with get_arxiv_metadata before citing it.

The higgsino SI prediction carries a large theoretical uncertainty from Higgs and gauge-loop cancellation, so 'at most 1e-48' is not a central value. Quote the Chen and Hill band with its uncertainty. A linear high-mass extrapolation of the LZ limit is acceptable if it is labeled, but the extrapolation formula must be stated.

issues.text: The central task question has not been answered quantitatively: where does the elastic SI cross section of the thermal higgsino sit relative to the LZ 4.2 t-yr and XENONnT 90% CL curves at 1.0-1.2 TeV? No finding gives either the higgsino SI value (loop and Higgs-mediated, around 1e-48 to 1e-49 cm^2 with possible cancellation) or the limit values at 1.1 TeV. d-11 is still open, and this comparison is the core of the headline answer.

The thermal mass of about 1159 GeV is set by the tool's hard-coded normalization (sigma_v = 2.5e-26 x (1100/m)^2). It is a calibration, not a computation. The report must not present it as an independent check of 1411.6930. The Sommerfeld/coannihilation step and the charged-splitting sensitivity in the brief were never done. A literature or analytic estimate (1008.2905 method) is needed if the task's 'with and without Sommerfeld' item is to be answered.

The tool's indirect-detection and CMB passes rest on a p-wave, splitting-suppressed annihilation today. This is unphysical for a higgsino, which annihilates s-wave to WW/ZZ at about 1-1.5e-26 cm^3/s. The 'VIABLE' label for indirect and CMB constraints should be replaced by a comparison of the s-wave rate with the Fermi dwarf and H.E.S.S. continuum and line limits at 1.1 TeV, together with f-026.

The claim that no LZ-reproducing point survives the neutrino limits is inferred from the 1.1 TeV kinematics and the single best fit. The 12 'best_fit_region' points were never listed. The npz file exists and should be loaded to confirm their (m_chi, delta) values. A second point needs checking: the tool gives zero events at 400 keV, while the profiled Maxwellian in 2609.01590 reaches 422 keV (1 sigma) and 457 keV (2 sigma). Either the tool's v_max = 776 km/s is lower than the profiled v_esc, or the treatments differ. This should be reconciled analytically.

Several headline literature numbers rest on text that was read but has no validated quote (x-04). Re-fetching narrower character windows around the relevant passages would let the excerpts carry the values even if the cite tool continues to reject garbled math.

turns.text: Survey recent arXiv work on the higgsino thermal relic target (1.0-1.2 TeV). Use the inelastic-DM tools to compute the relic density at several masses; compare with LZ/XENONnT sensitivities and the Planck abundance. Where does the higgsino sit relative to current limits?

**Survey** — 29 tools on 2 servers, 5 read-only probes, 11 papers found.

The literature agrees that a pure higgsino (an SU(2) doublet with Y=1/2) makes up all of the dark matter as a thermal relic at a mass of roughly 1.0-1.2 TeV. Sommerfeld-enhanced coannihilation calculations, for example 1411.6930, move the exact mass within that window, and 2606.31013 quotes about 1 TeV. Pure-higgsino scattering in direct detection comes from loops and is tiny: the one- and two-loop electroweak calculations (1104.0228 and 1007.2601) put the spin-independent cross section well below current xenon limits, near or inside the neutrino fog. I did not read those full texts, so the exact numbers need checking. The 2024 LZ result (2410.17036, 4.2 tonne-years) and the first XENONnT result (2303.14729) are tightest near 30-40 GeV. At 1 TeV their limits scale up roughly linearly with mass, to about 1e-46 to 1e-45 cm^2 (my estimate, not read from their tables). A thermal pure higgsino is therefore not excluded by elastic scattering. Direct detection can see it only if mixing with gauginos raises the Higgs coupling and the mass splittings (2606.31013), or if the splitting between the two neutral states is small enough (roughly up to a few hundred keV) that tree-level inelastic Z-exchange turns on. That inelastic case is already strongly constrained, and 2609.09830 recomputes it at one loop for LZ. Planck 2018 (1807.06209) sets the target abundance at Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001.

Quantities worth checking: Omega h^2 against higgsino mass at about 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV, with and without Sommerfeld enhancement; find the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120; Charged-neutral splitting (about 340 MeV from electroweak loops in the pure limit) and neutral-neutral splitting delta_m0 as functions of the gaugino masses M1 and M2; Elastic spin-independent cross section of the pure higgsino at 1.1 TeV compared with the LZ 2024 and XENONnT limits at the same mass, and with the xenon neutrino fog; Inelastic Z-exchange threshold: the largest delta_m0 at which xenon at about 1 TeV can still produce a recoil (scale set by the kinematic limit, about mu v^2 / 2), and the delta_m0 values LZ excludes; Rescaling of signal rate by (Omega h^2 / 0.12) for higgsinos lighter than the thermal mass that make up only part of the dark matter; Size of the tree-level Higgs coupling as a function of M1, M2 and tan(beta), to map where mixing makes higgsinos visible to LZ.

The minimum-velocity formula v_min = sqrt(2 delta/mu_A) is given in 2609.09830 Appendix A (Eq. A7).

**Finding:** 2609.09830 does not quote an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range. Its five benchmarks (|mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV; |M1|, M2 about 5.8-42 TeV; tan beta 10.9-26.5) have one-loop on-shell splittings delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. Each predicts at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, and probing them needs 9.4-65.5 tonne-years. All are consistent with the LZ bound. Inelastic events at NLO range from 0.00022 (BP1) to 0.18 (BP4). NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV come from partial cancellation of the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs.

**Finding:** 2606.31013: the SI coupling comes from Higgs exchange, f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta), so it is suppressed at large gaugino mass and at small tan beta with mu<0. Direct detection is sensitive mainly where higgsino-gaugino mixing produces sizable charged-neutral splittings, and reaches the thermal mass of about 1 TeV. Authors: Dimitrios Karamitros

Abstract: We consider cases where the dark matter-nucleon interaction is naturally suppressed. We explicitly show that by extending the standard model scalar sector by a number of singlets, can lead to a vanishing direct detection cross section, if some softly broken symmetries are imposed in the dark sector. In particular, it is shown that if said symmetries are $SU(2)$ ($SU(N)$) and $U(1) \times S_N$, then the resulting pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone bosons can constitute the dark matter of the Universe, while naturally explaining the missing signal in nuclear recoil experiments.

Abstract: Direct dark matter searches are promising techniques to identify the nature of dark matter particles. I describe the future of this field of research, focussing on the question of what can be achieved in the next decade. I will present the main techniques and R&D projects that will allow to build so-called ultimate WIMP detectors, capable of probing spin-independent interactions down to the unimaginably low cross section of 1e-48 cm2, before the irreducible neutrino background takes over. If a discovery is within the reach of a near-future dark matter experiment, these detectors will be able to constrain WIMP properties such as its mass, scattering cross section and possibly spin. With input from the LHC and from indirect searches, direct detection experiments will hopefully allow to determine the local density and to constrain the local phase-space structure of our dark matter halo.

Title: Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection
Authors: Koichi Hamaguchi, Natsumi Nagata, Genta Osaki

PDF URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.31013v1
Abstract: Although higgsinos are well motivated to be light from the viewpoint of naturalness, they remain difficult to detect experimentally because they interact only through electroweak interactions and typically possess a compressed mass spectrum. While higgsino dark matter can be efficiently probed by direct detection experiments when gauginos are relatively light, the sensitivity rapidly deteriorates for heavier gauginos due to the suppression of higgsino-gaugino mixing. In this paper, we investigate the prospects for probing light higgsinos through future electroweak precision measurements. Focusing on scenarios in which charginos and neutralinos are the only light electroweakly interacting superparticles, we evaluate their contributions to the electroweak oblique parameters as well as to the precision observables $M_W$ and $\sin^2θ_{\mathrm{eff}}$. We compare the projected sensitivities of future $e^+e^-$ colliders with those of dark matter direct detection experiments. We find that future electroweak precision measurements provide a powerful probe of higgsinos with masses $\lesssim 500~\mathrm{GeV}$, including parameter regions with highly compressed spectra and spin-independent scattering cross sections below the neutrino fog. On the other hand, dark matter direct detection experiments are particularly sensitive to scenarios with larger charged-neutral mass splittings induced by higgsino-gaugino mixing, and can probe higgsino dark matter all the way up to the thermal relic mass of $\simeq 1~\mathrm{TeV}$. Our results demonstrate the strong complementarity between electroweak precision measurements and dark matter direct detection experiments in exploring light higgsinos and testing supersymmetric scenarios motivated by naturalness.

Abstract: If there is a fifth force in the dark sector and dark sector particles interact non-gravitationally with ordinary matter, quantum corrections generically lead to a fifth force in the visible sector. Abstract: The inert higgs model is a minimal extension of the Standard Model that features a viable dark matter candidate, the so-called inert higgs ($H^0$). In this paper, we compute and analyze the dominant electroweak corrections to the direct detection cross section of dark matter within this model. These corrections arise from one-loop diagrams mediated by gauge bosons that, contrary to the tree-level result, do not depend on the unknown scalar coupling $λ$. We study in detail these contributions and show that they can modify in a significant way the prediction of the spin-independent direct detection cross section. In both viable regimes of the model, $\mh<M_W$ and $\mh\gtrsim 500 \gev$, we find regions where the cross section at one-loop is much larger than at tree-level. We also demonstrate that, over the entire viable parameter space of this model, these new contributions bring the spin-independent cross section within the reach of future direct detection experiments.

Abstract: We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new. A technique to actively tag background electronic recoils from $^{214}$Pb $β$ decays is featured for the first time. Enhanced electron-ion recombination is observed in two-neutrino double electron capture decays of $^{124}$Xe, representing a noteworthy new background. Abstract: The design and performance of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector is described as of March 2015 in this Conceptual Design Report. LZ is a second-generation dark-matter detector with the potential for unprecedented sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) of masses from a few GeV/c2 to hundreds of TeV/c2. With total liquid xenon mass of about 10 tonnes, LZ will be the most sensitive experiment for WIMPs in this mass region by the end of the decade. This report describes in detail the design of the LZ technical systems. Expected backgrounds are quantified and the performance of the experiment is presented. The LZ detector will be located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. The organization of the LZ Project and a summary of the expected cost and current schedule are given.

Abstract: We describe the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a proposed optical-near infrared survey of 5000 sq. deg of the South Galactic Cap to ~24th magnitude in SDSS griz, that would use a new 3 sq. deg CCD camera to be mounted on the Blanco 4-m telescope at Cerro Telolo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The survey data will allow us to measure the dark energy and dark matter densities and the dark energy equation of state through four independent methods: galaxy clusters, weak gravitational lensing tomography, galaxy angular clustering, and supernova distances. These methods are doubly complementary: they constrain different combinations of cosmological model parameters and are subject to different systematic errors. By deriving the four sets of measurements from the same data set with a common analysis framework, we will obtain important cross checks of the systematic errors and thereby make a substantial and robust advance in the precision of dark energy measurements.

Abstract: Direct dark matter searches are promising techniques to identify the nature of dark matter particles. I describe the future of this field of research, focussing on the question of what can be achieved in the next decade. I will present the main techniques and R&D projects that will allow to build so-called ultimate WIMP detectors, capable of probing spin-independent interactions down to the unimaginably low cross section of 1e-48 cm2, before the irreducible neutrino background takes over. If a discovery is within the reach of a near-future dark matter experiment, these detectors will be able to constrain WIMP properties such as its mass, scattering cross section and possibly spin. With input from the LHC and from indirect searches, direct detection experiments will hopefully allow to determine the local density and to constrain the local phase-space structure of our dark matter halo.

Abstract: The XENON experiment aims at the direct detection of dark matter in the form of WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) via their elastic scattering off Xenon nuclei. With a fiducial mass of 1000 kg of liquid xenon, a sufficiently low threshold of ~16 keV recoil energy and an un-rejected background rate of 10 events per year, XENON would be sensitive to a WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section of 10^(-46) cm^2, for WIMPs with masses above 50 GeV. The 1 tonne scale experiment (XENON1T) will be realized with an array of ten identical 100 kg detector modules (XENON100). The detectors are time projection chambers operated in dual (liquid/gas) phase, to detect simultaneously the ionization, through secondary scintillation in the gas, and primary scintillation in the liquid produced by low energy recoils. The distinct ratio of primary to secondary scintillation for nuclear recoils from WIMPs (or neutrons), and for electron recoils from background, is key to the event-by-event discrimination capability of XENON. A 3kg dual phase detector with light readout provided by an array of 7 photomultipliers is currently being tested, along with other prototypes dedicated to various measurements relevant to the XENON program. We present some of the results obtained to-date and briefly discuss the next step in the phased approach to the XENON experiment, i.e. the development and underground deployment of a 10 kg detector (XENON10) within 2005.

Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

Assuming that the lightest neutral component in an SU (2)L gauge multiplet is
the main ingredient of dark matter in the universe, we calcul ate the elastic scattering
cross section of the dark matter with nucleon, which is an imp ortant quantity for the
direct detection experiments. When the dark matter is a real scalar or a Majorana
fermion which has only electroweak gauge interactions, the scattering with quarks
and gluon are induced through one- and two-loop quantum proc esses, respectively,

section. We evaluate all of the contributions at the leading order and ﬁnd that there
is an accidental cancellation among them. As a result, the sp in-independent cross
section is found to be O(10− (46− 48)) cm2, which is far below the current experimental
bounds.

I. INTRODUCTION
Among the low-energy supersymmetric (SUSY) extensions of the Standard Model (SM), the
Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) with conservedR-parity provides a well-
motivated dark matter (DM) candidate. In large regions of the MSSM parameter space, the
lightest neutralino (˜χ0
1) is the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP). Owing to the conservation
ofR-parity, it is stable and can account for the observed DM relic abundance [1, 2]. In general,
˜χ0
1 can be characterised by one of the interaction states−Bino, Wino, or Higgsino, or by any of
their suitable admixtures. Among various possibilities, a nearly pure Higgsino LSP is favoured
as it offers a potential resolution to the naturalness problem [3–9]. The observed dark matter
(DM) relic abundance, (Ω DMh2 ≃0.12) [10, 11], can be naturally accommodated within the
Higgsino-like DM scenario [5, 12–18]. In particular, a nearly pure Higgsino-like ˜χ 0
1 with a mass
parameter (µ≃1 TeV) yields the correct thermal relic density owing to its sizable pair-annihilation
cross-sections into electroweak gauge bosons.
Fine-tuning measures, particularly those defined at the electroweak scale, generally favor a

Abstract
Although higgsinos are well motivated to be light from the viewpoint of nat-
uralness, they remain difficult to detect experimentally because they interact only
through electroweak interactions and typically possess a compressed mass spectrum.
While higgsino dark matter can be efficiently probed by direct detection exper-
iments when gauginos are relatively light, the sensitivity rapidly deteriorates for
heavier gauginos due to the suppression of higgsino-gaugino mixing. In this paper,
we investigate the prospects for probing light higgsinos through future electroweak
precision measurements. Focusing on scenarios in which charginos and neutralinos
are the only light electroweakly interacting superparticles, we evaluate their contri-
butions to the electroweak oblique parameters as well as to the precision observables
MW andsin 2θeff. We compare the projected sensitivities of futuree+e− colliders
with those of dark matter direct detection experiments. We find that future elec-
troweak precision measurements provide a powerful probe of higgsinos with masses
≲500 GeV, including parameter regions with highly compressed spectra and spin-
independent scattering cross sections below the neutrino fog. On the other hand,
dark matter direct detection experiments are particularly sensitive to scenarios with
larger charged-neutral mass splittings induced by higgsino-gaugino mixing, and can
probe higgsino dark matter all the way up to the thermal relic mass of≃1 TeV.
Our results demonstrate the strong complementarity between electroweak precision
measurements and dark matter direct detection experiments in exploring light hig-
gsinos and testing supersymmetric scenarios motivated by naturalness.

1 Introduction
The discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC [1, 2] completed the particle content of the
Standard Model (SM) and established the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking.
Nevertheless, the origin of the electroweak scale remains one of the central open questions
in particle physics. In particular, the Higgs boson mass is highly sensitive to ultraviolet
physics, and stabilizing the electroweak scale against large radiative corrections generally
requires new physics not far above the weak scale. Supersymmetry (SUSY) provides one
of the most compelling solutions to this naturalness problem by introducing superpartners
that cancel the quadratic sensitivity of the Higgs mass parameter to heavy scales.
Among SUSY particles, higgsinos play a particularly important role for naturalness.
In SUSY models, the electroweak scale is closely related to the higgsino mass parameter
µ, and avoiding significant fine-tuning typically requires higgsinos to remain relatively
light, often around the electroweak scale [3–8]. Consequently, light higgsinos are a generic
prediction of natural SUSY scenarios, even when other SUSY particles are substantially
heavier.
Despite their strong theoretical motivation, however, light higgsinos remain difficult
to probe experimentally. Since higgsinos carry only electroweak gauge charges, their
production cross sections at hadron colliders are relatively small. Furthermore, in many
realistic scenarios the charged and neutral higgsino states are highly degenerate in mass,
leading to soft visible decay products and reduced missing-energy signatures. As a result,
conventional searches at the LHC suffer from limited sensitivity to compressed higgsino
spectra. Althoughdedicatedsearchesbasedonsoftleptons[9–12], disappearingtracks[13,
14], or displaced tracks [15–18] have improved the sensitivity, a substantial region of
parameter space motivated by naturalness remains unexplored.
If the lightest SUSY particle (LSP) is a higgsino-like neutralino, it provides a well-
motivated dark matter candidate. In this case, dark matter direct detection experiments
offer a powerful and complementary probe of the higgsino sector. In the minimal super-
symmetric standard model (MSSM), the dominant contributions to the spin-independent
scattering cross section arise from Higgs-boson exchange and are induced by higgsino-
gaugino mixing. Consequently, when the gaugino masses are relatively light, current and
future direct detection experiments can impose stringent constraints on higgsino dark
matter [19–22]. On the other hand, as the gaugino masses increase, the higgsino-gaugino
mixing becomes suppressed, leading to a rapid decrease in the direct detection cross sec-
tion. Asaresult, evenfuturedarkmatterdirectdetectionexperimentsmaylosesensitivity
to light higgsinos.
In this situation, indirect probes based on precision measurements become increasingly
important. Electroweak precision observables (EWPOs) are sensitive to virtual effects
of new electroweakly interacting particles through radiative corrections to gauge boson
propagators [23–25]. Future circulare+e− colliders such as the FCC-ee [26] and CEPC [27]
are expected to achieve extremely precise determinations of electroweak observables. Such
measurements provide a promising opportunity to probe light electroweak multiplets even
when direct production or dark matter detection becomes challenging.
In this paper, we investigate the prospects for probing light higgsinos through elec-
troweak precision measurements1 and compare their sensitivity with that of dark matter

We show that future electroweak precision measurements provide a powerful probe of

6 Conclusion
In this paper, we have investigated the prospects for probing light higgsinos through future
electroweak precision measurements and dark matter direct detection experiments. We
compared the projected sensitivities of futuree+e− colliders with those of present and
future dark matter direct detection experiments. We found that the dominant sensitivity
to higgsinos arises through theWparameter, while the contributions to ˆSand ˆTare
typically suppressed once the current direct detection constraints are imposed. As a
result, futureelectroweakprecisionmeasurementscanprobehiggsinoswithmassesupto∼
500 GeV, including parameter regions in which the SI dark matter-nucleon scattering cross
section lies below the neutrino fog. By contrast, dark matter direct detection experiments
can efficiently probe scenarios with sizable charged-neutral mass splittings and are capable
oftestingthermalhiggsinodarkmatteruptoM ~χ0
1
≃1 TeV. Ourresultsthereforehighlight
the strong complementarity between electroweak precision measurements and dark matter
direct detection experiments in exploring light higgsino scenarios. We also showed that
the predicted shifts inMW andsin 2θeff exhibit a strong correlation characteristic of the
higgsino scenario considered in this work.
Finally, we emphasized that future improvements in theoretical calculations will play
an essential role in fully exploiting the precision reach of futuree+e− colliders. In partic-
ular, reductions in the theoretical uncertainties of EWPOs will be crucial for establishing
sensitivity to the small deviations predicted in light higgsino scenarios.

VI. SUMMAR Y AND CONCLUSION
In this work, a comprehensive study of the spin-independent direct detection of Higgsino-like
neutralino DM in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model has been presented, incorporating
both elastic and inelastic scattering channels. While conventional direct-detection analyses typi-
cally focus on elastic scattering, the presence of a nearly degenerate Higgsino-like next-to-lightest
neutralino can render inelastic processes phenomenologically relevant when the mass splitting be-
tween the two lightest neutralinos is comparable to the typical kinetic energy of galactic DM
particles.
To obtain precise predictions for the direct-detection rates, we have computed the complete set

Our analysis demonstrates that radiative corrections can substantially modify both the neu-
tralino mass splitting and the effective Higgs couplings, thereby significantly affecting the relative
importance of elastic and inelastic scattering channels. In particular, for scenarios with mass split-
tings of (O(100) keV) or smaller, the inelastic contribution to scattering events in the detector can
become comparable to the corresponding elastic contribution (BP2). Consequently, a consistent
interpretation of direct-detection limits and future sensitivities in compressed Higgsino scenarios

The results presented here highlight the importance of precision calculations for Higgsino-like

sensitivities to spin-independent DM–nucleon cross-sections. These experiments are expected to
probe cross-sections approaching the neutrino floor over a broad range of DM masses, including
the TeV-scale region relevant for Higgsino-like DM.
Given their large target masses and increased exposure, future experiments will also become
increasingly sensitive to compressed electroweakino spectra in which inelastic up-scattering is kine-
matically accessible. The recently reported LZ nuclear-recoil event near 248 keV provides an
additional motivation for studying this possibility. While its interpretation as a dark-matter signal
remains premature, recent studies have pointed out that TeV-scale Higgsino dark matter can be
relevant in this context [57–59]. A dedicated analysis of this event within the radiatively corrected
inelastic Higgsino framework developed here, including the recoil-energy spectrum and the com-
bined elastic and inelastic contributions, would therefore be an interesting direction for future work.
Consequently, radiatively corrected predictions for both elastic and inelastic scattering processes
will be essential for robust interpretations of experimental results and for accurately assessing the

searches, these studies provide a complementary avenue to probe natural supersymmetric scenarios,
which are characterized by a compressed Higgsino spectrum and suppressed tree-level interactions.

combined with precision theoretical predictions, will not only extend the reach for DM discov-

Title: Unveiling the Vanishing Higgsino-Nucleon Scattering in the MSSM at Next-to-Leading Order
Authors: Subhadip Bisal, Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: Higgsino dark matter (DM) is considered one of the most well-motivated and minimal DM scenarios arising from supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model. Motivated by the requirement of electroweak naturalness, Higgsinos are expected to be relatively light, with masses close to the weak scale. While a pure Higgsino state typically evades current direct detection limits, next-to-leading (NLO) order radiative corrections may bring it within the sensitivity of upcoming experiments. On the contrary, a more important consequence, observed specifically near the kinematic threshold for the production of two particles, is that the NLO corrections lower the DM-nucleon cross section below the neutrino floor. We explicitly examine the cancellation mechanism responsible for suppressed Higgsino-nucleon scattering and identify regions of MSSM parameter space where spin-independent cross-sections may vanish.

Astrophysical observations provide strong evidence for
the existence of dark matter and its dominance of the
matter density of the Universe [1–4]. Well-motivated
as a thermal relic, the weakly interacting massive par-
ticle (WIMP) is a leading hypothesis for dark matter,
arising in a number of beyond-the-standard-model the-
ories [5–7]. The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration op-
erates the world’s largest two-phase xenon time pro-
jection chamber (TPC), with the primary aim of di-
rectly detecting WIMPs through their interactions with
xenon nuclei. This technology has produced the most
stringent constraints on spin-independent (SI) WIMP-
nucleon interactions for ≳5 GeV/c2 masses, with all
three current-generation experiments having reported re-
sults [8–10]. In this Letter we present the latest WIMP
analysis from LZ, combining a new 220 live-day expo-
sure (WS2024) with the 60 live-day exposure from the
first result (WS2022) [8] to perform the most sensitive
direct search for WIMPs to date.
The LZ experiment [11] is located 4850 ft underground,
shielded by a 4300 meter water equivalent rock overbur-
den in the Davis Cavern at the Sanford Underground
Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota, USA.
Its TPC, containing seven tonnes of active liquid xenon
(LXe), is surrounded by a dual-detector veto system
comprising a two-tonne LXe “Skin,” designed to tag γ
rays, and an outer detector (OD) containing 17 tonnes of
gadolinium-loaded liquid scintillator (GdLS), optimized
for the detection of neutrons.
Interactions in the LXe target that fills the TPC create
light in the form of prompt vacuum ultraviolet (VUV)
scintillation (S1) and delayed electroluminescence (S2),
both observed by the top and bottom photomultiplier
tube (PMT) arrays. The S2 signal is generated by ion-
ization electrons as they traverse a thin layer of gaseous
xenon above the liquid, having been drifted upwards from
the interaction site under an applied electric field and ex-
tracted from the liquid phase. The measured time inter-
val between the S1 and the S2 pulses, referred to as the
“drift time”, corresponds to the depth, z, of the interac-
tion, while the hit pattern of S2 light in the top PMT
array allows for position reconstruction in the transverse
(x,y ) plane. The ratio of S2 to S1 signal sizes is used to
discriminate between background electronic recoils (ERs)
and nuclear recoils (NRs), the latter of which is expected
for WIMP-nucleus scatters. Background events are fur-
ther rejected if they exhibit multiple scatters (MS) rather
than a single scatter (SS) in the TPC, or through the

Abstract
Many viable dark matter models contain a WIMP candidate that is a component of a new elec-
troweak multiplet whose massM is large compared to the electroweak scalemW . A generic amplitude-
level cancellation in such models yields a severe suppression of the cross section for WIMP-nucleon
scattering, making it important to assess the impact of formally subleading eﬀects. The power cor-
rection of order mW/M to the heavy WIMP limit is computed for electroweak doublet (Higgsino-like)
dark matter candidates, and a modern model of nuclear modiﬁcations to the free nucleon cross section
is evaluated. Corrections to the pure Higgsino limit are determined by a single parameter through ﬁrst
order in the heavy WIMP expansion. Current and projected experimental bounds on this parameter
are investigated. The direct detection signal in the pure Higgsino limit remains below neutrino back-
grounds for WIMPs in the TeV mass range. Nuclear corrections are applied also to the heavy Wino
case, completing the investigation of combined subleading eﬀects from perturbative QCD, 1 /M power
corrections, and nuclear modiﬁcations.

1 Introduction
The Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) has long been considered as a well-motivated dark mat-
ter candidate [1–11] but remains experimentally undetected [12]. WIMPs naturally ﬁt in the paradigm
of supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model [13] yet we haven’t found evidence at the LHC for
supersymmetric particles at the electroweak scale [14, 15]. Within the WIMP paradigm, the situation
is suggestive that new particles are somewhat heavy compared to the electroweak scale, and in particu-
lar, MWIMP≫MW±,MZ0. In this mass regime, heavy WIMP eﬀective ﬁeld theory becomes a powerful
method to study the universal behavior in low energy WIMP-nucleus scattering processes [16–18], predict-
ing cross sections for dark matter direct detection experiments that are minimally sensitive to unknown
ultraviolet (UV) physics.
Explicit calculations in heavy WIMP eﬀective theory [17–19] reveal an amplitude level cancellation [16,
19, 20] that results in cross section predictions for electroweak triplet (Wino-like) and electroweak doublet
(Higgsino-like) WIMPs that are below the sensitivity of current direct detection experiments [21]. Such
particles thus remain as viable dark matter candidates but it is important to understand whether naively
subleading eﬀects could alter the predicted cross section and hence their experimental observability.
To improve the leading order calculation and to compare with next-generation experiments [22–25]
approaching the neutrino ﬂoor [26], we consider subleading eﬀects from the following sources. First, 1 /M
power corrections in the heavy WIMP expansion depend on the speciﬁc representation of electroweak
SU(2)× U(1) symmetry, and on the detailed UV completion of the WIMP theory. For the case of
electroweak triplet, power corrections for the pure Wino case were themselves found to exhibit a surprising
level of cancellation [27], yielding a cross section prediction for low velocity WIMP-nucleon scattering of
σ∼ 10−47 cm2, for M & 500 GeV. Given that Higgsino-nucleon scattering suﬀers an even more severe
amplitude cancellation compared to the Wino case [18], it is important to study the power corrections
in this case. We also explore the consequences of structure beyond the pure Higgsino limit. Second,

6 Summary
We have computed subleading corrections to the cross sections for Wino-like and Higgsino-like WIMP
particles scattering on nuclear targets. The doublet result shows that order 1 /M corrections do not
signiﬁcantly enhance the small leading order cross section. The upper limit for the pure doublet is less
than 10−48 cm2 in the TeV mass regime, consistent with the leading order estimate [18, 19], and lower
than the estimated Xenon neutrino ﬂoor [26]. We also investigated the impact of nuclear eﬀects by
employing a modern EFT-based model in place of the standard nuclear form factor. Although individual
nuclear response channels have signiﬁcant contributions, cancellations occur in the total nuclear response.
The overall eﬀect of the new nuclear model is comparable to other uncertainties for both Wino-like
and Higgsino-like WIMP candidates, leaving the TeV scale pure Wino within striking distance of next
generation experiments, and the pure Higgsino well below the neutrino ﬂoor. The small cross section in
the pure Higgsino limit can be modiﬁed by non-decoupled states in the UV completion. For WIMP masses
of orderM = 500 GeV, current experiments constrain the dimensionless Higgs-WIMP-WIMP coupling as
˜cH ≲ 0.04.

Abstract
We point out that thermal relic abundance of the dark matter i s strongly
altered by a non-perturbative eﬀect called the Sommerfeld en hancement, when
constituent particles of the dark matter are non-singlet un der the SU(2)L gauge
interaction and much heavier than the weak gauge bosons. Typ ical candidates
for such dark matter particles are the heavy wino- and higgsi no-like neutrali-
nos. We investigate the non-perturbative eﬀect on the relic a bundance of dark
matter for the wino-like neutralino as an example. We show th at its ther-
mal abundance is reduced by 50% compared to the perturbative result. The
wino-like neutralino mass consistent with the observed dar k matter abundance
turns out to be 2.7 TeV ≲ m ≲ 3.0 TeV.
