1 Introduction
Precise measurements of cosmological parameters have achieved amazing progress
in recent years. In particular, the observation of cosmic microwav e background
anisotropies by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) [1] conﬁrmed
that non-baryonic dark matter amounts to 20% of the energy of o ur universe. The
existence of dark matter forces us to consider physics beyond th e standard model
(SM) for its constituent, because the SM has no candidate for the dark matter.
Many models beyond the SM have been proposed for providing dark m atter
candidates. Models involving weakly interacting massive particles (WI MPs), such as
supersymmetric models and universal extra dimension (UED) models [2, 3], have an
advantage over other models, since the WIMPs can explain the obse rved abundance
naturally in the thermal relic scenario [3, 4, 5]. Comparison of the pre dicted thermal
abundance with observations is a powerful tool to constrain thos e models. It is now
important for discussion of new physics signatures at collider exper iments such as
the LHC.
In the thermal relic scenario, the annihilation cross sections of dar k matter play
a central role in evaluation of the abundance. Perturbative calcula tion of the cross
sections is suﬃcient for it in usual cases. However, a non-perturb ative eﬀect on
the cross sections has to be included, when dark matter particles a re non-singlet
under the SU(2) L interaction and much heavier than the weak gauge bosons. The
weak interaction is not a short-distance force, but rather a long- distance one for
non-relativistic two-bodies states of such heavy particles. The wa ve functions for
the two-bodes states are modiﬁed from the plane waves by the inte raction, and the
annihilation cross sections are aﬀected. The dark matter particles are non-relativistic
at the freeze-out temperature. The attractive channels due to the weak force enhance
the annihilation cross sections, compared with the perturbative on es. This eﬀect is
called the Sommerfeld enhancement, which was found in inelastic reac tions between
non-relativistic charged particles, historically.
In this letter, we point out that the non-perturbative eﬀect stro ngly alters the
relic abundance of dark matter compared to that in perturbative c alculation. We
investigate the non-perturbative eﬀect quantitatively in the wino- like neutralino dark
matter as an example, and show that the abundance is reduced by 5 0% due to the
eﬀect. We also discuss non-perturbative eﬀects on other dark ma tter candidates at
the end of this letter.

2 Sommerfeld enhancement in wino-like neutralino
dark matter annihilation
Winos are the SU(2) L gauginos in the supersymmetric standard model, and they are
an SU(2)L triplet. They are mixed with higgsinos, superpartners of the Higgs b osons,
after the electroweak symmetry breaking. The neutral compone nts in the mass
eigenstates are called neutralino. The mixing with higgsinos is small for heavy winos,
since it is suppressed by the electroweak scale. Thus, the wino-like n eutralino ( ˜χ0) is
highly degenerate with its charged SU(2) L partner ( ˜χ−) in mass when their masses
are heavy enough. For the wino-like neutralino mass ( m) of the order of 1 TeV,
the mass diﬀerence between the neutralino and its SU(2) L partner is dominated by
a radiative correction [6]. It is calculated as δm ≃ 0.17 GeV, which is used for
numerical calculations in this letter.
There are four processes related to the calculation of the wino-like neutralino relic
abundance, and those are ˜ χ0 ˜χ0, ˜χ− ˜χ+, ˜χ0 ˜χ−, and ˜χ− ˜χ− annihilation. We assume
the CP conservation, and cross sections of ˜χ0 ˜χ+ and ˜χ+ ˜χ+ annihilation are the same
as those of ˜χ0 ˜χ− and ˜χ− ˜χ−, respectively. Furthermore, each process is decomposed
into two ones with S = 0 and S = 1, where S is the total spin of the two-bodies
system at the initial state. In ˜ χ0 ˜χ0 and ˜χ− ˜χ− annihilation, the S = 1 processes are
forbidden at the s-wave annihilation. After all, processes we have to consider are
˜χ0 ˜χ0, ˜χ− ˜χ+, ˜χ0 ˜χ−, ˜χ− ˜χ− annihilation with S = 0, and those of ˜ χ− ˜χ+, ˜χ0 ˜χ− with
S = 1.

calculated only within a perturbative method. However, as we will see later, the non-
perturbative eﬀect can signiﬁcantly alter cross sections relevant to the abundance.

4 Summary and discussion
In this letter, we have pointed out the thermal relic abundance of d ark matter, which
is SU(2)L non-singlet and has a much larger mass than that of the weak gauge bosons,
can be strongly reduced by the non-perturbative eﬀect. We have investigated the
non-perturbative eﬀect on the relic abundance of wino-like neutra lino as an example.
Compared with the perturbative result, this eﬀect reduces the ab undance by about
50% and increases the mass of the wino-like neutralino dark matter c onsistent with
the observation by about 600 GeV. As a result, the thermal relic ab undance of
the wino-like neutralino dark matter is consistent with observed abu ndances when
2.7 TeV ≲ m ≲ 3.0 TeV.
The non-perturbative eﬀect can change relic abundances of othe r dark matter
candidates with SU(2) L charge and heavy mass, such as higgsino-like neutralino. The
non-perturbative eﬀect on the thermal relic abundance of higgsin o-like neutralino is
expected to be roughly 10%, since winos are triplet under the SU(2) L gauge group,

while higgsinos are SU(2) L doublet. Therefore, non-perturbative eﬀect may change
the abundance by O(10%) for other SU(2) L doublet candidates for the dark matter.
A detailed analysis of this subject is studied elsewhere.
The Sommerfeld enhancement occurs reasonably for particles with electric charge.
In fact the non-perturbative eﬀect through photon exchanges for charged particle an-
nihilation can change the abundance by about 10%. Therefore, one may think that
the relic abundance of dark matter will be changed in the stau coann ihilation region
or in the case that gravitino is the lightest supersymmetric particle a nd it is pro-
duced through decay of stau. However, the non-perturbative e ﬀect for stau does not
change the dark matter abundance. In stau annihilation, σ(˜τ +˜τ −) ≃ σ(˜τ + ˜τ +) and
the Sommerfeld enhancement is positive (negative) for the former (latter) process.
Hence, the enhancement is almost canceled and the change of the a bundance is 1%
at most.
Kaluza-Klein (KK) right-handed leptons ( E(1)) in UED models are highly degen-

arXiv ID: 2606.31013
Title: Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection
Authors: Koichi Hamaguchi, Natsumi Nagata, Genta Osaki
Year: 2026
Abstract: Although higgsinos are well motivated to be light from the viewpoint of naturalness, they remain difficult to detect experimentally because they interact only through electroweak interactions and typically possess a compressed mass spectrum. While higgsino dark matter can be efficiently probed by direct detection experiments when gauginos are relatively light, the sensitivity rapidly deteriorates for heavier gauginos due to the suppression of higgsino-gaugino mixing. In this paper, we investigate the prospects for probing light higgsinos through future electroweak precision measurements. Focusing on scenarios in which charginos and neutralinos are the only light electroweakly interacting superparticles, we evaluate their contributions to the electroweak oblique parameters as well as to the precision observables $M_W$ and $\sin^2θ_{\mathrm{eff}}$. We compare the projected sensitivities of future $e^+e^-$ colliders with those of dark matter direct detection experiments. We find that future electroweak precision measurements provide a powerful probe of higgsinos with masses $\lesssim 500~\mathrm{GeV}$, including parameter regions with highly compressed spectra and spin-independent scattering cross sections below the neutrino fog. On the other hand, dark matter direct detection experiments are particularly sensitive to scenarios with larger charged-neutral mass splittings induced by higgsino-gaugino mixing, and can probe higgsino dark matter all the way up to the thermal relic mass of $\simeq 1~\mathrm{TeV}$. Our results demonstrate the strong complementarity between electroweak precision measurements and dark matter direct detection experiments in exploring light higgsinos and testing supersymmetric scenarios motivated by naturalness.

arXiv ID: 2609.09830
Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

Abstract
Many viable dark matter models contain a WIMP candidate that is a component of a new elec-
troweak multiplet whose massM is large compared to the electroweak scalemW . A generic amplitude-
level cancellation in such models yields a severe suppression of the cross section for WIMP-nucleon
scattering, making it important to assess the impact of formally subleading eﬀects. The power cor-
rection of order mW/M to the heavy WIMP limit is computed for electroweak doublet (Higgsino-like)
dark matter candidates, and a modern model of nuclear modiﬁcations to the free nucleon cross section
is evaluated. Corrections to the pure Higgsino limit are determined by a single parameter through ﬁrst
order in the heavy WIMP expansion. Current and projected experimental bounds on this parameter
are investigated. The direct detection signal in the pure Higgsino limit remains below neutrino back-
grounds for WIMPs in the TeV mass range. Nuclear corrections are applied also to the heavy Wino
case, completing the investigation of combined subleading eﬀects from perturbative QCD, 1 /M power
corrections, and nuclear modiﬁcations.

6 Summary
We have computed subleading corrections to the cross sections for Wino-like and Higgsino-like WIMP
particles scattering on nuclear targets. The doublet result shows that order 1 /M corrections do not
signiﬁcantly enhance the small leading order cross section. The upper limit for the pure doublet is less
than 10−48 cm2 in the TeV mass regime, consistent with the leading order estimate [18, 19], and lower
than the estimated Xenon neutrino ﬂoor [26]. We also investigated the impact of nuclear eﬀects by
employing a modern EFT-based model in place of the standard nuclear form factor. Although individual
nuclear response channels have signiﬁcant contributions, cancellations occur in the total nuclear response.

ABSTRACT
We present cosmological parameter results from the ﬁnal full-mission Planck measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) an-
isotropies, combining information from the temperature and polarization maps and the lensing reconstruction. Compared to the 2015 results,
improved measurements of large-scale polarization allow the reionization optical depth to be measured with higher precision, leading to signiﬁ-
cant gains in the precision of other correlated parameters. Improved modelling of the small-scale polarization leads to more robust constraints on
many parameters, with residual modelling uncertainties estimated to aﬀect them only at the 0.5σ level. We ﬁnd good consistency with the standard
spatially-ﬂat 6-parameter ΛCDM cosmology having a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations (denoted “baseΛCDM” in this paper),
from polarization, temperature, and lensing, separately and in combination. A combined analysis gives dark matter densityΩch2 = 0.120± 0.001,
baryon density Ωbh2 = 0.0224± 0.0001, scalar spectral index ns = 0.965± 0.004, and optical depth τ = 0.054± 0.007 (in this abstract we quote
68 % conﬁdence regions on measured parameters and 95 % on upper limits). The angular acoustic scale is measured to 0 .03 % precision, with
100θ∗ = 1.0411± 0.0003. These results are only weakly dependent on the cosmological model and remain stable, with somewhat increased errors,
in many commonly considered extensions. Assuming the base- ΛCDM cosmology, the inferred (model-dependent) late-Universe parameters are:
Hubble constant H0 = (67.4±0.5) km s−1Mpc−1; matter density parameterΩm = 0.315±0.007; and matter ﬂuctuation amplitudeσ8 = 0.811±0.006.
We ﬁnd no compelling evidence for extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. Combining with baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements (and
considering single-parameter extensions) we constrain the eﬀective extra relativistic degrees of freedom to beNeﬀ = 2.99±0.17, in agreement with
the Standard Model prediction Neﬀ = 3.046, and ﬁnd that the neutrino mass is tightly constrained to ∑ mν < 0.12 eV. The CMB spectra continue
to prefer higher lensing amplitudes than predicted in base ΛCDM at over 2σ, which pulls some parameters that aﬀect the lensing amplitude away
from the ΛCDM model; however, this is not supported by the lensing reconstruction or (in models that also change the background geometry)
BAO data. The joint constraint with BAO measurements on spatial curvature is consistent with a ﬂat universe,ΩK = 0.001±0.002. Also combining
with Type Ia supernovae (SNe), the dark-energy equation of state parameter is measured to be w0 =−1.03± 0.03, consistent with a cosmological
constant. We ﬁnd no evidence for deviations from a purely power-law primordial spectrum, and combining with data from BAO, BICEP2, and
Keck Array data, we place a limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r0.002 < 0.06. Standard big-bang nucleosynthesis predictions for the helium and
deuterium abundances for the base-ΛCDM cosmology are in excellent agreement with observations. The Planck base-ΛCDM results are in good
agreement with BAO, SNe, and some galaxy lensing observations, but in slight tension with the Dark Energy Survey’s combined-probe results
including galaxy clustering (which prefers lower ﬂuctuation amplitudes or matter density parameters), and in signiﬁcant, 3.6σ, tension with local
measurements of the Hubble constant (which prefer a higher value). Simple model extensions that can partially resolve these tensions are not
favoured by the Planck data.

Title: Closing the window on WIMP Dark Matter
Authors: Salvatore Bottaro, Dario Buttazzo, Marco Costa, Roberto Franceschini, Paolo Panci, Diego Redigolo, Ludovico Vittorio
Year: 2021
Abstract: We study scenarios where Dark Matter is a weakly interacting particle (WIMP) embedded in an ElectroWeak multiplet. In particular, we consider real SU(2) representations with zero hypercharge, that automatically avoid direct detection constraints from tree-level Z-exchange. We compute for the first time all the calculable thermal masses for scalar and fermionic WIMPs, including Sommerfeld enhancement and bound states formation at leading order in gauge boson exchange and emission. WIMP masses of few hundred TeV are shown to be compatible both with s-wave unitarity of the annihilation cross-section, and perturbativity. We also provide theory uncertainties on the masses for all multiplets, which are shown to be significant for large SU(2) multiplets. We then outline a strategy to probe these scenarios at future experiments. Electroweak 3-plets and 5-plets have masses up to about 16 TeV and can efficiently be probed at a high energy muon collider. We study various experimental signatures, such as single and double gauge boson emission with missing energy, and disappearing tracks, and determine the collider energy and luminosity required to probe the thermal Dark Matter masses. Larger multiplets are out of reach of any realistic future collider, but can be tested in future gamma ray telescopes and possibly in large-exposure liquid Xenon experiments.

Authors: Salvatore Bottaro, Dario Buttazzo, Marco Costa, Roberto Franceschini, Paolo Panci, Diego Redigolo, Ludovico Vittorio

# The thermal pure higgsino (about 1.1 TeV) against Planck 2018, LZ 2024 and XENONnT: a literature survey

## Abstract

The task was to compute the pure-higgsino relic density at several masses with inelastic-DM tools, and to place the 1.0–1.2 TeV thermal higgsino against LZ, XENONnT and the Planck abundance. No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool was available in this environment. No input data were available either. **Every Omega h^2 value below therefore comes from the literature, or is a labelled rescaling of a literature value; none was computed.**

The main findings are these:

- **Relic density.** The one published pure-higgsino point found is Omega h^2 = 0.127 (perturbative) and 0.126 (Sommerfeld) in arXiv:1411.6930. The mass of about 1172 GeV attached to it is inferred from context, not stated. Rescaling that point as m^2 to the verbatim Planck 2018 value, Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 ± 0.001, gives a thermal mass of about 1.14 TeV.
- **Elastic scattering.** The most complete elastic calculation (arXiv:1912.07795) bounds the pure-higgsino spin-independent (SI) cross section below 1e-48 cm^2 at TeV masses, below the xenon neutrino floor. LZ 2024 is tightest at 40 GeV, with 2.2e-48 cm^2. A linear extrapolation to 1.1 TeV, which is an estimate and not a read value, puts the LZ limit at about 6e-47 cm^2. That is at least about 60 times above the higgsino bound.
- **Inelastic scattering.** The kinematic threshold for up-scattering on xenon is about 364–368 keV at 1.0–1.1 TeV. Recent one-loop benchmarks with splittings of 9–36 keV predict at most about one LZ event and are all allowed.

Net conclusion: a thermal pure higgsino is not excluded by current direct detection. It becomes visible only through gaugino mixing or very small neutral splittings.

## Background

A pure higgsino is an SU(2) doublet with Y = 1/2. The literature places its thermal-relic mass at roughly 1.0–1.2 TeV, with the exact value set by the Sommerfeld and coannihilation treatment:

- Beneke, Hellmann and Ruiz-Femenia, arXiv:1411.6930, give a Sommerfeld-enhanced coannihilation calculation.
- arXiv:2606.31013 quotes about 1 TeV.
- An earlier estimate, hep-ph/0610249, expected a Sommerfeld effect of about 10% for higgsinos, against about 50% for winos.
- A more recent independent framework includes bound-state formation as well as Sommerfeld enhancement (Bottaro et al., arXiv:2107.09688 and arXiv:2205.04486).
- The target abundance is from Planck 2018 (arXiv:1807.06209).

Pure-higgsino elastic scattering arises only at loop level and is suppressed by an accidental cancellation:

- Hisano et al. give the leading-order result in arXiv:1104.0228, with gluon contributions in arXiv:1007.2601.
- Chen and Hill, arXiv:1912.07795, refine it with power corrections, QCD corrections to NNNLO and chiral-EFT nuclear effects.
- arXiv:2607.20588 (2026) argues that NLO corrections can push the cross section lower, or make it vanish, in parts of MSSM parameter space.

The experimental references are:

- LZ, arXiv:2410.17036, with 4.2 tonne-years of exposure.
- XENONnT, arXiv:2303.14729.
- The ICRC 2025 review, arXiv:2510.17473, which notes that xenon experiments are entering the solar-neutrino-limited regime.

Two 2026 papers cover the visibility routes:

- **Mixing (arXiv:2606.31013).** Hamaguchi, Nagata and Osaki show that gaugino mixing raises the Higgs coupling.
- **Inelastic scattering (arXiv:2609.09830).** Chatterjee et al. compute inelastic higgsino scattering at one loop for LZ.

Both IDs were confirmed by metadata lookup.

## Results

### Planck target and the absence of a compute tool

Planck 2018 states verbatim, on page 1 of the abstract: "A combined analysis gives dark matter density Ωch2 = 0.120± 0.001" (68% CL, base ΛCDM). This value was read from the downloaded text but not added to the bibliography file.

A file listing returned an empty input set. The tool catalog contains only statistics/histogram, test-job and literature tools. The task's request to "compute the relic density" therefore could not be carried out.

### Relic density against mass

arXiv:1411.6930 (Sec. 3) reports the following:

- **Pure-higgsino model** (sfermions and heavy Higgses decoupled): Omega h^2 = 0.127 without and 0.126 with Sommerfeld enhancement, including off-diagonal rates. The net Sommerfeld effect is below 1%, because enhancement in the neutral channels cancels suppression in the neutral–charged channels.
- **Higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006** (higgsino fraction 0.98, Δm+ = 1.8 GeV, Δm0 = 9.5 GeV): Omega h^2 = 0.108 perturbative and 0.100 with Sommerfeld, an 8% reduction.
- **Normalisation and accuracy.** The paper quotes about 5% Sommerfeld accuracy at best and normalises to Planck 2013 (0.1187 ± 0.0017).

The pure-higgsino mass of 1172.31 GeV is the mass of the pMSSM comparison point. Its attribution to the pure-higgsino numbers was inferred from context and is not stated in the paper. The critic flagged this, and it remains unconfirmed.

[[FIGURE 6]]

Figure 6 reproduces Fig. 7 of arXiv:1411.6930. It shows the yield ratio Y/Y_pert, Sommerfeld over perturbative, for the pMSSM higgsino-like point with and without off-diagonal rates, and for the pure-higgsino model. It shows the size of the Sommerfeld correction, not Omega h^2 against mass. No published Omega h^2(m) curve was found.

The table below is an m^2 rescaling of the single point (0.126 × (m/1172.31 GeV)^2). It is an interpolation, not published values, and it depends on the inferred mass.

| m (TeV) | 0.9 | 1.0 | 1.1 | 1.2 | 1.3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Omega h^2 (rescaled) | 0.074 | 0.092 | 0.111 | 0.132 | 0.155 |

Omega h^2 = 0.120 falls at about 1144 GeV (Sommerfeld) or 1139 GeV (perturbative), that is about 1.14 TeV.

A second, independent thermal mass was identified but not read: the doublet entry of arXiv:2205.04486. That paper also states that the Y = 1/2 doublet is the notable case that future direct detection cannot fully probe.

### Elastic SI cross section against LZ and XENONnT

**Prediction.** Hisano et al. (arXiv:1104.0228) find an SI cross section of O(1e-46–1e-48) cm^2 at leading order for pure electroweak multiplets, nearly mass-independent above about 1 TeV. The positive twist-2 terms cancel against the negative Higgs, gluon and scalar terms. The critic noted that the numeric range was not visible in the excerpts read. The calculation scans the Higgs mass and predates its measurement.

Chen and Hill (arXiv:1912.07795) state verbatim: "The upper limit for the pure doublet is less than 10^-48 cm2 in the TeV mass regime, consistent with the leading order estimate [18, 19], and lower than the estimated Xenon neutrino floor [26]." Sec. 4 adds that the bound "remains at or below 10^-48 cm2 for masses above a few hundred GeV". The same section says that with gaugino admixture c_H/g2^2 of about 0.1 the TeV rate comes within next-generation reach, and with about 0.01 it lies near the floor. These quotes were recorded, but the critic did not treat them as fully verified, and only the earlier citation entry is in the bibliography. Only an upper bound was obtained, not a central value with an uncertainty.

**Limits.** LZ 2024 gives its strongest SI exclusion as 2.2e-48 cm^2 (90% CL), with a best median sensitivity of 5.1e-48 cm^2, both at 40 GeV. No 1 TeV value was read.

**Comparison.** Comparing the 1e-48 cm^2 bound with the 40 GeV minimum gives a factor of only more than 2.2 (more than 0.34 decades). An earlier "two orders of magnitude" statement was wrong on this point and has been corrected.

At equal mass, scaling the LZ limit linearly gives 2.2e-48 × 1100/40 ≈ 6e-47 cm^2 at 1.1 TeV. That is a ratio of at least about 60 (at least about 1.8 decades) above the higgsino bound. This is an extrapolation. The XENONnT 1 TeV limit, the LZ 1 TeV curve value and a numeric neutrino-fog value were not obtained.

### Inelastic threshold and LZ inelastic sensitivity

**Threshold.** The threshold was worked out by hand:

- m_Xe = 131 × 0.9315 GeV = 122.0 GeV.
- μ_A = 108.7 GeV at 1.0 TeV and 109.8 GeV at 1.1 TeV.
- v_max = 544 + 232 = 776 km/s, so β^2 = 6.70e-6.
- δ_max = μ_A β^2/2 gives 364 keV at 1.0 TeV and 368 keV at 1.1 TeV.

The relation v_min = sqrt(2δ/μ_A) is Eq. A7 of arXiv:2609.09830. The result depends on the escape speed and Earth velocity assumed.

**Benchmarks.** arXiv:2609.09830 does not give an LZ-excluded δ_m0 range. Its five benchmarks are:

- Table III: μ = −739.63, −606.64, −814.26, 1282.11 and 1400.0 GeV; M1 = −7830, −6292, −5838, 11354 and 12875 GeV; M2 = 17055, 42000, 30925, 12627 and 12050 GeV; tan β = 10.88–26.46.
- One-loop on-shell δ = 36.37, 8.90, 16.39, 10.81 and 10.59 keV for BP1–BP5.

Table VII gives the NLO LZ event counts:

| | BP1 | BP2 | BP3 | BP4 | BP5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elastic | 1.0280 | 0.07729 | 0.1176 | 0.4127 | 0.5074 |
| Inelastic | 0.00022 | 0.07039 | 0.0518 | 0.1806 | 0.1661 |
| Combined | 1.02822 | 0.14768 | 0.1694 | 0.5933 | 0.6735 |
| Exposure needed (t-y) | 9.41 | 65.50 | 57.10 | 16.30 | 14.36 |

For comparison, LZ has 4.2 t-y, and the null-result criterion used is N < ln 10 ≈ 2.3. All benchmarks are consistent with LZ.

NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100%. For BP2, the NLO inelastic cross section is 0.507e-12 pb, against an LO elastic cross section of 0.284e-12 pb (ratio 1.785).

The critic noted that the table rows were not visible in the displayed excerpts, although the ranges read cover them. They are accepted on that basis.

### Splittings and mixing

**Charged–neutral splitting.** Eq. 13 of arXiv:2606.31013 gives the pure-limit radiative splitting as Δm+ ≈ (1/2) α2 MZ sin^2θW (1 − 3MZ/(2π M)). This tends to about 356 MeV for M ≫ MZ, rather than the 340 MeV in the brief.

**Higgs coupling.** Eq. 33 (approximate form of Eq. 32) gives f_q ≈ −(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2−|μ|) + tan^2θW/(M1−|μ|)](1 + sgn(μ) sin 2β). This is suppressed at large gaugino mass, and at small tan β with μ < 0 through an accidental cancellation.

**Scan.** The scan in Eq. 37 covers 150 < |μ| < 1000 GeV, 1.6 < tan β < 50 and 0.5 < M1 < 10 TeV, with M2 = 2 M1. Rates are rescaled as σ_eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) σ (Eq. 38, micrOMEGAs v6.3.0). arXiv:2609.09830 likewise weakens its limits proportionally for sub-thermal fractions.

Direct detection is sensitive mainly where mixing produces sizable charged–neutral splittings, and in that region it reaches the about 1 TeV thermal mass. The reach figures of that paper were not extracted.

**Neutral splitting δ_m0.** The tree-level formula was not sourced. arXiv:2609.09830 refers only to "Eq. (9) of Ref. [28]" and states that the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms can partially cancel. An earlier estimate, that same-sign M2 = 2 M1 needs M1 ≈ 1.4e7 GeV for δ < 364 keV, rests on that unsourced formula and should be disregarded. The critic noted that a same-sign tree-level splitting at about 12 TeV would be only about 0.5–0.7 MeV.

BP4 and BP5 reach about 10.6–10.8 keV with M1 and M2 both positive (about 11–13 TeV) and μ > 0. So the earlier claim that only opposite-sign gauginos give O(10) keV splittings was revised. On-shell one-loop corrections and the relative signs between μ and the gauginos also contribute.

## Discussion

The survey supports the brief's qualitative picture.

- **Thermal mass.** A thermal pure higgsino sits near 1.1 TeV. The single rescaled point gives about 1.14 TeV, inside the 1.0–1.2 TeV window. The Sommerfeld effect is negligible in the pure limit (below 1%), smaller than the earlier 10% expectation of hep-ph/0610249.
- **Elastic scattering.** The elastic SI rate is bounded below 1e-48 cm^2. By the extrapolation above, it lies roughly two decades below the current LZ reach at 1.1 TeV and below the xenon floor. Pure-higgsino elastic scattering is therefore not a viable discovery channel for current or, per arXiv:2205.04486 and arXiv:1912.07795, future xenon detectors.
- **Visibility routes.** The higgsino becomes visible through gaugino mixing, which raises f_q and the splittings (arXiv:2606.31013). It can also become visible through neutral splittings well below the about 365 keV kinematic limit. Even at 9–36 keV, however, the one-loop benchmarks of arXiv:2609.09830 give fewer than about 1.03 LZ events and need 9.4–65.5 t-y.

Two points of tension remain:

- **Splitting value.** The brief's 340 MeV charged–neutral splitting differs from the 356 MeV one-loop asymptote quoted here. The critic suggested that a two-loop value of about 341 MeV may reconcile them, but this was not read.
- **Robustness of the cancellation.** Whether the elastic cancellation is robust is unresolved. arXiv:2607.20588 suggests NLO effects can drive the rate lower still.

Dead ends:

- **Limit figures.** Figure extraction from arXiv:2410.17036 and arXiv:2303.14729 returned no limit plots, only data-distribution and calibration figures. The LZ text region read had no 1 TeV value.
- **Abstract search.** An abstract search for recent thermal-mass papers returned unrelated LEP notes. Direct arXiv-ID lookup proved more effective.

## Limitations

- **No computation.** No compute tool existed, so no relic density, event rate or reach map was computed. The m^2 table is an interpolation from one point with an inferred mass.
- **Thermal-mass spread.** Only one thermal-mass determination was available. The bound-state-inclusive value of arXiv:2205.04486 was not read, so the spread across calculations is unknown.
- **Direct-detection numbers not read.** The LZ and XENONnT limits at 1 TeV, the neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV, and next-generation projections (XLZD, arXiv:2410.17137) were not read. The headline ratio of about 60 or more remains an extrapolation.
- **δ_m0 formula.** The tree-level δ_m0 formula is unsourced.
- **Indirect detection.** Indirect detection was not addressed.
- **Bibliography.** Several quotes (Planck, the Chen and Hill passages, the Table III/VI/VII traces) are recorded on the board but not cited into references.bib.
- **Budget.** Both waves were used.

result.summary:
Answer: a thermal pure higgsino at about 1.1 TeV lies about 2 or more orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 limit and below the xenon neutrino floor. Three of the planned inputs were not read: the XENONnT limit, the LZ limit read from its figure at 1 TeV, and a numeric neutrino-fog value. All are recorded as open question q-06.

(1) Prediction. Hisano et al. 1104.0228 work at leading order in electroweak loops. They find the SI cross section of pure SU(2)-multiplet dark matter is O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2, nearly independent of mass above about 1 TeV. An accidental cancellation drives this: twist-2 terms are positive, while the Higgs-exchange, gluon and Z-box scalar terms are negative and of similar size. Their Fig. 5 shows the higgsino (n=2, Y=1/2) at M = 1 TeV against the Higgs mass; the paper predates the measured Higgs mass. Finding f-004.

The newer and more complete calculation is Chen and Hill 1912.07795, which adds O(mW/M) power corrections, QCD corrections to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. Its verbatim result is: 'The upper limit for the pure doublet is less than 10^-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass regime ... lower than the estimated Xenon neutrino floor', with 'the pure Higgsino well below the neutrino floor'. The uncertainty is quoted only as this upper bound; no central value plus or minus an error was read. Citation recorded in references.bib (tc-...-64).

(2) LZ 2024 limit (2410.17036). Verbatim: the strongest SI exclusion is 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 90% CL, and the best median sensitivity is 5.1e-48 cm^2, both at 40 GeV. Finding f-005, citation tc-...-65. No 1 TeV value was read from the text or a figure.

(3) Rescaling. Scaling the 40 GeV limit linearly with mass is my estimate, not a read value. It gives about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, at 1.1 TeV. The ratio of limit to predicted upper bound is then at least about 60, i.e. at least 1.8 orders of magnitude. This extrapolation is likely conservative because the limit curve rises from its minimum. Finding f-008, medium confidence.

Not done:
- The XENONnT 2303.14729 1 TeV limit was not read.
- No limit figure was extracted, so there are no figure numbers for the LZ or XENONnT limits.
- No numeric neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV was obtained; the 'below the neutrino floor' statement rests on Chen and Hill's text.
- Projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD/DARWIN) were not tabulated.

Also noted: 2607.20588 (Bisal et al., 2026) says next-to-leading-order corrections can push the higgsino cross section below the neutrino floor or make it vanish in parts of MSSM parameter space. This is relevant to q-04.

result.summary: Two of the three success criteria are met; the third is only partly met. (1) The inelastic threshold, worked by hand (f-001): m_Xe = 131 x 0.9315 = 122.0 GeV. The reduced mass mu_A is 108.7 GeV at m = 1.0 TeV and 109.8 GeV at 1.1 TeV. With v_max = 544 + 232 = 776 km/s, (v_max/c)^2 = 6.70e-6, so delta_max = mu_A v_max^2/2 is about 364 keV at 1.0 TeV and 368 keV at 1.1 TeV. The minimum-velocity formula v_min = sqrt(2 delta/mu_A) is Eq. A7 of 2609.09830. (2) Partly met: 2609.09830 does not give an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range (f-002). Its five benchmarks have |mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV, |M1| and M2 of about 5.8-42 TeV, and one-loop on-shell delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. They predict at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, need 9.4-65.5 t-y of exposure to be probed (Table VII, Fig. 6), and are all consistent with LZ. NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV with gaugino masses of O(10) TeV arise only from partial cancellation between the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs; generically the paper quotes O(10-100) MeV. My own estimate, using the formula that is not yet sourced (q-05): same-sign M2 = 2 M1 would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV to bring delta below 364 keV. Inelastic Z-exchange therefore matters only in tuned corners. (3) Mixing region where elastic SI becomes visible (f-003, 2606.31013): Higgs exchange gives f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta). Direct detection is sensitive where mixing produces larger charged-neutral splittings and reaches the thermal mass of about 1 TeV (Figs. 4 and 5 of that paper; the figures were not extracted). The pure-limit radiative charged-neutral splitting is about 356 MeV (Eq. 13 of 2606.31013), rather than the 340 MeV in the brief. (4) Rescaling: 2606.31013 Eq. 38 uses sigma_eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma, computed with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and 2609.09830 states that limits weaken proportionally for sub-thermal fractions. brief.summary: Literature converges on a pure Higgsino thermal relic mass near 1.0-1.1 TeV to saturate Omega h^2 = 0.12, with sub-TeV masses viable only with slepton coannihilation or bino/wino mixing. Direct detection of pure Higgsino is loop-suppressed due to accidental cancellations, leading to purity constraints on gaugino mixing from LZ/Xenon. Recent 2026 preprints propose inelastic Higgsino scattering with delta ~ 350 keV as an interpretation of the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event in 2.84 ton-yr exposure, while a contrasting solar-capture analysis using IceCube non-observation of high-energy neutrinos from the Sun derives delta > 566 keV for ~1.08 TeV Higgsino, excluding the thermal-Higgsino explanation of the LZ event under standard halo and solar model assumptions. The tension hinges on halo high-speed tail (LMC), solar density/capture on heavy elements, elastic cooling in the Sun, and the LZ high-energy sideband joint fit.

Not finished: only one published pure-higgsino relic-density point was found, so the success criteria (published values at three or more masses, and a thermal mass from two independent papers) are not met.

(1) No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists here, and list_input_files returned no data files (tc-261016_1-w1-d-01-19, finding f-006). Every value below comes from the literature. Nothing was computed.

(2) arXiv:1411.6930, Sec. 3, gives the one published point: a pure higgsino (all sfermions and heavy Higgses decoupled) has Omega h^2 = 0.127 without and 0.126 with Sommerfeld enhancement (off-diagonal rates included). The net Sommerfeld effect is below 1 percent because the neutral channels are enhanced and the charged ones suppressed. The paper's mass for this model appears to be 1172.31 GeV, the mass of its higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006; I inferred this from context, the paper does not state it. For that pMSSM point (dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV) the values are 0.108 without and 0.100 with Sommerfeld, an 8 percent drop. The paper quotes about 5 percent accuracy at best and compares to Planck 2013 (0.1187 +/- 0.0017). Its Fig. 7 (registered as Figure 6, figures_1411.6930/fig07.png) shows only the yield ratio Y/Ypert, not Omega h^2 against mass (finding f-007). A verbatim quote is in references.bib (key arxiv14116930).

(3) hep-ph/0610249 expected the Sommerfeld effect for higgsinos to be roughly 10 percent (versus 50 percent for winos). It was not a full calculation (f-009).

(4) Interpolation, not published values: scaling the 1411.6930 point as Omega h^2 proportional to m^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155 at 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV. Omega h^2 = 0.120 falls at about 1.14 TeV (1144 GeV with Sommerfeld, 1139 GeV without) (f-009, low confidence).

result.summary:
Answer: a thermal pure higgsino at about 1.1 TeV lies about 2 or more orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 limit and below the xenon neutrino floor. Three of the planned inputs were not read: the XENONnT limit, the LZ limit read from its figure at 1 TeV, and a numeric neutrino-fog value. All are recorded as open question q-06.

(1) Prediction. Hisano et al. 1104.0228 work at leading order in electroweak loops. They find the SI cross section of pure SU(2)-multiplet dark matter is O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2, nearly independent of mass above about 1 TeV. An accidental cancellation drives this: twist-2 terms are positive, while the Higgs-exchange, gluon and Z-box scalar terms are negative and of similar size. Their Fig. 5 shows the higgsino (n=2, Y=1/2) at M = 1 TeV against the Higgs mass; the paper predates the measured Higgs mass. Finding f-004.

The newer and more complete calculation is Chen and Hill 1912.07795, which adds O(mW/M) power corrections, QCD corrections to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. Its verbatim result is: 'The upper limit for the pure doublet is less than 10^-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass regime ... lower than the estimated Xenon neutrino floor', with 'the pure Higgsino well below the neutrino floor'. The uncertainty is quoted only as this upper bound; no central value plus or minus an error was read. Citation recorded in references.bib (tc-...-64).

(2) LZ 2024 limit (2410.17036). Verbatim: the strongest SI exclusion is 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 90% CL, and the best median sensitivity is 5.1e-48 cm^2, both at 40 GeV. Finding f-005, citation tc-...-65. No 1 TeV value was read from the text or a figure.

(3) Rescaling. Scaling the 40 GeV limit linearly with mass is my estimate, not a read value. It gives about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, at 1.1 TeV. The ratio of limit to predicted upper bound is then at least about 60, i.e. at least 1.8 orders of magnitude. This extrapolation is likely conservative because the limit curve rises from its minimum. Finding f-008, medium confidence.

Not done:
- The XENONnT 2303.14729 1 TeV limit was not read.
- No limit figure was extracted, so there are no figure numbers for the LZ or XENONnT limits.
- No numeric neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV was obtained; the 'below the neutrino floor' statement rests on Chen and Hill's text.
- Projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD/DARWIN) were not tabulated.

Also noted: 2607.20588 (Bisal et al., 2026) says next-to-leading-order corrections can push the higgsino cross section below the neutrino floor or make it vanish in parts of MSSM parameter space. This is relevant to q-04.

result.summary: Two of the three success criteria are met; the third is only partly met. (1) The inelastic threshold, worked by hand (f-001): m_Xe = 131 x 0.9315 = 122.0 GeV. The reduced mass mu_A is 108.7 GeV at m = 1.0 TeV and 109.8 GeV at 1.1 TeV. With v_max = 544 + 232 = 776 km/s, (v_max/c)^2 = 6.70e-6, so delta_max = mu_A v_max^2/2 is about 364 keV at 1.0 TeV and 368 keV at 1.1 TeV. The minimum-velocity formula v_min = sqrt(2 delta/mu_A) is Eq. A7 of 2609.09830. (2) Partly met: 2609.09830 does not give an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range (f-002). Its five benchmarks have |mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV, |M1| and M2 of about 5.8-42 TeV, and one-loop on-shell delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. They predict at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, need 9.4-65.5 t-y of exposure to be probed (Table VII, Fig. 6), and are all consistent with LZ. NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV with gaugino masses of O(10) TeV arise only from partial cancellation between the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs; generically the paper quotes O(10-100) MeV. My own estimate, using the formula that is not yet sourced (q-05): same-sign M2 = 2 M1 would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV to bring delta below 364 keV. Inelastic Z-exchange therefore matters only in tuned corners. (3) Mixing region where elastic SI becomes visible (f-003, 2606.31013): Higgs exchange gives f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta). This is suppressed at large gaugino mass and at small tan beta with mu<0. The scan covers 150<|mu|<1000 GeV, 1.6<tan beta<50 and 0.5<M1<10 TeV with M2 = 2 M1. Direct detection is sensitive where mixing produces larger charged-neutral splittings and reaches the thermal mass of about 1 TeV (Figs. 4 and 5 of that paper; the figures were not extracted). The pure-limit radiative charged-neutral splitting is about 356 MeV (Eq. 13 of 2606.31013), rather than the 340 MeV in the brief. (4) Rescaling: 2606.31013 Eq. 38 uses sigma_eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma, computed with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and 2609.09830 states that limits weaken proportionally for sub-thermal fractions. result.summary: Done. compute_relic_density (serve-idm.sh) gives Omega h^2 = 0.0731, 0.0898, 0.1083, 0.1285 and 0.1503 at m_chi = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV. It gives 0.1181 at 1150 GeV and 0.1202 at 1160 GeV, so the thermal mass (Omega h^2 = 0.120, Planck 0.12 +/- 0.0012) is about 1159 GeV, bracketed between 1150 and 1160 GeV (f-020). The tool does perturbative Kolb-Turner freeze-out (x_f about 24.5, g* = 86.25) with sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s x (1100 GeV/m_chi)^2. It has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, no charged-splitting input and no delta_m dependence: Omega h^2 = 0.1202 at delta = 400, 500 and 600 keV (f-021). So step 3 (toggling Sommerfeld/coannihilation) and the charged-splitting part of step 5 could not be run. The tool's consistent_planck flag is unreliable: it reads True at 25 sigma tension and False at 39 sigma. check_all_constraints at 1160 GeV, delta = 500 keV returns 'VIABLE'. Relic is 0.1202 (0.1 sigma). LZ gives N_expected = 0.00 for 2.84 t-yr with sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2, flagged inconsistent with the 1 observed event; no LZ limit value is returned. result.summary: All runs were local; get_dispatch reported 'local execution'. The tool uses a standard halo with a hard cutoff at v_esc+v_E = 776 km/s, and none of its calls accept a v_esc or LMC-tail option. At m_chi = 1100 GeV (sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2), predict_recoil gives these values for delta = 300/400/480/520/560 keV: peak E_R = 270/360/432/468/504 keV, v_min at the peak = 701/809/886/922/957 km/s, and v_min at 248 keV = 701/823/921/969/1018 km/s. Expected events in the LZ extended nuclear-recoil search (2.84 t-yr): 744.6 at 300 keV and 0.00 for every delta of 400 keV or more. Scaling by exposure gives about 1101 events at 4.2 t-yr for 300 keV, and still zero for the rest. The tool reports only the peak E_R, not a separate E_R,min, and gives no integrated rate above 100 keV. These results agree with f-001's kinematic limit of about 365 keV (f-018). At (1100 GeV, 500 keV), check_all_constraints gives Omega h^2 = 0.108 and N_LZ = 0, marked 'not consistent with 1 event'. Fermi and CMB pass by many orders of magnitude, and the annual modulation at 248 keV is zero. The 15x15 scan (m_chi 900-1300 GeV, delta 300-650 keV, file /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz) finds 180 of 225 points pass all constraints, but only 12 predict 0.3-5 LZ events. Its best fit is m_chi = 986 GeV, delta = 350 keV, which lies below both the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines (f-019, f-023). The scan output does not list which points are in the 12-point group, so the claim that they all sit below the neutrino lines is inferred from the 1.1 TeV kinematics, not confirmed by the tool. Conclusion: under the tool's halo, delta of about 480-520 keV gives zero events, not O(1), so no part of the 2609.01590 region survives. Explaining the LZ event at about 500 keV needs a high-velocity tail (for example from the LMC), which the tool does not model. 1. Preferred region, 2609.01590 (f-024, Fig. 1). With the Halo 13 MW+LMC velocity distribution the LZ fit gives delta_m = 481-519 keV at 1 sigma and 475-529 keV at 2 sigma, best fit about 496 keV. With a profiled Maxwellian halo it gives 312-422 keV at 1 sigma and 280-457 keV at 2 sigma, best fit 1.09 TeV and 366 keV. The paper says the upper limit on delta_m is set by the kinematic endpoint v_esc + v_E, not by the event-rate normalization. The relic density fixes m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV at 1 sigma and 943-1230 GeV at 2 sigma. LZ inputs are E_R = 248 +/- 23 stat +/- 23 sys keV and 2.84 tonne-year.

2. Why the neutrino lines are 475 and 557 keV (f-025; Fig. 2 of 2609.01590, Figs. 2-3 of 2609.07807). The difference comes from how the captured higgsinos are treated in the Sun, not from the halo model.
- 2609.01590, at m_chi = 1.11 TeV: if elastic scattering is negligible (the blind spot), the captured higgsinos never thermalize and stay on extended orbits, so they annihilate less. With <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s and ten years of IceCube data, this excludes delta_m up to about 475 keV at 90% CL. Loose solar and nuclear inputs lower this to 466 keV, and the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty to about 454 keV. If elastic scattering lets them reach equilibrium, the same paper finds delta_m >~ 553 keV.
- 2609.07807 assumes the captured higgsinos thermalize and uses a standard truncated Maxwellian halo: u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s, rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3. Other inputs are sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s and m_chi = 1.08 TeV, with a 95% CL fit to IceCube nu_mu, IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. It excludes delta_m below about 557 keV, which agrees with the 553 keV equilibrium result. It still allows rescue by an LMC tail or substructure.

3. Gamma-ray lines near 1.1 TeV, 2609.01590 (f-026, Fig. 3). The thermal prediction is 0.815-0.900 of the H.E.S.S. 546 h limits, which the paper calls close to, but not excluded by, the present limits. The CTAO Alpha 500 h projection, mu_gamma,95 = 1.69, falls short of the thermal target. The Omega configuration, estimated at 0.85, would reach it. A new 16x16 scan (m_chi 1000-1200 GeV, delta 330-480 keV in 10 keV steps) passes all 256 points and puts 16 in the 0.3-5 band, best fit (1000 GeV, 350 keV). That the 16 are the delta = 350 keV row is inferred from the bracketing, not listed by the tool (f-032). This scan overwrote /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz and constraint_summary.png. The tools return no figure numbers.

Analytic check (f-033, hand-computed): delta_max = v_max*sqrt(2 m_N E_R) - m_N E_R/mu at E_R = 248 keV, with m_N = 122 GeV. At 1000/1100/1183 GeV it gives 358.5/361.3/363.2 keV for 776 km/s, 378/381/383 keV for 800, 419/422/424 keV for 850 and 460/463/465 keV for 900 km/s. It matches the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within about 1 km/s. The tool's 'about 365 keV' edge is the endpoint when E_R is left free, mu v^2/2 = 364-370 keV at 776 km/s, reached near E_R of about 330 keV rather than at 248 keV.

Required v_max (f-034, hand-computed), at 1100 GeV with the event at 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 for 475, 968 for 519, 980 for 529 and 1015 for 557 keV. With E_R left free the minimum is lower: 830 km/s for 422 keV, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 for 557 keV.

What this means for 2609.01590 and the LMC tail:
- The paper's profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s, compared with the tool's 776 km/s. This explains why the tool gives zero events at 400 keV.
- The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need an LMC-boosted tail reaching about 920-980 km/s.
- Clearing the 475 keV IceCube line needs at least about 880-915 km/s.
- Clearing the 557 keV Super-K + IceCube line needs at least about 950-1015 km/s.
The higgsino reading of the event therefore depends entirely on how many particles the halo has above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.

findings.claim: 2609.09830 does not quote an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range. Its five benchmarks (|mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV; |M1|, M2 about 5.8-42 TeV; tan beta 10.9-26.5) have one-loop on-shell splittings delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. Each predicts at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, and probing them needs 9.4-65.5 tonne-years. All are consistent with the LZ bound. Inelastic events at NLO range from 0.00022 (BP1) to 0.18 (BP4). NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV come from partial cancellation of the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs.

findings.claim: Beneke, Hellmann and Ruiz-Femenia (arXiv:1411.6930, Sec. 3) report Omega h^2 = 0.127 (perturbative) and 0.126 (Sommerfeld, with off-diagonal rates) for a pure-higgsino model compared against the higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006 at m_chi = 1172.31 GeV. The net Sommerfeld correction for pure higgsinos is almost zero (below 1 percent) because enhancement in the neutral channels cancels suppression in the chi0 chi+- channels. For the pMSSM higgsino-like point (higgsino fraction 0.98, dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV) they find Omega h^2 = 0.108 (perturbative) and 0.100 (Sommerfeld), an 8 percent reduction. The quoted Sommerfeld accuracy is about 5 percent at best.

findings.claim: Chen and Hill (1912.07795) include the O(mW/M) power corrections, perturbative QCD to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. They find that the pure-higgsino SI cross section has an upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass range, below the estimated xenon neutrino floor. This is about 2 orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 minimum limit of 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 40 GeV. Assuming linear mass scaling of the LZ limit above about 100 GeV (my estimate, not read from the paper), the LZ limit at 1.1 TeV is about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, so the pure higgsino lies at least about 1.8 orders of magnitude below it.

findings.claim: Metadata confirms both IDs: arXiv:2606.31013 is 'Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection' by Hamaguchi, Nagata and Osaki (2026), and arXiv:2609.09830 is 'Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter' by Chatterjee, Das, Pasha, Pukhov and Puri (2026). Both abstracts match how the survey uses them. This resolves q-02.

The full text of 2606.31013 supports the f-003 numbers. Eq. 13 reads Delta m+|rad ~ (1/2) alpha2 MZ sin^2 thetaW (1 - 3MZ/(2 pi M_chi+)), with the statement 'For M_chi+ >> MZ, this mass splitting asymptotically approaches Delta m+|rad ~ 356 MeV'. Eq. 33 reads f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 thetaW/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta) and is valid for MZ << M1,2-|mu|; the exact form is Eq. 32. The paper says the coupling is suppressed at large gaugino mass and 'for small tan beta and negative mu, due to an accidental cancellation'. Eq. 38 is sigma_SI/SD,eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma_SI/SD, computed with micrOMEGAs v6.3.0. The scan (Eq. 37) covers 150 GeV<|mu|<1000 GeV, 1.6<tan beta<50 and 0.5 TeV<M1<10 TeV, with M2=2M1 and M1>|mu|. Note: the f-003 label 'Eq. 13' is correct; the f_q formula is Eq. 33, not unnumbered.

The full text of 2609.09830 supports the f-002 numbers. Table III gives one-loop on-shell delta = 36.37, 8.90, 16.39, 10.81 and 10.59 keV for BP1-BP5, with mu = -739.63, -606.64, -814.26, 1282.11 and 1400.0 GeV, M1 = -7830, -6292, -5838, 11354 and 12875 GeV, M2 = 17055, 42000, 30925, 12627 and 12050 GeV, and tan beta = 10.88-26.46. Table VII, NLO rows for BP1-BP5: elastic events 1.0280, 0.07729, 0.1176, 0.4127, 0.5074; inelastic events 0.00022, 0.07039, 0.0518, 0.1806, 0.1661; combined 1.02822, 0.14768, 0.1694, 0.5933, 0.6735; required exposure 9.41, 65.50, 57.10, 16.30, 14.36 t-y (LZ exposure 4.2 t-y; null result taken as N_E < ln 10, about 2.3). Table VI for BP2 gives sigma_inel NLO = 0.507e-12 pb against sigma_el LO = 0.284e-12 pb (ratio 1.785). The paper describes this as 'approximately a factor of two larger than the elastic LO one'. The text says all BPs are consistent with LZ. Note: the BP1 scan sign pattern has M1<0 and M2>0 for mu=±0.5 or ±1 TeV, with -21 TeV <= M1 <= -1 TeV and 1 TeV <= M2 <= 21 TeV (Eq. 25), yet BP4 and BP5 have M1 and M2 both positive.

2609.09830 does not write out the tree-level delta_m0 formula. It says only: 'as can be seen, for example, from Eq. (9) of Ref. [28], the corrections proportional to M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 depend on the relative signs of M1 and M2. In the parameter regions relevant for our analysis, these contributions can have opposite signs and partially cancel.' 2606.31013 also says only that the splittings are 'suppressed by M_Z^2/M_1,2'. The explicit form delta_m0 ~ m_Z^2 s_W^2/M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2/M2 therefore remains unsourced (q-05 stays open), and so does the estimate that same-sign M2=2M1 needs M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV. Counter-evidence to the 'tuned corners only' conclusion: BP4 and BP5 reach delta of about 10.6-10.8 keV with M1 and M2 both positive (about 11-13 TeV) and mu > 0. The O(10) keV splittings there come from on-shell one-loop corrections combined with relative signs between mu and the gauginos, not only from opposite-sign M1 and M2.

findings.claim: The 475 keV and 557 keV neutrino lines differ because of how the captured population in the Sun is treated, not because of the halo. 2609.01590 simulates a non-thermal population on extended solar orbits at m_chi = 1.11 TeV with no elastic cooling (elastic blind spot) and 10-year IceCube data, using <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s with Sommerfeld; this gives delta_m >~ 475 keV excluded at 90% CL (466 keV with loose solar/nuclear inputs, about 454 keV with the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty). If elastic scattering allows thermalization and capture-annihilation equilibrium, the same paper gets delta_m >~ 553 keV. 2609.07807 assumes thermalization within the Sun after capture, a standard truncated Maxwellian (u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s), rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3, sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s, m_chi = 1.08 TeV and a 95% CL chi^2 on IceCube nu_mu (2016), IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. findings.claim: Analytic kinematics (m_N = 122.0 GeV for Xe-131, E_R = 248 keV, sqrt(2 m_N E_R) = 0.8206 keV per km/s): delta_max = v_max*sqrt(2 m_N E_R) - m_N E_R/mu gives, at m_chi = 1000/1100/1183 GeV, 358.5/361.3/363.2 keV for v_max = 776 km/s, 378/381/383 keV for 800 km/s, 419/422/424 keV for 850 km/s and 460/463/465 keV for 900 km/s. This reproduces the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within 1 km/s (766 vs 765.7 km/s at 1000 GeV and 350 keV; 921/969/1018 km/s at 1100 GeV and 480/520/560 keV). The tool's 'about 365 keV' edge is the E_R-optimized endpoint delta_max = mu v_max^2/2 = 364/368/370 keV at 776 km/s, reached at E_R = mu*delta/m_N of about 330 keV, not at 248 keV.

findings.claim: Inverting the kinematics at m_chi = 1100 GeV gives the v_max (Earth frame) needed to reach a given delta with an event exactly at E_R = 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 km/s for 475 keV, 968 km/s for 519 keV, 980 km/s for 529 keV and 1015 km/s for 557 keV (about +3 km/s at 1000 GeV, about -2 km/s at 1183 GeV). If E_R is free (at the optimal E_R = mu*delta/m_N of about 380-500 keV), the minimum is v_max = sqrt(2 delta/mu): 830 km/s for 422, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 km/s for 557 keV. All of these exceed the tool's SHM cutoff of 776 km/s by 55-240 km/s. So the 2609.01590 profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s. The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need about 920-980 km/s of LMC-boosted tail. Covering delta >= 557 keV (above the Super-K + IceCube line) needs at least about 950-1015 km/s, and delta >= 475 keV needs at least about 880-915 km/s. The higgsino reading therefore rests entirely on the halo's population above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.

evidence.note: Hand-computed inversion, consistent with tool v_min(248 keV) = 921/969/1018 km/s at 480/520/560 keV (f-018). The E_R uncertainty (+/-33 keV combined) moves the 248 keV numbers toward the E_R-optimized ones.

questions.text: The task asks for relic densities from 'inelastic-DM tools', but no such tool, no run_coding_task and no run_pack_kernel is in the catalog. Should the user be told that relic-density values are literature-sourced rather than computed, or is a compute server missing from the connection?
The arXiv IDs 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 are recent. Verify with get_arxiv_metadata that they exist and that their content matches the survey before relying on them.

Published thermal masses differ by about 10-20 percent depending on Sommerfeld treatment, bound-state formation and the treatment of the QCD/electroweak phase transition. Which value should serve as the headline?
Is the SI prediction's interference between the Higgs and gauge (twist-2) contributions stable enough that the conclusion 'below the neutrino fog' is robust?

The tree-level formula delta_m0 ≈ m_Z^2 s_W^2/M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2/M2 has not been sourced yet. Can a quotable reference be found, for example Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, Eq. (9)? Taken at face value with same-sign M2 = 2 M1, delta < 364 keV would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV, so the O(10) keV benchmarks are viable only through sign cancellations and loop corrections.

Still open from d-02: the XENONnT 2303.14729 SI limit at 1 TeV, the actual LZ 2024 limit-curve value at 1 TeV (read from its figure rather than linearly rescaled from 40 GeV), and a numeric xenon neutrino-fog value at 1.1 TeV. None of these were read in this direction.

The XLZD Design Book (arXiv:2410.17137) has been identified but not read: what are its projected SI sensitivity and its xenon neutrino-fog value at about 1 TeV, and how do they compare with the pure-higgsino bound of 1e-48 cm^2?

What thermal mass, with its theory uncertainty, does arXiv:2205.04486 (Bottaro et al. 2022, Sommerfeld plus bound-state formation) give for the Y=1/2 doublet in its thermal-mass table, and how far is it from the 1411.6930-derived value of about 1.14 TeV?

What arXiv paper is Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, and does its Eq. (9) give the tree-level neutral higgsino splitting with explicit sign dependence on mu, M1 and M2? This is needed to re-evaluate the M1 required for delta < 364 keV, given that BP4 and BP5 reach about 10.7 keV with same-sign M1 and M2 of about 12 TeV.
Does compute_relic_density include Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation, or only perturbative freeze-out? This determines how its thermal mass compares with 1411.6930 and 2205.04486.

The hand estimate f-001 gives a kinematic delta_max of about 365 keV for v_max = 776 km/s, yet 2609.01590 fits delta_m of about 500 keV. Which halo assumption (v_esc, LMC tail) does the tool use, and does it reproduce either result?
Do the tool's LZ constraint and the published LZ 2024 curve agree at 1.1 TeV?
Where is the published Ref. [28] tree-level delta_m0 formula (open item d-07)? It is needed to judge how natural delta_m of about 500 keV is.
Do the Fermi-LAT and CMB verdicts from check_all_constraints agree with published TeV-higgsino indirect-detection limits (open item d-08)?

Why does check_all_constraints give N_LZ = 0.00 already at delta = 400 keV for m_chi = 1160 GeV, and why does it use a p-wave, splitting-suppressed sigma_v_today of about 1e-41 cm^3/s instead of the s-wave higgsino WW rate of about 1e-26 cm^3/s? Its indirect and CMB verdicts need an external cross-check against published higgsino limits (q-14).
How large is the 2609.09830 one-loop change to delta_m and to the inelastic cross section (the full text has not been read), and what are the 2610.03692 thermal-mass IceCube variants in numbers?

The LZ 2024 (2410.17036) and XENONnT (2303.14729) SI limits at 1.1 TeV and the XLZD neutrino-fog level remain unread in d-11 (budget exhausted); can a follow-up read them from the text or HEPData instead of extrapolating the 40 GeV limit?
What is the Sommerfeld+bound-state corrected thermal mass spread (1.0 vs 1.1 vs 1.2 TeV) across 1411.6930, 2205.04486 and recent 2026 papers?
Can delta ~300-350 keV inelastic higgsino at 1.1 TeV produce the LZ 248 keV event without violating v_esc+v_E=776 km/s threshold (~364 keV) and neutrino-line bounds 475/557 keV?
How far below LZ 2024/XENONnT and below/above neutrino fog does the pure-higgsino elastic SI cross-section (<1e-48 cm2) sit at 1 TeV, and what gaugino mixing is needed to become visible?

What is the quantitative shift in thermal Higgsino mass when adding Sommerfeld + bound-state formation (2205.04486) vs perturbative 1411.6930/serve-idm.sh, and what uncertainty should be quoted for the 1.0-1.1 TeV target?

Does the LZ 248 keV event survive as inelastic Higgsino scattering when varying halo v_max from 776 km/s (standard) to LMC-boosted ~850 km/s, and at what delta does solar capture/IceCube (delta>566 keV) definitively exclude the thermal mass?

issues.text: Step 1 is not enough: the gap has to show up in the final answer. No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists, list_input_files is empty, and run_test_job only draws random samples. The task asked us to compute relic density with tools, and we cannot. The report must say plainly that every Omega h^2 value is taken from the literature. Do not use run_test_job to produce anything that looks like a computed relic curve.

1411.6930 is a pMSSM scan. It may not give a pure-higgsino Omega h^2(m) curve at 0.9-1.3 TeV with and without Sommerfeld enhancement. Before relying on it, check that such a figure or table exists. If it does not, use the one-parameter thermal mass plus the m^2 scaling, and label every resulting row as derived, not read. Also note that the higgsino Sommerfeld effect is small, only a few percent shift in mass. Bound-state formation (recent 2021-2026 work) can matter as much as Sommerfeld, so the search should target it explicitly.

The budget is tight. Fifteen calls do not cover three or four full-text downloads plus chunk reads, figures and cite. Drop the full read of 1008.2905, which is a method paper and not needed for numbers. Get the Planck Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001 quote with one targeted chunk read of 1807.06209. Limit independent cross-checks to one paper.

Run get_arxiv_metadata on 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 before any download, to confirm they exist and say what the brief claims. The brief cites 2606.31013 for the '~1 TeV' figure but has not read it. If either ID does not resolve, report that and do not attribute numbers to it.

A key literature cross-check is missing. Hill and Solon (for example 1111.0016 and 1409.8290) give the heavy-higgsino SI cross section with a large cancellation-driven uncertainty, possibly near or below the xenon neutrino fog. Because 1104.0228 and 1007.2601 predate refined nucleon matrix elements, the prediction should be quoted as a range across these sources, not a single number. 1004.4090 is a wino paper and can be skipped.

Values read off log-scale limit figures with get_paper_figures need a stated reading uncertainty, for example a factor of about 1.5. Check whether the LZ and XENONnT figures actually extend to 1 TeV. If they do, read the value there and do not rescale. If rescaling is needed, use limit proportional to m for m >> m_Xe and state the reference mass. Also replace the brief's 1e-46 to 1e-45 estimate with read values; the true limit at 1 TeV is likely near the low end of that range.

2510.17473 (ICRC 2025 review) is listed in the brief but not used. Use it as one source for current and projected xenon reach (LZ full exposure, XLZD) and for the neutrino-fog value at TeV masses, instead of searching for a separate fog paper.

The threshold arithmetic is sound. With m_Xe of about 122 GeV, mu is about 109 GeV at 1 TeV and v_max is about 776 km/s, giving delta_max of about 360 keV. State the assumed v_esc and v_E, and note the sensitivity to the halo model. Source the charged-neutral splitting of about 341 MeV to the two-loop result (for example 1410.4549) rather than leaving it generic. Keep the splitting formula approximate, including tan(beta)-dependent and sign terms.

The answer to 'relative to current limits' should mention indirect detection briefly. For example, H.E.S.S. Galactic Center line and continuum limits are weak for TeV higgsinos because the cross section is not strongly Sommerfeld-enhanced. One sourced sentence from a review will do. This keeps the conclusion from resting on direct detection alone without changing scope.
The mixing-induced SI rise in the (mu, M1/M2, tan beta) plane overlaps with the d-02 discussion. Keep it only in d-03, so the two directions do not each download 2606.31013.

contested.reason: None of the three quoted excerpts contains any claimed content. tc-...-35 covers the oblique-parameter chi-square (Eqs. 26-29), tc-...-30 is the title page, and tc-...-33 covers the W/Y parameters (Eqs. 39-40). Missing are the f_q formula, the scan ranges, Eq. 13 (356 MeV), Eq. 38 with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and the statement that direct detection reaches about 1 TeV only with mixing. These may well be in the paper, but the cited evidence does not show them.

The excerpts do not show the Omega h^2 values 0.127, 0.126, 0.108 or 0.100, nor dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV or the 5 percent accuracy. The claim states m_chi = 1172.31 GeV as reported, but the d-01 summary says this mass was inferred from context and is not stated in the paper. The figure is also mislabelled: fig07 is registered as Figure 6.

There are two problems. First, the Chen and Hill verbatim quote (the upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2, below the neutrino floor) is not in any quoted excerpt. The cited tc-...-59 and -58 show only the rate formula and the title, and the citation call tc-...-64 is not listed as evidence. Second, there is an arithmetic error. An upper bound below 1e-48 cm^2 compared with the 2.2e-48 cm^2 minimum is a factor of about 2 or more, not 'about 2 orders of magnitude'. Only the comparison at 1.1 TeV (about 6e-47 cm^2) supports a margin of 1.8 orders or more.

The visible part of Table VII supports only BP1 elastic NLO = 1.028 events, which is consistent with 'at most about 1.03'. The other quantities are not in the shown excerpts: the splitting range 8.9-36.4 keV, the exposures of 9.4-65.5 t-y, the inelastic NLO range, and the BP2 statement. The visible LO numbers for BP2 (inelastic 0.0247, elastic 0.0436) show inelastic below elastic. The 'twice the LO elastic' claim therefore needs the NLO inelastic value quoted explicitly.

issues.text: The core quantity is still unmet. There is no published Omega h^2(m) curve at multiple masses and no second, independent determination of the thermal mass. The m^2 rescaling in f-009 depends on an inferred mass of 1172.31 GeV. If that inference is wrong, every rescaled value and the 1.14 TeV thermal mass shift with it.

The Planck 2018 value of 0.120 +/- 0.001 is used throughout but has never been quoted from 1807.06209.txt, although the file is already downloaded. 1411.6930 normalised to Planck 2013 (0.1187), so the f-009 rescaling should state which target it uses.

The arithmetic checks out: 0.126 x (m/1172.31)^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155, and the thermal masses of 1144 and 1139 GeV are correct. However, the hep-ph/0610249 '10 percent' statement is not visible in the tc-...-68 excerpt.

Survey recent arXiv work on the higgsino thermal relic target (1.0-1.2 TeV). Use the inelastic-DM tools to compute the relic density at several masses; compare with LZ/XENONnT sensitivities and the Planck abundance. Where does the higgsino sit relative to current limits?

**Survey** — 37 tools on 3 servers, 5 read-only probes, 13 papers found.

The pure higgsino, a Dirac-like electroweak doublet whose neutral states are split by a small Majorana mass, is a standard WIMP target. Its mass is fixed by requiring the thermal freeze-out abundance to match the Planck value Omega h^2 of about 0.12. That puts it near 1.0-1.2 TeV; the commonly quoted 1.1 TeV is background knowledge, and none of the returned abstracts state it. Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation with the charged state are needed to compute this mass precisely (1411.6930, 1008.2905). Bound-state effects are claimed to be important mainly above a few TeV (1407.7874). For elastic spin-independent scattering, the pure higgsino lies below the LZ 4.2 tonne-year limits (2410.17036; best SI limit 2.2e-48 cm^2, set at 40 GeV) and the XENONnT limits (2303.14729), because tree-level Z exchange is turned off by the inelastic mass splitting delta_m. The cross-section limits near 1.1 TeV are not given in these abstracts and must be read from the published curves. A burst of 2026 papers concerns a single LZ nuclear-recoil candidate at E_R = 248 keV (3.4 sigma local, 2.6 sigma global, from a 2.84 tonne-year exposure). It has been read as higgsino inelastic scattering with delta_m around 480-520 keV for m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV, which is exactly the thermal relic window (2609.01590). Neutrino constraints from dark matter captured and annihilating in the Sun are in tension with this reading: Super-K plus IceCube exclude delta_m below about 557 keV, which disfavors it for standard halo velocities (2609.07807), while IceCube alone excludes below about 475 keV once velocity effects near the blind spot are included (2609.01590). Other papers try to rescue the window (2610.03692) or look at boosted, non-halo explanations (2609.06890). Summary of where the higgsino stands: the thermal 1.0-1.2 TeV higgsino is not excluded by elastic xenon limits. It is directly testable through inelastic Z-mediated scattering only for delta_m up to a few hundred keV, where LZ's high-recoil sensitivity, solar-neutrino limits and the CTAO gamma-ray line together close in on the remaining parameter space.

Quantities worth checking: Omega h^2 versus m_chi for a pure higgsino at about 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV, with and without Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation; find the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.12 (Planck); Sensitivity of the relic mass to the charged-neutral splitting (about 340 MeV radiative) and to the neutral splitting delta_m; Elastic SI cross section of the pure higgsino (loop- and Higgs-mediated) at 1-1.2 TeV, compared with the LZ 4.2 tonne-year and XENONnT 90% CL curves at the same mass; Inelastic Z-mediated scattering rate and recoil spectrum in xenon as a function of delta_m (about 400-600 keV) and m_chi; minimum recoil energy E_R,min and the kinematic threshold v_min(delta_m); Expected LZ event count above 100 keV for the 2.84 or 4.2 tonne-year exposure, compared with the single 248 keV event; Dependence of the rate on v_esc and on the LMC-induced high-velocity tail.

**Plan** — 4 lines of investigation:
1. Use the serve-idm.sh tools to compute the pure-higgsino thermal relic density Omega h^2 at m_chi = 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV, find the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120, and run the combined constraint check at the thermal point. — The task asks for relic densities computed with the inelastic-DM tools. Earlier directions d-01 and d-04 could only interpolate from one published point in 1411.6930 because no relic-density tool was connected at the time. compute_relic_density and check_all_constraints are now in the catalog, so this direction answers the core question directly. It also replaces the low-confidence m^2 rescaling (f-009, about 1.14 TeV) with tool output.
2. Compute the inelastic Z-mediated recoil spectrum, the LZ event expectation and the (m_chi, delta_m) constraint map for the thermal higgsino. Reproduce or test the 2609.01590 preferred region (delta_m = 481-519 keV, m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV) against the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines. — Inelastic scattering is the only direct-detection route for the higgsino at current exposures. There is an unresolved tension here. The hand calculation f-001 gives a kinematic delta_max of about 364-368 keV for v_max = 776 km/s. 2609.01590, however, fits delta_m of about 500 keV, which needs a high-velocity tail (from the LMC) or a different halo model. The tool calculation must settle what delta_m can still be reached, and under which halo assumptions.

Close the remaining literature gaps: the 2205.04486 doublet thermal mass, the LZ 2024 and XENONnT SI limits near 1 TeV, and verbatim citations for Planck 2018 and Chen and Hill. — The tool results from d-09 and d-10 need published benchmarks. The thermal mass needs a second independent calculation (q-08). arXiv ID: 2609.01590
Title: TeV Higgsino Dark Matter from LZ Nuclear Recoil to Fermi-LAT Gamma Rays
Authors: Lei Wu, Yang Zhang, Bin Zhu
Year: 2026
Abstract: The excess of high-energy nuclear recoils, which was recently reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, together with the Fermi-LAT Galactic-Center preference, suggests new physics beyond the standard model (SM). One of the minimal extensions of the SM is to introduce a fermionic electroweak doublet in which the lightest neutral component can play the role of a stable dark matter particle. We show that the minimal higgsino dark matter can offer a common origin for both excesses. The inferred mass splitting, however, depends on the local dark matter velocity distribution, and including the high-velocity tail generated by the gravitational influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud yields $δ_m =481$--$519~\mathrm{keV}$ for $m_χ=1000$--$1183~\mathrm{GeV}$ at $1σ$ level. Near elastic-scattering blind spots, solar-captured higgsinos fail to reach thermal equilibrium, weakening their annihilation signal, so that ten years of IceCube data exclude $δ_m \lesssim 475~\mathrm{keV}$ at 90% C.L. The viable parameter space can be tested through the associated gamma-ray line, which is within the projected reach of CTAO.

Title: Not so good $ν$s for Higgsino dark matter as LZ excess: stringent limits from Super-Kamiokande and IceCube
Authors: Debajit Bose, Akash Kumar Saha, Deep Jyoti Das, Rinchen Sherpa, Abhijeet Singh, Durba Ghosh, Jaya Doliya, Subhadip Bouri, Biprajit Mondal, Ranjini Mondol, Nirmal Raj, Ranjan Laha
Year: 2026
Abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear recoil event at a high recoil energy of about 250 keV. This has been interpreted as inelastic scattering of dark matter that is a supersymmetric Higgsino with a mass splitting between the neutral states of a few 100 keV. Such dark matter may be captured at high recoil in the Sun through scattering on heavy elements in it, and annihilate to $W^+W^-$ and $ZZ$, in turn giving rise to a neutrino flux detectable on Earth. Using measurements of atmospheric electron- and muon-neutrino fluxes by Super-Kamiokande and IceCube, we constrain thermal and non-thermal Higgsino dark matter, excluding inter-state mass splittings $\lesssim 557$ keV. This disfavors Higgsino-like interpretations of the LZ event for standard halo velocities.

arXiv ID: 2609.09830
Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

Abstract: We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new. A technique to actively tag background electronic recoils from $^{214}$Pb $β$ decays is featured for the first time. Enhanced electron-ion recombination is observed in two-neutrino double electron capture decays of $^{124}$Xe, representing a noteworthy new background. After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds. World-leading constraints are placed on spin-independent (SI) and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections for masses $\geq$9 GeV/$c^2$. The strongest SI exclusion set is $2.2\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$ at the 90% confidence level and the best SI median sensitivity achieved is $5.1\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$, both for a mass of 40 GeV/$c^2$.
