Abstract: The design and performance of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector is described as of March 2015 in this Conceptual Design Report. LZ is a second-generation dark-matter detector with the potential for unprecedented sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) of masses from a few GeV/c2 to hundreds of TeV/c2. With total liquid xenon mass of about 10 tonnes, LZ will be the most sensitive experiment for WIMPs in this mass region by the end of the decade. This report describes in detail the design of the LZ technical systems. Expected backgrounds are quantified and the performance of the experiment is presented. The LZ detector will be located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. The organization of the LZ Project and a summary of the expected cost and current schedule are given.

Abstract: We report results from searches for new physics models through electron recoils using data collected by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment during its first two science runs, with a total exposure of 4.2 tonne-years. The observed data are consistent with a background-only hypothesis. Constraints are derived for electromagnetic interactions of solar neutrinos, solar axion-like particles (ALPs), mirror dark matter, and the absorption of bosonic dark matter candidates. Abstract: We describe the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a proposed optical-near infrared survey of 5000 sq. deg of the South Galactic Cap to ~24th magnitude in SDSS griz, that would use a new 3 sq. deg CCD camera to be mounted on the Blanco 4-m telescope at Cerro Telolo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The survey data will allow us to measure the dark energy and dark matter densities and the dark energy equation of state through four independent methods: galaxy clusters, weak gravitational lensing tomography, galaxy angular clustering, and supernova distances. These methods are doubly complementary: they constrain different combinations of cosmological model parameters and are subject to different systematic errors. By deriving the four sets of measurements from the same data set with a common analysis framework, we will obtain important cross checks of the systematic errors and thereby make a substantial and robust advance in the precision of dark energy measurements.

Abstract: Dark matter interacts gravitationally, but it presumably interacts weakly through other channels, especially with respect to regular luminous matter. We look at different ways in which dark matter may couple to other fields. We briefly review some example approaches in the literature for modeling the coupling between dark energy and dark matter and examine the possibility of an arguably better-motivated approach via non-minimal coupling between a scalar field and the Ricci scalar, which is necessary for renormalization of the scalar field in curved space-time. We also show an example of a theory beyond the Standard Model in which dark matter is uniquely connected to the inflaton, and we use observational astrophysical constraints to specify an upper bound on the dark matter mass. In turn, this mass constraint implies a limit on the unification scale of the theory, a decoupling scale of the theory, and the number of $e$-folds of inflation allowed.

Authors: Lei Wu, Yang Zhang, Bin Zhu

TeV Higgsino Dark Matter from LZ Nuclear Recoil to Fermi-LAT Gamma Rays
Lei Wu, 1,∗ Yang Zhang, 2,† and Bin Zhu 3,‡
1Department of Physics and Institute of Theoretical Physics,
Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, 210023, China
2Center for Theoretical Physics, Henan Normal University, Xinxiang 453007, China
3School of Physics, Yantai University, Yantai 264005, China
(Dated: September 18, 2026)
The excess of high-energy nuclear recoils, which was recently reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ)
experiment, together with the Fermi-LAT Galactic-Center preference, suggests new physics beyond
the standard model (SM). One of the minimal extensions of the SM is to introduce a fermionic
electroweak doublet in which the lightest neutral component can play the role of a stable dark
matter particle. We show that the minimal higgsino dark matter can offer a common origin for
both excesses. The inferred mass splitting, however, depends on the local dark matter velocity
distribution, and including the high-velocity tail generated by the gravitational influence of the
Large Magellanic Cloud yieldsδ m = 481–519 keV form χ = 1000–1183 GeV at 1σlevel. Near
elastic-scattering blind spots, solar-captured higgsinos fail to reach thermal equilibrium, weakening
their annihilation signal, so that ten years of IceCube data excludeδ m ≲475 keV at 90% C.L. The
viable parameter space can be tested through the associated gamma-ray line, which is within the
projected reach of CTAO.
Introduction.The existence of dark matter (DM)
is firmly established by gravitational evidence spanning
galactic rotation curves, cluster lensing, the cosmic mi-
crowave background, and the growth of large-scale struc-
ture [1]. Its identity, however, remains one of the central
open questions of particle physics and cosmology. Weakly
interacting massive particles (WIMPs) are among the
most studied candidates, since masses and interactions
at the weak scale, from a few tens of GeV to several
TeV, reproduce the observed relic abundance and provide
concrete targets for direct, indirect, and collider searches
[2]. Recently, a single high-energy nuclear recoil in LUX-
ZEPLIN and a gamma-ray excess toward the Galactic
Center in Fermi-LAT data may point to the upper end
of this mass range.
The LZ candidate is a single nuclear recoil atE R =
248±23 stat±23 sys keVnr and has a local significance
of about 3.4σand a global significance of 2.6σ[3]. This
event is kinematically compatible with TeV-scale DM,
though standard elastic scenarios are disfavored by null
results in the low energy nuclear recoils. Meanwhile,
the Fermi-LAT excess is a broad spectral component at
multi-GeV energies, reported in 14 years of data with
a significance of about 2σ[4]. Its morphology follows
a steeply rising, approximately squared Navarro–Frenk–
White profile, and its spectrum is broader and harder
than the diffuse emission that accounts for the rest of
the Galactic plane, so that an interpretation in terms
of unresolved astrophysical sources becomes increasingly
strained at the highest energies. A TeV-scale WIMP an-
nihilating into gauge-boson and Higgs-boson pairs pro-
duces just such a component, since gauge-boson fragmen-
tation yields a continuum peaking nearE γ∼m χ/50≃
20 GeV and spanning about a decade in energy, match-
ing both the position and the width of the excess. Both
observations, despite their modest significance, are thus
compatible with a common origin in a TeV-scale WIMP.
In thisLetter, we propose minimal higgsino dark mat-
ter as an explanation of the above two intriguing ex-
cesses. In the pure-doublet limit, the observed thermal
relic abundance fixes its mass near 1 TeV [2, 5], the
very scale the two observations favor. It can inelasti-
cally scatter off xenon nuclei, reproducing the LZ recoil,
and annihilate intoW +W− andZZ, enhanced by the
Sommerfeld effect at halo velocities [6, 7], generating the
continuum underlying the Fermi-LAT preference. Note
that kinematics of endothermic inelastic scattering ties
the 248 keV recoil to the mass splittingδ m through the
incident velocity, which must grow withδ m. The ac-
cessibleδ m is therefore bounded by the largest veloci-
ties available in the local dark matter distribution. We
find that the high-velocity tail of this distribution, gen-
erated by the gravitational influence of the Large Mag-
ellanic Cloud (LMC) [8], yields the favored parameter
space:δ m = 481–519 keV form χ = 1000–1183 GeV at
1σlevel. On the other hand, such a TeV-scale higgsino
is captured in the Sun and subsequently annihilates into
neutrinos. The large inelastic splitting that explains the
LZ event makes inelastic scattering the dominant process
governing the captured population, which therefore does
not reach thermal equilibrium within the solar age. The
resulting nonthermal distribution suppresses the annihi-
lation rate relative to the equilibrium assumption and
weakens the corresponding IceCube bounds. Simulat-
ing the nonthermal evolution, we find that ten years of
IceCube data excludeδ m ≲475 keV at 90% C.L.. In
addition, higgsino annihilation yields gamma-ray signals
within the projected reach of Cherenkov Telescope Array
Observatory (CTAO) [9].

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear recoil event at a high
recoil energy of about 250 keV. This has been interpreted as inelastic scattering of dark matter that
is a supersymmetric Higgsino with a mass splitting between the neutral states of a few 100 keV.
Such dark matter may be captured at high recoil in the Sun through scattering on heavy elements
in it, and annihilate to W +W − and ZZ , in turn giving rise to a neutrino flux detectable on Earth.
Using measurements of atmospheric electron- and muon-neutrino fluxes by Super-Kamiokande and
IceCube, we constrain thermal and non-thermal Higgsino dark matter, excluding inter-state mass
splittings ≲ 557 keV. This disfavors Higgsino-like interpretations of the LZ event for standard halo
velocities.
==================================================================== One of the authors is convinced that this is a background event as it is too close to the upper energy cut ==================================================================.
I. INTRODUCTION
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, seeking direct de-
tection of dark matter (DM), has seen a 248 ± 23 (stat)
± 23 (sys) keV nuclear recoil energy event, LZ230616, in
its 2.84 tonne-year dataset at a global (local) significance
of 2.6σ (3.4σ) [1]. The collaboration interpreted this as
induced by effective operators that lead to momentum-
dependent elastic scattering (via a magnetic moment)
or endothermic inelastic scattering; other operators such
as scalar-scalar interactions would have produced events
at low recoils that were not observed. One particularly
attractive explanation of LZ230616 [ 2–7] is, with an in-
elastic mass splitting δ≃ 350 keV, the thermal Higgsino,
a 1.08 TeV mass supersymmetric partner of the Higgs
boson – arising in weak-scale supersymmetric extensions
of the Standard Model (SM) [8–10] – that freezes out to
the right DM abundance via co-annihilations with slightly
heavier neutral and charged Higgsino states, dubbed the
“last-standing electroweak WIMP” and a poster child
for electroweak multiplets in the so-called minimal DM
paradigm [11]. Such Higgsino-like dark matter is accessi-
ble at collider energies, is being sought in indirect searches
for its annihilation products [ 12–15], and possibly large
δs may be cornered in compact stars [16–21].
While the thermal Higgsino DM interpretation is in
slight tension with a lack of events in LZ’s high-energy
sideband [23, 24] (which could be tested in LZ’s upcoming
runs and relaxed by considering a lighter non-thermal
Higgsino DM), a more urgent tension has been pointed
out. The 1.08 TeV Higgsino DM can be captured in
the Sun for δ <566 keV by scattering on its constituent
heavy elements, e.g., lead, thermalize within the solar
core, and subsequently annihilate to W +W−/ ZZ giving
rise to a high-energy neutrino flux that is constrained by
FIG. 1: Solar opening angle event distribution of our νµ
signal at IceCube [ 22] from the thermal Higgsino. Our

several bins and is hence disfavored. See Sec. III for more
details.

Higgsino interpretation of LZ230616, as the event may still
have been produced from the high-speed tail of the local
DM velocity distribution after accounting for possible

atmospheric neutrinos at Super-Kamiokande (Super-K)
and other IceCube datasets [22, 27, 28], applying angular

In Fig. 2 we show for thermal Higgsino DM our limits,
as well as a band enclosing δ = 340− 360 keV preferred
by LZ230616. The slope of these limits can be understood
from the tree-level vs loop-level scattering of χ. For
the heaviest solar nuclei, tree-level inelastic scattering is
suppressed due to kinematic threshold when χ reaches a
radius∼ 0.2R⊙ after losing kinetic energy via repeated
scatters. If the loop-level SI and SD cross sections are
then large enough, χ can scatter further and settle into
smaller volumes within the Sun, which would enhance its
annihilation rates. This is reflected in Fig. 2, where for SI
(SD) cross sections up to ∼ 2× 10−52 cm2 (∼ 2× 10−48
cm2) loop-level elastic scattering is inefficient for the
thermalization of χ, and the limit on δ is flat. As these
cross sections are increased, rχ shrinks and saturates to

The hierarchy of our limits is understood from detector

1.08 TeV thermal Higgsino produces a broad neutrino

spectrum, containing a significant fraction of the signal

hence the smaller detector of Super-K registers much
fewer events – though thanks to its lower threshold it can
access the softer part of the signal spectrum that IceCube
cannot reach. Together, these effects make Super-K limits
weaker than those from IceCube. Further, IceCube – νµ
measurements benefit from a significantly better angular

V. DISCUSSION
Our results show that high-energy νe and νµ measure-
ments at IceCube and Super-K disfavor the Higgsino inter-
pretation of the anomalous LZ230616 event. Our results
complement Ref. [25], which used the latest IceCube mea-
surements of νµs from the solar direction. We have also
ruled out a significant parametric region of a non-thermal
Higgsino DM interpretation of LZ230616. Future observa-
tions by upcoming telescopes such as Hyper-Kamiokande
and KM3NeT can further improve these bounds and
potentially discover the existence of a (non-)thermal Hig-
gsino – as could direct detectors such as LZ, XENONnT,
and PandaX-4T.
We re-state that our results do not completely rule
out the thermal Higgsino interpretation of LZ230616. It
could remain viable if the local DM velocity distribution
receives non-standard contributions such as from the mo-
tion of the LMC [ 2] or unvirialized substructure, e.g.,
tidal streams [54–56]. Moreover, for ∼250 keV recoils of
xenon the Helm form factor is in a region where it rapidly

Conclusions.We have investigated a thermal higgsino
interpretation of the LZ high-energy recoil and the Fermi-
LAT Galactic-center preference. Thermal freeze-out fixes
the higgsino mass near 1.1 TeV, while the LZ recoil se-
lects the neutral-state splitting through the high-velocity
tail of the local dark-matter distribution. With the LMC-
enhanced Halo 13 distribution, the joint 1σregion gives
481≲δ m/keV≲519. Solar-neutrino searches provide
a decisive complementary test. A thermalizing captured
population requiresδ m ≳553 keV, outside the LZ 2σre-
gions. Near the blind spot of elastic scattering, however,
the captured higgsinos remain on extended nonthermal
orbits, lowering the IceCube boundary to 475 keV, or to
466 keV with the loose solar and nuclear inputs. The full
Halo 13 LZ 2σinterval can therefore remain compatible
with IceCube when the residual elastic scattering is neg-
ligible. The same region predicts a Galactic-center line
and endpoint signal close to the present H.E.S.S. limits
and within the projected reach of CTAO, providing a
direct test of this interpretation.
Note added.Ref. [43] pointed out that the higgsino
interpretation of the LZ event can predict additional nu-
clear recoils in the high-energy sideband. For the Halo 13
MW+LMC, the smallest mass splittingδ m = 475 keV
givesN raw
SB /NROI ≃3.39. The high-energy sideband
therefore provides an important additional test of this
scenario, but does not by itself establish an exclusion
without the corresponding detector acceptance.

In Fig. 2 we show for thermal Higgsino DM our limits,
as well as a band enclosing δ = 340− 360 keV preferred
by LZ230616. The slope of these limits can be understood
from the tree-level vs loop-level scattering of χ. For
the heaviest solar nuclei, tree-level inelastic scattering is
suppressed due to kinematic threshold when χ reaches a
radius∼ 0.2R⊙ after losing kinetic energy via repeated
scatters. If the loop-level SI and SD cross sections are
then large enough, χ can scatter further and settle into
smaller volumes within the Sun, which would enhance its
annihilation rates. This is reflected in Fig. 2, where for SI
(SD) cross sections up to ∼ 2× 10−52 cm2 (∼ 2× 10−48
cm2) loop-level elastic scattering is inefficient for the
thermalization of χ, and the limit on δ is flat. As these
cross sections are increased, rχ shrinks and saturates to

The hierarchy of our limits is understood from detector
sizes, energy thresholds, and angular resolutions. The
1.08 TeV thermal Higgsino produces a broad neutrino

spectrum, containing a significant fraction of the signal
flux. However, this flux is rapidly falling with energy,
hence the smaller detector of Super-K registers much
fewer events – though thanks to its lower threshold it can
access the softer part of the signal spectrum that IceCube
cannot reach. Together, these effects make Super-K limits
weaker than those from IceCube. Further, IceCube – νµ
measurements benefit from a significantly better angular
resolution than the νe cascade observations, explaining
its slightly stronger limits. Now between the Super-K
datasets, although the atmospheric νµ flux is smaller

strongest (IceCube –νµ) and weakest (Super-K –νe) limits

arXiv ID: 2610.03692
Title: Higgsino dark matter compatible with the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy nuclear-recoil event and IceCube constraints
Authors: Katherine Freese, Dionysios P. Theodosopoulos
Year: 2026
Abstract: We examine Higgsino dark matter (DM) as a potential explanation of the $248~\mathrm{keV}$ nuclear-recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, taking into account IceCube constraints on DM annihilation in the Sun. In the nearly pure Higgsino limit, two neutral Majorana states separated by a small mass splitting $δ$ are connected by an off-diagonal coupling to the $Z$ boson, providing a natural realization of inelastic DM. Using a likelihood analysis, we identify 90\% confidence regions compatible with the LZ event and consistent with the null results of IceCube searches, both with and without including a constraint from the absence of events in the LZ high-energy sideband. In our LZ analysis, we consider the DM distribution in the Standard Halo Model alone as well as possible enhancements of the high-speed tail induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We present four variants of bounds from IceCube on Higgsino dark matter, depending on various assumptions on cooling channels in the Sun, motivated by severe theoretical uncertainties about Higgsino-nucleon elastic scattering (unimportant for direct detection but crucial for IceCube bounds). Whereas the thermal Higgsino with a mass of $1.1~\mathrm{TeV}$ remains only marginally compatible with both the LZ event and the IceCube limits when the LMC-induced high-speed tail is included and both elastic cooling in the Sun and the LZ high-energy sideband constraint are neglected, higher mass Higgsinos are excellent candidates for the LZ event in light of IceCube constraints. Depending on the halo distribution, cooling interactions, and whether the LZ high-energy sideband is included, the compatible regions in the Higgsino parameter space $(m_χ,δ)$ extend from masses of $\sim2~\mathrm{TeV}$ to hundreds of TeV or higher, with mass splittings ranging approximately from $350$ to $525~\mathrm{keV}$.

arXiv ID: 2609.09830
Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

arXiv ID: 2609.06890
Title: High-Energy Nuclear Recoils from Boosted Dark Matter for the LZ 248-keV Event: Beyond the Halo-Dependent High-Velocity Tail
Authors: Haider Alhazmi, Doojin Kim, Kyoungchul Kong, Jong-Chul Park, Seodong Shin
Year: 2026
Abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a nuclear-recoil candidate at $E_R=248\pm23_{\rm stat}\pm23_{\rm sys}$ keV, with a maximum local significance of $3.4σ$ and a global significance of $2.6σ$. A prominent interpretation invokes heavy halo dark matter near an inelastic threshold and therefore depends sensitively on the poorly constrained high-speed tail of the Galactic velocity distribution. In this Letter, we propose a qualitatively different possibility based on light boosted dark matter (BDM), whose incident energy is determined primarily by the dark-sector mass spectrum. We consider multi-component scenarios in which the boosted state scatters elastically or inelastically off xenon nuclei. For elastic scattering, pseudoscalar-mediated momentum dependence suppresses low-energy recoils. Near-threshold endothermic scattering of a nearly monochromatic BDM flux can instead confine the signal between kinematically determined recoil endpoints, suppressing events in both the low- and high-energy sidebands. The upscattered state may furthermore decay invisibly within the dark sector, preserving a single-nuclear-recoil signature without requiring it to be detector-stable. We present representative benchmark spectra and discuss complementary tests using other target nuclei and large-volume liquid-scintillator experiments.

We continue the study of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMP) started in [1], focusing
on a single complex electroweak n-plet with non-zero hypercharge added to the Standard Model.
The minimal splitting between the Dark Matter and its electroweak neutral partner required to
circumvent direct detection constraints allows only multiplets with hypercharge smaller or equal to
1. We compute for the ﬁrst time all the calculable WIMP masses up to the largest multiplet allowed
by perturbative unitarity. For the minimal allowed splitting, most of these multiplets can be fully
probed at future large-exposure direct detection experiments, with the notable exception of the
doublet with hypercharge 1/2. We show how a future muon collider can fully explore the parameter
space of the complex doublet combining missing mass, displaced track and long-lived track searches.
In the same spirit, we study how a future muon collider can probe the parameter space of complex
WIMPs in regions where the direct detection cross section drops below the neutrino ﬂoor. Finally,
we comment on how precision observables can provide additional constraints on complex WIMPs.

The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering
processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass
splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be re-

vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic

We examine Higgsino dark matter (DM) as a potential explanation of the 248 keV nuclear-
recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, taking into account IceCube
constraints on DM annihilation in the Sun. In the nearly pure Higgsino limit, two neutral Majorana
states separated by a small mass splittingδare connected by an off-diagonal coupling to theZ
boson, providing a natural realization of inelastic DM. Using a likelihood analysis, we identify 90%
confidence regions compatible with the LZ event and consistent with the null results of IceCube
searches, both with and without including a constraint from the absence of events in the LZ high-
energy sideband. In our LZ analysis, we consider the DM distribution in the Standard Halo Model
alone as well as possible enhancements of the high-speed tail induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud
(LMC). We present four variants of bounds from IceCube on Higgsino dark matter, depending on
various assumptions on cooling channels in the Sun, motivated by severe theoretical uncertainties
about Higgsino-nucleon elastic scattering (unimportant for direct detection but crucial for IceCube
bounds). Whereas the thermal Higgsino with a mass of 1.1 TeV remains only marginally compatible
with both the LZ event and the IceCube limits when the LMC-induced high-speed tail is included
and both elastic cooling in the Sun and the LZ high-energy sideband constraint are neglected, higher
mass Higgsinos are excellent candidates for the LZ event in light of IceCube constraints. Depending
on the halo distribution, cooling interactions, and whether the LZ high-energy sideband is included,
the compatible regions in the Higgsino parameter space (m χ,δ) extend from masses of∼2 TeV to
hundreds of TeV or higher, with mass splittings ranging approximately from 350 to 525 keV.

Although Dark Matter (DM) constitutes most (∼
85%) of the mass of the Universe, its nature remains a

posed to exist within several scenarios from Beyond the
Standard Model (BSM) of particle physics.
Direct detection laboratory experiments, originally
proposed in the 1980s [1, 2], are designed to probe the
interactions of WIMP dark matter with atomic nuclei in
terrestrial detectors situated deep underground. Despite
decades of experimental searches with continuously im-

particle nature of dark matter remains unsolved. Over
the years there have been hints of detection, but conclu-

NaI detectors consistent with a WIMP interpretation[3],
but these results are in tension with recent experiments
made of the same material [4].
Recently, a single unexplained event found by the

Many viable dark matter models contain a WIMP candidate that is a component of a new elec-
troweak multiplet whose massM is large compared to the electroweak scalemW . A generic amplitude-
level cancellation in such models yields a severe suppression of the cross section for WIMP-nucleon
scattering, making it important to assess the impact of formally subleading eﬀects. The power cor-
rection of order mW/M to the heavy WIMP limit is computed for electroweak doublet (Higgsino-like)
dark matter candidates, and a modern model of nuclear modiﬁcations to the free nucleon cross section
is evaluated. Corrections to the pure Higgsino limit are determined by a single parameter through ﬁrst
order in the heavy WIMP expansion. Current and projected experimental bounds on this parameter
are investigated. The direct detection signal in the pure Higgsino limit remains below neutrino back-
grounds for WIMPs in the TeV mass range. Nuclear corrections are applied also to the heavy Wino
case, completing the investigation of combined subleading eﬀects from perturbative QCD, 1 /M power
corrections, and nuclear modiﬁcations.

V. HIGH-ENERGY SIDEBAND IN LZ DA T A
Rodd et al. suggested that any explanation of the LZ
event atδ= 350 keV should also be consistent with the
lack of events in the LZ experiment at higher energies,
in its “sideband” at recoil energies∼350–650 keV [14].
However, the LZ collaboration has not published the ac-
ceptance in this sideband and did not include it in the
DM signal likelihood. The nuclear recoil response of the
detector up at those high recoil energies has not yet been
calibrated and is the subject of current work by the LZ
collaboration. Hence in this paper we will present results
both with and without the empty sideband taken into
account.
In those cases where we do require compatibilty of
our model with an empty sideband, we extend our LZ
likelihood to include the sideband. We can then iden-
tify regions in the (m χ,δ) plane compatible with the
LZ region of interest (ROI) as well as the empty side-
band. We extend our 96-bin likelihood by a Poisson
factorL SB = exp(−N SB), modeling the sideband as
350< E R <650 keV with zero observed events, zero
expected background, and unit signal acceptance. Here
NSB is the predicted differential recoil rate integrated
over this interval and multiplied by the exposure. Be-
cause the acceptance for DM-induced recoils in the exper-
imental sideband has not been published, the resulting
constraint is conditional on our acceptance and energy-
window approximations [14].
Fig. 2 illustrates the effect of the sideband on the LZ
confidence regions at 90% CL in the Higgsino parameter
space. The upper (lower) panel uses the SHM (SHM +
LMC) velocity distribution for the LZ prediction. Or-
ange dashed and blue solid contours show the approx-
imate joint 90% confidence regions in (m χ,δ) obtained
from our likelihood analysis with and without the high-
energy sideband, respectively, at fixed Higgsino coupling.
The star and diamond mark the corresponding best-fit
points, respectively. We note that there are two regions
compatible with empty sideband events. One region cor-
responds to lower DM massm χ <1 TeV, in which case
very few high energy recoil events are produced; but this
low mass region is ruled out by IceCube neutrino bounds
described in the next Section. The second region cor-
responds to higher Higgsino mass, and it is compatible
with the empty sideband because the particle abundance
and hence expected count rate decreases∼1/m χ.
In the rest of the paper we will present results both
with and without the empty sideband taken into account.
VI. SOLAR BOUNDS FROM NEUTRINO
TELESCOPES
Neutrino telescopes provide complementary probes of
dark matter particles through searches for neutrinos from
DM annihilation in the Sun 7. In particular, the absence
of a neutrino excess from the direction of the Sun in Ice-
Cube and Super-Kamiokande places strong constraints
on the DM particles studied in this paper. The same
inelastic DM–nucleus scattering process that could ex-
plain the LZ event can also occur as DM traverses the
Sun. Inelastic interactions with solar nuclei cause DM
particles to lose energy, allowing some to become gravi-
tationally bound to the Sun when their speeds fall below
the local solar escape speed. Because the solar gravi-
tational field accelerates incident DM particles, inelastic
scattering on heavy solar nuclei can occur at mass split-
tings beyond the reach of terrestrial xenon experiments.
Once captured, DM particles can cool by losing energy
through repeated scattering with solar nuclei. Inelas-
tic cooling stops when scattering becomes kinematically
inaccessible, while elastic interactions can allow further
energy loss. This cooling concentrates the captured pop-
ulation closer to the solar center, increasing its density
and enhancing the annihilation rate. If the Higgsino in-
teractions are sufficiently effective, cooling can proceed
rapidly enough for Higgsino capture and annihilation to
approach equilibrium. Capture–annihilation equilibrium
implies that the number of Higgsinos captured per unit
time equals the number lost to annihilation, yielding the
maximum annihilation rate sustained by a capture rate.
Understanding when cooling becomes inefficient or ceases
is essential, as well as identifying whether or not capture–
annihilation equilibrium is reached. DM annihilation in
the Sun produces neutrinos that can be detected by neu-
trino telescopes. The absence of a DM-induced solar neu-
trino excess in IceCube can therefore constrain Higgsino
properties, specifically the particle mass and mass split-
ting [12, 13]. Here we estimate these constraints under
different assumptions about the interactions responsible

B. DM distribution in the Sun: cooling and
possible thermalization
To compute the DM annihilation rate in the Sun, we
need the spatial distribution of the captured DM pop-
ulation. Captured Higgsinos can lose energy through
repeated scattering on solar nuclei, sinking towards the
center of the Sun. The key question in this subsection
is the spatial distribution of DM after cooling. We ap-
proximate the resulting DM population as uniformly dis-
tributed within a sphere of radiusR, which we determine
in the remainder of this subsection.
A bound Higgsino traverses the Sun repeatedly, in-
creasing the probability of undergoing multiple scatter-

turns.report:
# The thermal higgsino at 1.0–1.2 TeV: relic mass, inelastic LZ rates and neutrino limits

## Abstract

This run surveyed recent work on the pure-higgsino thermal relic, used the inelastic-DM tool server to compute relic densities and xenon recoil rates, and checked the 2026 reading of the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event as higgsino inelastic scattering.

- **Relic mass from the tool.** The tool's perturbative freeze-out gives Omega h^2 = 0.120 at m_chi ≈ 1159 GeV (bracketed by 1150 and 1160 GeV). This is a calibration of the tool's built-in cross-section normalisation, not an independent calculation. The independent Sommerfeld plus bound-state value from the literature is 1.08 ± 0.02 TeV.
- **LZ event under the tool's halo.** With a standard halo cut off at 776 km/s, the tool predicts zero LZ events for every delta_m ≥ 380 keV at 1.0–1.2 TeV. LZ-compatible event counts appear only near delta_m ≈ 350 keV, which lies below both the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) solar-neutrino exclusions.
- **What the literature region requires.** Analytic kinematics show that the published preferred region (481–519 keV) needs Earth-frame dark-matter speeds of about 920–980 km/s, and clearing the 557 keV line needs about 950–1015 km/s. The higgsino reading of the event therefore depends entirely on the halo's high-velocity tail.
- **Not done.** The elastic spin-independent comparison against the LZ and XENONnT curves at 1.1 TeV was not completed.

## Background

The pure higgsino is an electroweak doublet whose neutral states are split by a small Majorana mass, delta_m. Its thermal mass is fixed by matching the Planck abundance, Omega h^2 ≈ 0.12. A precise value needs Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation with the charged state (arXiv:1411.6930; analytic method in arXiv:1008.2905). Bound-state formation is claimed to matter mainly above a few TeV (arXiv:1407.7874).

Bottaro et al. (arXiv:2205.04486, Table I) give M_DM = 1.08 ± 0.02 TeV for the Dirac Y=1/2 doublet. That value includes Sommerfeld enhancement and bound-state formation and is normalised to Omega_DM h^2 = 0.11933 ± 0.00091. The same paper states that the doublet's direct-detection cross section "lies well below the neutrino" floor. Chen and Hill (arXiv:1912.07795) state: "The direct detection signal in the pure Higgsino limit remains below neutrino backgrounds for WIMPs in the TeV mass range." The relic density also sets the upper mass limit relevant to collider disappearing-track searches (arXiv:1901.02987).

For elastic scattering, the higgsino lies below the LZ 4.2 tonne-year limits (arXiv:2410.17036; best SI limit 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 40 GeV) and the XENONnT limits (arXiv:2303.14729). Tree-level Z exchange is removed by the inelastic splitting.

**The LZ event.** LZ reported a nuclear-recoil candidate at E_R = 248 ± 23 stat ± 23 sys keV, with 3.4σ local and 2.6σ global significance, in a 2.84 tonne-year exposure (arXiv:2609.06890, arXiv:2609.02608).

**Papers interpreting or constraining the event:**
- Wu, Zhang and Zhu (arXiv:2609.01590) fit the event with a higgsino.
  - With a Milky Way plus Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) velocity distribution ("Halo 13"), they find delta_m = 481–519 keV at 1σ and 475–529 keV at 2σ.
  - With a profiled Maxwellian halo they find 312–422 keV at 1σ and 280–457 keV at 2σ, with best fit 1.09 TeV and 366 keV.
  - The relic density fixes m_chi = 1000–1183 GeV at 1σ and 943–1230 GeV at 2σ.
- Solar-capture neutrino limits:
  - arXiv:2609.07807 excludes delta_m ≲ 557 keV, assuming captured higgsinos thermalise in a standard truncated Maxwellian halo.
  - arXiv:2609.01590 excludes delta_m ≲ 475 keV at 90% CL with IceCube when captured particles stay on extended orbits without elastic cooling. Loose inputs give 466 keV and the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty gives about 454 keV. Assuming equilibrium instead, the same paper finds about 553 keV.
- Freese and Theodosopoulos (arXiv:2610.03692) find the 1.1 TeV thermal higgsino only marginally compatible with the event and IceCube. Their compatible regions run from about 2 TeV to hundreds of TeV with delta ≈ 350–525 keV.
- arXiv:2609.09830 computes one-loop electroweak corrections to delta_m and to the scattering rates.
- arXiv:2609.06890 proposes boosted dark matter, which does not depend on the halo tail.

Several of these literature numbers were read directly in the full texts but could not be validated as verbatim quotes, because PDF extraction garbles math symbols and en-dash ranges. Treat them as read but not independently verified.

## Results

### Relic density versus mass (tool)

The tool's `compute_relic_density` uses perturbative Kolb–Turner freeze-out (x_f ≈ 24.4–24.8, g* = 86.25) with sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s × (1100 GeV/m_chi)^2.

| m_chi (GeV) | Omega h^2 |
|---|---|
| 900 | 0.0731 |
| 1000 | 0.0898 |
| 1100 | 0.1083 |
| 1150 | 0.1181 |
| 1160 | 0.1202 |
| 1200 | 0.1285 |
| 1300 | 0.1503 |

The Planck crossing (0.120 ± 0.0012) is at about 1159 GeV.

- **Comparison with the literature.** This is about 1% below the 1172 GeV inferred, not quoted, from arXiv:1411.6930. It is about 7% above the 1.08 TeV of arXiv:2205.04486.
- **Why it is not a check.** The agreement follows from the hard-coded normalisation; it is not independent physics.
- **Missing inputs.** The tool has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, no charged-splitting input and no delta_m dependence: Omega h^2 = 0.1202 at 1160 GeV for delta = 400, 500 and 600 keV. The "with and without Sommerfeld/coannihilation" and charged-splitting sensitivity items could not be run.
- **Unreliable flag.** The tool's `consistent_planck` flag reads True at 25σ tension and False at 39σ.

### Inelastic recoil kinematics and LZ event counts (tool)

The tool's halo is a standard halo with a hard cutoff at v_esc + v_E = 776 km/s. No call exposes halo parameters. Results at m_chi = 1100 GeV, sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2:

| delta (keV) | E_R,peak (keV) | v_min at peak (km/s) | v_min at 248 keV (km/s) | N_LZ (2.84 t-yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 270 | 701 | 701 | 744.6 |
| 400 | 360 | 809 | 823 | 0.00 |
| 480 | 432 | 886 | 921 | 0.00 |
| 520 | 468 | 922 | 969 | 0.00 |
| 560 | 504 | 957 | 1018 | 0.00 |

Scaling by exposure gives about 1101 events at 4.2 t-yr for 300 keV and zero for the rest. The tool does not report a separate E_R,min or an integrated rate above 100 keV. The annual-modulation output at (1100 GeV, 500 keV, 248 keV) is identically zero, because the rate is zero.

Bracketing near the edge with `predict_recoil` (2.84 t-yr):

| delta (keV) | events at 1000 GeV | events at upper mass |
|---|---|---|
| 340 | 10.67 | 17.30 (1183 GeV) |
| 350 | 1.13 | 2.90 (1200 GeV) |
| 360 | 0.03 | 0.158 (1183 GeV) |
| 380 | 0.00 | 0.00 (1183 GeV) |

**Scans.**
- A 15×15 scan (900–1300 GeV, 300–650 keV) found 180 of 225 points passing all constraints. Only 12 points predict 0.3–5 LZ events, with best fit (986 GeV, 350 keV).
- A 16×16 scan (1000–1200 GeV, 330–480 keV) passed all 256 points. It placed 16 points in the 0.3–5 band, with best fit (1000 GeV, 350 keV).
- That those 16 points form the delta = 350 keV row is inferred from the bracketing above. The binary scan file could not be read, so this was not listed directly by the tool.
- The second scan overwrote the first scan's file (`.../inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz`) and its summary plot (`constraint_summary.png`). A recoil-spectrum plot for 1100 GeV / 500 keV is at `.../output/recoil_spectrum.png`.
- No numbered figures were produced.

**Interpretation.** Under the truncated halo, no LZ-compatible point reaches delta ≥ 360 keV. In particular none reaches the 475 or 557 keV neutrino lines, so no tool point that reproduces the event survives the neutrino limits. The critic stressed that the band near 350 keV is an artefact of the hard cutoff, where N falls from 10.7 to 1.1 to 0.03 over 20 keV. It is not a physical preferred region.

### Analytic kinematic check

The maximum splitting that can produce a recoil at E_R = 248 keV for a given maximum speed is

delta_max = v_max·sqrt(2 m_N E_R) − m_N E_R/mu,

with m_N = 122.0 GeV (Xe-131) and sqrt(2 m_N E_R) = 0.8206 keV per km/s.

| v_max (km/s) | delta_max at 1000 GeV (keV) | at 1100 GeV | at 1183 GeV |
|---|---|---|---|
| 776 | 358.5 | 361.3 | 363.2 |
| 800 | 378 | 381 | 383 |
| 850 | 419 | 422 | 424 |
| 900 | 460 | 463 | 465 |

- **Agreement with the tool.** This reproduces the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within about 1 km/s.
- **Origin of the "about 365 keV" edge.** That figure is the endpoint with E_R left free, mu v_max^2/2 = 364–370 keV at 776 km/s, reached near E_R ≈ 330 keV rather than at 248 keV.

Inverting at 1100 GeV gives the Earth-frame v_max needed to reach a given splitting:

| delta (keV) | v_max with event at 248 keV (km/s) | v_max with E_R free (km/s) |
|---|---|---|
| 422 | — | 830 |
| 457 | 893 | 864 |
| 475 | 915 | 881 |
| 519 | 968 | 921 |
| 529 | 980 | 930 |
| 557 | 1015 | 954 |

At 1000 GeV these values shift by about +3 km/s, and at 1183 GeV by about −2 km/s.

What this implies:
- The profiled-Maxwellian edges of arXiv:2609.01590 (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830–890 km/s.
- The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need an LMC-boosted tail reaching about 920–980 km/s.
- Clearing 475 keV needs at least about 880–915 km/s, and clearing 557 keV needs at least about 950–1015 km/s.

The critic noted two sources of uncertainty that make these thresholds uncertain by roughly ±10–20 km/s:
- The calculation assumes a single isotope. Natural xenon spans A = 124–136, and Xe-134 raises delta_max by about 7 keV at 776 km/s and 1.1 TeV.
- The ±23 keV statistical and systematic energy uncertainty also enters.

### Combined constraint check (tool)

At 1160 GeV, `check_all_constraints` returns "VIABLE" for delta = 400, 500 and 600 keV:

| Quantity | delta = 400 keV | 500 keV | 600 keV | Tool's limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Omega h^2 | 0.1202 (0.1σ) | 0.1202 | 0.1202 | — |
| N_LZ (2.84 t-yr) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | flagged inconsistent with 1 observed event |
| sigma_v today (cm^3/s) | 6.7e-42 | 1.04e-41 | 1.50e-41 | 2.48e-25 (Fermi) |
| CMB p_ann | 0.86e-45 | 1.35e-45 | 1.94e-45 | 3.2e-28 |

At (1100 GeV, 500 keV) the check gives Omega h^2 = 0.1083, N_LZ = 0 and sigma_v = 1.29e-41 against a Fermi limit of 2.3e-25.

Warning: these verdicts are not physically reliable. The tool treats annihilation today as p-wave and splitting-suppressed, whereas the higgsino annihilates s-wave to WW/ZZ at about 1e-26 cm^3/s. The "viable" label therefore means invisible, not allowed. The critic contested this finding, and no s-wave replacement was computed.

### Literature: why the two neutrino lines differ, and gamma-ray lines

The 475 vs 557 keV difference comes from how captured particles are treated in the Sun, not from the halo model (read in the full texts; not independently verified).

- **arXiv:2609.01590 (475 keV).** At 1.11 TeV it uses a non-thermal captured population on extended orbits, <sigma v>_eff ≈ 1.5e-26 cm^3/s with Sommerfeld, and ten years of IceCube data.
- **arXiv:2609.07807 (557 keV).** It assumes thermalisation, a truncated Maxwellian (u0 = 220, v_esc = 544, v_sun = 232 km/s; rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3), sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s and m_chi = 1.08 TeV. It uses a 95% CL fit to IceCube nu_mu, IceCube nu_e and Super-K. It still allows rescue by an LMC tail or substructure.
- **arXiv:2610.03692.** It shows four 90% CL IceCube cooling treatments in its Fig. 2:
  - capture–annihilation equilibrium;
  - spin-independent (SI) inelastic cooling only;
  - SI inelastic plus spin-dependent (SD) elastic cooling;
  - SI inelastic plus SD plus SI elastic cooling, with sigma_SI,el = 4e-50 cm^2.

  Its other inputs are a standard halo with rho = 0.3 GeV/cm^3, sigma_Hn = 7.43e-39 cm^2 and an LMC tail cut at 950 km/s. It states the solar limits "remain unchanged by adding the effects of the LMC". The delta values at 1.1 TeV for each treatment appear only in the figure and were not quantified.

**Gamma-ray lines (arXiv:2609.01590).** The thermal line prediction is 0.815–0.900 of the H.E.S.S. 546 h limits, which the paper describes as close to but not excluded. The CTAO Alpha 500 h projection gives mu_gamma,95 = 1.69, which falls short of the thermal target. An Omega-configuration estimate of 0.85 would reach it, but it is unverified whether that number comes from the paper or from the agent's own 1.69/2 scaling. Dwarf, CMB and ATLAS disappearing-track limits do not exclude the region.

**Radiative corrections (arXiv:2609.09830).** Its benchmarks have one-loop on-shell splittings of 36.37, 8.90, 16.39, 10.81 and 10.59 keV at |mu| = 0.61–1.40 TeV, all with Omega h^2 < 0.12. It gives no delta_m shift in the 475–557 keV window. A tree-to-one-loop shift of order 0.1 GeV was read off its mass table by the agent; the paper does not state it. It therefore does not bear on rescuing the window.

## Discussion

**Relic mass.** The tool's 1159 GeV is a normalisation echo. The best independent anchor in the record is 1.08 ± 0.02 TeV (arXiv:2205.04486), which includes Sommerfeld enhancement and bound states. The 1172 GeV figure attributed to arXiv:1411.6930 is inferred rather than quoted. Which value to use as the headline remains open, since published thermal masses differ by roughly 10–20% depending on treatment.

**The LZ event.** Our computations and the literature agree on one point: the LZ reading requires a population of halo particles above roughly 880 km/s in the Earth frame. A standard halo truncated at 776 km/s caps the splitting at about 360 keV at 248 keV recoil. That is below every neutrino exclusion line. This is consistent with arXiv:2609.07807's statement that the reading is disfavoured for standard halo velocities, and with arXiv:2610.03692's "marginal" verdict.

What the run could not do is decide between the published analyses. They differ in the solar treatment (thermalised or not) and in how much LMC tail they assume. Our tool can vary neither.

**Current limits.** The task asked where the higgsino sits relative to current limits. Only qualitative literature statements are available for the elastic channel: below the LZ and XENONnT reach, and below the neutrino floor according to arXiv:1912.07795 and arXiv:2205.04486. No numerical limit at 1.1 TeV was read. For indirect detection, the only computed numbers come from the tool's unphysical p-wave treatment. The literature gamma-ray line ratio (0.815–0.900 of H.E.S.S.) suggests the thermal higgsino is close to current sensitivity, but that number is not independently verified.

**Dead ends.**
- No tool exposes halo parameters, so the dependence on v_esc and on an LMC tail could not be tested. A custom rate code is needed.
- `load_table_data` cannot read the binary scan file, so scan-band membership had to be inferred by bracketing.
- Verbatim quotes from arXiv:2609.01590 failed because of garbled math: the endpoint sentence, the H.E.S.S. ratio, the 553 keV bound, the Maxwellian best fit and the relic ranges.
- The Planck 2018 quote "0.120 \pm 0.001" was not found in the extracted text, so Planck is not yet cited in the reference file.
- The tool budget ran out before narrow re-reads of arXiv:2609.01590 and arXiv:2609.07807 and before an s-wave indirect-detection comparison.

## Limitations

- **Relic density.** The tool is perturbative only, with no Sommerfeld, coannihilation, charged-splitting or delta_m dependence. The relic mass is therefore not an independent computation.
- **Event counts.** Counts assume the tool's unstated LZ acceptance in its extended nuclear-recoil search and a single halo with a hard 776 km/s cutoff. There is no isotope averaging, and the critic noted thresholds carry about ±10–20 km/s.
- **Elastic SI comparison.** Not done: the LZ 4.2 t-yr and XENONnT 90% CL values near 1.1 TeV, the higgsino sigma_SI band and the neutrino-fog level were never read. The critic flagged this as the main missing piece.
- **Indirect and CMB.** These rest on an unphysical p-wave assumption. No s-wave comparison was made.
- **Unverified literature numbers.** Several literature numbers (preferred regions, 553 keV, the H.E.S.S. ratio, the CTAO Omega estimate, the doublet mass, the arXiv:2610.03692 and arXiv:2609.09830 details) were not independently verified. The critic contested them, mostly because of failed verbatim quotes or abstract-only reading.
- **Reproducibility.** The first scan's outputs were overwritten and cannot be reproduced from disk.
- **Compute.** All computation ran locally. No HPC facility was used.

brief.summary: Literature converges on a pure Higgsino thermal relic mass near 1.0-1.1 TeV to saturate Omega h^2 = 0.12, with sub-TeV masses viable only with slepton coannihilation or bino/wino mixing. Direct detection of pure Higgsino is loop-suppressed due to accidental cancellations, leading to purity constraints on gaugino mixing from LZ/Xenon. Recent 2026 preprints propose inelastic Higgsino scattering with delta ~ 350 keV as an interpretation of the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event in 2.84 ton-yr exposure, while a contrasting solar-capture analysis using IceCube non-observation of high-energy neutrinos from the Sun derives delta > 566 keV for ~1.08 TeV Higgsino, excluding the thermal-Higgsino explanation of the LZ event under standard halo and solar model assumptions. The tension hinges on halo high-speed tail (LMC), solar density/capture on heavy elements, elastic cooling in the Sun, and the LZ high-energy sideband joint fit.

result.summary:
Not finished: only one published pure-higgsino relic-density point was found, so the success criteria (published values at three or more masses, and a thermal mass from two independent papers) are not met.

(1) No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists here, and list_input_files returned no data files (tc-261016_1-w1-d-01-19, finding f-006). Every value below comes from the literature. Nothing was computed.

(2) arXiv:1411.6930, Sec. 3, gives the one published point: a pure higgsino (all sfermions and heavy Higgses decoupled) has Omega h^2 = 0.127 without and 0.126 with Sommerfeld enhancement (off-diagonal rates included). The net Sommerfeld effect is below 1 percent because the neutral channels are enhanced and the charged ones suppressed. The paper's mass for this model appears to be 1172.31 GeV, the mass of its higgsino-like pMSSM point 1627006; I inferred this from context, the paper does not state it. For that pMSSM point (dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV) the values are 0.108 without and 0.100 with Sommerfeld, an 8 percent drop. The paper quotes about 5 percent accuracy at best and compares to Planck 2013 (0.1187 +/- 0.0017). Its Fig. 7 (registered as Figure 6, figures_1411.6930/fig07.png) shows only the yield ratio Y/Ypert, not Omega h^2 against mass (finding f-007). A verbatim quote is in references.bib (key arxiv14116930).

(3) hep-ph/0610249 expected the Sommerfeld effect for higgsinos to be roughly 10 percent (versus 50 percent for winos). It was not a full calculation (f-009).

(4) Interpolation, not published values: scaling the 1411.6930 point as Omega h^2 proportional to m^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155 at 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV. Omega h^2 = 0.120 falls at about 1.14 TeV (1144 GeV with Sommerfeld, 1139 GeV without) (f-009, low confidence).

Still to do: the Planck 2018 text was downloaded but not yet read or quoted; 1008.2905 was not read; no independent recent thermal-mass determination was found.

result.summary:
Answer: a thermal pure higgsino at about 1.1 TeV lies about 2 or more orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 limit and below the xenon neutrino floor. Three of the planned inputs were not read: the XENONnT limit, the LZ limit read from its figure at 1 TeV, and a numeric neutrino-fog value. All are recorded as open question q-06.

(1) Prediction. Hisano et al. 1104.0228 work at leading order in electroweak loops. They find the SI cross section of pure SU(2)-multiplet dark matter is O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2, nearly independent of mass above about 1 TeV. An accidental cancellation drives this: twist-2 terms are positive, while the Higgs-exchange, gluon and Z-box scalar terms are negative and of similar size. Their Fig. 5 shows the higgsino (n=2, Y=1/2) at M = 1 TeV against the Higgs mass; the paper predates the measured Higgs mass. Finding f-004.

The newer and more complete calculation is Chen and Hill 1912.07795, which adds O(mW/M) power corrections, QCD corrections to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. Its verbatim result is: 'The upper limit for the pure doublet is less than 10^-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass regime ... lower than the estimated Xenon neutrino floor', with 'the pure Higgsino well below the neutrino floor'. The uncertainty is quoted only as this upper bound; no central value plus or minus an error was read. Citation recorded in references.bib (tc-...-64).

(2) LZ 2024 limit (2410.17036). Verbatim: the strongest SI exclusion is 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 90% CL, and the best median sensitivity is 5.1e-48 cm^2, both at 40 GeV. Finding f-005, citation tc-...-65. No 1 TeV value was read from the text or a figure.

(3) Rescaling. Scaling the 40 GeV limit linearly with mass is my estimate, not a read value. It gives about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, at 1.1 TeV. The ratio of limit to predicted upper bound is then at least about 60, i.e. at least 1.8 orders of magnitude. This extrapolation is likely conservative because the limit curve rises from its minimum. Finding f-008, medium confidence.

Not done:
- The XENONnT 2303.14729 1 TeV limit was not read.
- No limit figure was extracted, so there are no figure numbers for the LZ or XENONnT limits.
- No numeric neutrino-fog value at 1 TeV was obtained; the 'below the neutrino floor' statement rests on Chen and Hill's text.
- Projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD/DARWIN) were not tabulated.

Also noted: 2607.20588 (Bisal et al., 2026) says next-to-leading-order corrections can push the higgsino cross section below the neutrino floor or make it vanish in parts of MSSM parameter space. This is relevant to q-04.

result.summary: Two of the three success criteria are met; the third is only partly met. (1) The inelastic threshold, worked by hand (f-001): m_Xe = 131 x 0.9315 = 122.0 GeV. The reduced mass mu_A is 108.7 GeV at m = 1.0 TeV and 109.8 GeV at 1.1 TeV. With v_max = 544 + 232 = 776 km/s, (v_max/c)^2 = 6.70e-6, so delta_max = mu_A v_max^2/2 is about 364 keV at 1.0 TeV and 368 keV at 1.1 TeV. The minimum-velocity formula v_min = sqrt(2 delta/mu_A) is Eq. A7 of 2609.09830. (2) Partly met: 2609.09830 does not give an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range (f-002). Its five benchmarks have |mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV, |M1| and M2 of about 5.8-42 TeV, and one-loop on-shell delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. They predict at most about 1.03 combined NLO events in LZ, need 9.4-65.5 t-y of exposure to be probed (Table VII, Fig. 6), and are all consistent with LZ. NLO vertex corrections can exceed 100 percent, and in BP2 the inelastic cross section is about twice the LO elastic one. Splittings of O(10) keV with gaugino masses of O(10) TeV arise only from partial cancellation between the M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 terms when M1 and M2 have opposite signs; generically the paper quotes O(10-100) MeV. My own estimate, using the formula that is not yet sourced (q-05): same-sign M2 = 2 M1 would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV to bring delta below 364 keV. Inelastic Z-exchange therefore matters only in tuned corners. (3) Mixing region where elastic SI becomes visible (f-003, 2606.31013): Higgs exchange gives f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 theta_W/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta). Analytic check (f-033, hand-computed): delta_max = v_max*sqrt(2 m_N E_R) - m_N E_R/mu at E_R = 248 keV, with m_N = 122 GeV. At 1000/1100/1183 GeV it gives 358.5/361.3/363.2 keV for 776 km/s, 378/381/383 keV for 800, 419/422/424 keV for 850 and 460/463/465 keV for 900 km/s. It matches the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within about 1 km/s. The tool's 'about 365 keV' edge is the endpoint when E_R is left free, mu v^2/2 = 364-370 keV at 776 km/s, reached near E_R of about 330 keV rather than at 248 keV.

Required v_max (f-034, hand-computed), at 1100 GeV with the event at 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 for 475, 968 for 519, 980 for 529 and 1015 for 557 keV. With E_R left free the minimum is lower: 830 km/s for 422 keV, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 for 557 keV.

What this means for 2609.01590 and the LMC tail:
- The paper's profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s, compared with the tool's 776 km/s. This explains why the tool gives zero events at 400 keV.
- The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need an LMC-boosted tail reaching about 920-980 km/s.
- Clearing the 475 keV IceCube line needs at least about 880-915 km/s.
- Clearing the 557 keV Super-K + IceCube line needs at least about 950-1015 km/s.
The higgsino reading of the event therefore depends entirely on how many particles the halo has above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.

findings.claim: 2609.09830 does not quote an LZ-excluded delta_m0 range. Its five benchmarks (|mu| = 0.61-1.40 TeV; |M1|, M2 about 5.8-42 TeV; tan beta 10.9-26.5) have one-loop on-shell splittings delta = 8.9-36.4 keV. findings.claim: Chen and Hill (1912.07795) include the O(mW/M) power corrections, perturbative QCD to NNNLO and ChEFT nuclear effects. They find that the pure-higgsino SI cross section has an upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass range, below the estimated xenon neutrino floor. This is about 2 orders of magnitude below the LZ 2024 minimum limit of 2.2e-48 cm^2 at 40 GeV. Assuming linear mass scaling of the LZ limit above about 100 GeV (my estimate, not read from the paper), the LZ limit at 1.1 TeV is about 2.2e-48 x (1100/40), roughly 6e-47 cm^2, so the pure higgsino lies at least about 1.8 orders of magnitude below it.

findings.claim: Hisano et al. (hep-ph/0610249) expect the Sommerfeld effect on the higgsino-like relic abundance to be roughly 10 percent, compared with a 50 percent reduction for the wino. 1411.6930 later found the net pure-higgsino effect is below 1 percent (Omega h^2 = 0.127 perturbative, 0.126 Sommerfeld). findings.claim: Metadata confirms both IDs: arXiv:2606.31013 is 'Complementary Probes of Light Higgsinos: Electroweak Precision Measurements and Dark Matter Direct Detection' by Hamaguchi, Nagata and Osaki (2026), and arXiv:2609.09830 is 'Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter' by Chatterjee, Das, Pasha, Pukhov and Puri (2026). Both abstracts match how the survey uses them. This resolves q-02.

The full text of 2606.31013 supports the f-003 numbers. Eq. 13 reads Delta m+|rad ~ (1/2) alpha2 MZ sin^2 thetaW (1 - 3MZ/(2 pi M_chi+)), with the statement 'For M_chi+ >> MZ, this mass splitting asymptotically approaches Delta m+|rad ~ 356 MeV'. Eq. 33 reads f_q ~ -(g^2/8M_h^2)[1/(M2-|mu|) + tan^2 thetaW/(M1-|mu|)](1 + sgn(mu) sin 2beta) and is valid for MZ << M1,2-|mu|; the exact form is Eq. 32. The paper says the coupling is suppressed at large gaugino mass and 'for small tan beta and negative mu, due to an accidental cancellation'. Eq. 38 is sigma_SI/SD,eff = (Omega_H h^2/0.12) sigma_SI/SD, computed with micrOMEGAs v6.3.0. The scan (Eq. 37) covers 150 GeV<|mu|<1000 GeV, 1.6<tan beta<50 and 0.5 TeV<M1<10 TeV, with M2=2M1 and M1>|mu|. Note: the f-003 label 'Eq. 13' is correct; the f_q formula is Eq. 33, not unnumbered.

The full text of 2609.09830 supports the f-002 numbers. Table III gives one-loop on-shell delta = 36.37, 8.90, 16.39, 10.81 and 10.59 keV for BP1-BP5, with mu = -739.63, -606.64, -814.26, 1282.11 and 1400.0 GeV, M1 = -7830, -6292, -5838, 11354 and 12875 GeV, M2 = 17055, 42000, 30925, 12627 and 12050 GeV, and tan beta = 10.88-26.46. Table VII, NLO rows for BP1-BP5: elastic events 1.0280, 0.07729, 0.1176, 0.4127, 0.5074; inelastic events 0.00022, 0.07039, 0.0518, 0.1806, 0.1661; combined 1.02822, 0.14768, 0.1694, 0.5933, 0.6735; required exposure 9.41, 65.50, 57.10, 16.30, 14.36 t-y (LZ exposure 4.2 t-y; null result taken as N_E < ln 10, about 2.3). Table VI for BP2 gives sigma_inel NLO = 0.507e-12 pb against sigma_el LO = 0.284e-12 pb (ratio 1.785). The paper describes this as 'approximately a factor of two larger than the elastic LO one'. The text says all BPs are consistent with LZ. Note: the BP1 scan sign pattern has M1<0 and M2>0 for mu=±0.5 or ±1 TeV, with -21 TeV <= M1 <= -1 TeV and 1 TeV <= M2 <= 21 TeV (Eq. 25), yet BP4 and BP5 have M1 and M2 both positive.

2609.09830 does not write out the tree-level delta_m0 formula. It says only: 'as can be seen, for example, from Eq. (9) of Ref. [28], the corrections proportional to M_Z^2/M1 and M_Z^2/M2 depend on the relative signs of M1 and M2. In the parameter regions relevant for our analysis, these contributions can have opposite signs and partially cancel.' 2606.31013 also says only that the splittings are 'suppressed by M_Z^2/M_1,2'. The explicit form delta_m0 ~ m_Z^2 s_W^2/M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2/M2 therefore remains unsourced (q-05 stays open), and so does the estimate that same-sign M2=2M1 needs M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV. Counter-evidence to the 'tuned corners only' conclusion: BP4 and BP5 reach delta of about 10.6-10.8 keV with M1 and M2 both positive (about 11-13 TeV) and mu > 0. The O(10) keV splittings there come from on-shell one-loop corrections combined with relative signs between mu and the gauginos, not only from opposite-sign M1 and M2.

findings.claim: The 475 keV and 557 keV neutrino lines differ because of how the captured population in the Sun is treated, not because of the halo. 2609.01590 simulates a non-thermal population on extended solar orbits at m_chi = 1.11 TeV with no elastic cooling (elastic blind spot) and 10-year IceCube data, using <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s with Sommerfeld; this gives delta_m >~ 475 keV excluded at 90% CL (466 keV with loose solar/nuclear inputs, about 454 keV with the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty). If elastic scattering allows thermalization and capture-annihilation equilibrium, the same paper gets delta_m >~ 553 keV. 2609.07807 assumes thermalization within the Sun after capture, a standard truncated Maxwellian (u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s), rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3, sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s, m_chi = 1.08 TeV and a 95% CL chi^2 on IceCube nu_mu (2016), IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. It excludes delta_m <~ 557 keV and states the interpretation could remain viable with an LMC tail or substructure.

findings.claim: Inverting the kinematics at m_chi = 1100 GeV gives the v_max (Earth frame) needed to reach a given delta with an event exactly at E_R = 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 km/s for 475 keV, 968 km/s for 519 keV, 980 km/s for 529 keV and 1015 km/s for 557 keV (about +3 km/s at 1000 GeV, about -2 km/s at 1183 GeV). If E_R is free (at the optimal E_R = mu*delta/m_N of about 380-500 keV), the minimum is v_max = sqrt(2 delta/mu): 830 km/s for 422, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 km/s for 557 keV. All of these exceed the tool's SHM cutoff of 776 km/s by 55-240 km/s. So the 2609.01590 profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s. The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need about 920-980 km/s of LMC-boosted tail. Covering delta >= 557 keV (above the Super-K + IceCube line) needs at least about 950-1015 km/s, and delta >= 475 keV needs at least about 880-915 km/s. The higgsino reading therefore rests entirely on the halo's population above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.

questions.text: The task asks for relic densities from 'inelastic-DM tools', but no such tool, no run_coding_task and no run_pack_kernel is in the catalog. Should the user be told that relic-density values are literature-sourced rather than computed, or is a compute server missing from the connection?
The arXiv IDs 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 are recent. Verify with get_arxiv_metadata that they exist and that their content matches the survey before relying on them.

Published thermal masses differ by about 10-20 percent depending on Sommerfeld treatment, bound-state formation and the treatment of the QCD/electroweak phase transition. Which value should serve as the headline?
Is the SI prediction's interference between the Higgs and gauge (twist-2) contributions stable enough that the conclusion 'below the neutrino fog' is robust?

The tree-level formula delta_m0 ≈ m_Z^2 s_W^2/M1 + m_Z^2 c_W^2/M2 has not been sourced yet. Can a quotable reference be found, for example Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, Eq. (9)? Taken at face value with same-sign M2 = 2 M1, delta < 364 keV would need M1 of about 1.4e7 GeV, so the O(10) keV benchmarks are viable only through sign cancellations and loop corrections.

Still open from d-02: the XENONnT 2303.14729 SI limit at 1 TeV, the actual LZ 2024 limit-curve value at 1 TeV (read from its figure rather than linearly rescaled from 40 GeV), and a numeric xenon neutrino-fog value at 1.1 TeV. None of these were read in this direction.

The XLZD Design Book (arXiv:2410.17137) has been identified but not read: what are its projected SI sensitivity and its xenon neutrino-fog value at about 1 TeV, and how do they compare with the pure-higgsino bound of 1e-48 cm^2?

What thermal mass, with its theory uncertainty, does arXiv:2205.04486 (Bottaro et al. 2022, Sommerfeld plus bound-state formation) give for the Y=1/2 doublet in its thermal-mass table, and how far is it from the 1411.6930-derived value of about 1.14 TeV?

What arXiv paper is Ref. [28] of 2609.09830, and does its Eq. (9) give the tree-level neutral higgsino splitting with explicit sign dependence on mu, M1 and M2? issues.text: Step 1 is not enough: the gap has to show up in the final answer. No relic-density or inelastic-DM compute tool exists, list_input_files is empty, and run_test_job only draws random samples. The task asked us to compute relic density with tools, and we cannot. The report must say plainly that every Omega h^2 value is taken from the literature. Do not use run_test_job to produce anything that looks like a computed relic curve.

1411.6930 is a pMSSM scan. It may not give a pure-higgsino Omega h^2(m) curve at 0.9-1.3 TeV with and without Sommerfeld enhancement. Before relying on it, check that such a figure or table exists. If it does not, use the one-parameter thermal mass plus the m^2 scaling, and label every resulting row as derived, not read. Also note that the higgsino Sommerfeld effect is small, only a few percent shift in mass. Bound-state formation (recent 2021-2026 work) can matter as much as Sommerfeld, so the search should target it explicitly.

The budget is tight. Fifteen calls do not cover three or four full-text downloads plus chunk reads, figures and cite. Drop the full read of 1008.2905, which is a method paper and not needed for numbers. Get the Planck Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001 quote with one targeted chunk read of 1807.06209. Limit independent cross-checks to one paper.

Run get_arxiv_metadata on 2606.31013 and 2609.09830 before any download, to confirm they exist and say what the brief claims. The brief cites 2606.31013 for the '~1 TeV' figure but has not read it. If either ID does not resolve, report that and do not attribute numbers to it.

A key literature cross-check is missing. Hill and Solon (for example 1111.0016 and 1409.8290) give the heavy-higgsino SI cross section with a large cancellation-driven uncertainty, possibly near or below the xenon neutrino fog. Because 1104.0228 and 1007.2601 predate refined nucleon matrix elements, the prediction should be quoted as a range across these sources, not a single number. 1004.4090 is a wino paper and can be skipped.

Values read off log-scale limit figures with get_paper_figures need a stated reading uncertainty, for example a factor of about 1.5. Check whether the LZ and XENONnT figures actually extend to 1 TeV. If they do, read the value there and do not rescale. If rescaling is needed, use limit proportional to m for m >> m_Xe and state the reference mass. Also replace the brief's 1e-46 to 1e-45 estimate with read values; the true limit at 1 TeV is likely near the low end of that range.

2510.17473 (ICRC 2025 review) is listed in the brief but not used. Use it as one source for current and projected xenon reach (LZ full exposure, XLZD) and for the neutrino-fog value at TeV masses, instead of searching for a separate fog paper.

The threshold arithmetic is sound. With m_Xe of about 122 GeV, mu is about 109 GeV at 1 TeV and v_max is about 776 km/s, giving delta_max of about 360 keV. State the assumed v_esc and v_E, and note the sensitivity to the halo model. Source the charged-neutral splitting of about 341 MeV to the two-loop result (for example 1410.4549) rather than leaving it generic. Keep the splitting formula approximate, including tan(beta)-dependent and sign terms.

The answer to 'relative to current limits' should mention indirect detection briefly. For example, H.E.S.S. Galactic Center line and continuum limits are weak for TeV higgsinos because the cross section is not strongly Sommerfeld-enhanced. One sourced sentence from a review will do. This keeps the conclusion from resting on direct detection alone without changing scope.
The mixing-induced SI rise in the (mu, M1/M2, tan beta) plane overlaps with the d-02 discussion. Keep it only in d-03, so the two directions do not each download 2606.31013.

contested.reason: None of the three quoted excerpts contains any claimed content. tc-...-35 covers the oblique-parameter chi-square (Eqs. 26-29), tc-...-30 is the title page, and tc-...-33 covers the W/Y parameters (Eqs. 39-40). Missing are the f_q formula, the scan ranges, Eq. 13 (356 MeV), Eq. 38 with micrOMEGAs 6.3.0, and the statement that direct detection reaches about 1 TeV only with mixing. These may well be in the paper, but the cited evidence does not show them.

The excerpts do not show the Omega h^2 values 0.127, 0.126, 0.108 or 0.100, nor dm+ = 1.8 GeV, dm0 = 9.5 GeV or the 5 percent accuracy. The claim states m_chi = 1172.31 GeV as reported, but the d-01 summary says this mass was inferred from context and is not stated in the paper. The figure is also mislabelled: fig07 is registered as Figure 6.

There are two problems. First, the Chen and Hill verbatim quote (the upper limit below 1e-48 cm^2, below the neutrino floor) is not in any quoted excerpt. The cited tc-...-59 and -58 show only the rate formula and the title, and the citation call tc-...-64 is not listed as evidence. Second, there is an arithmetic error. An upper bound below 1e-48 cm^2 compared with the 2.2e-48 cm^2 minimum is a factor of about 2 or more, not 'about 2 orders of magnitude'. Only the comparison at 1.1 TeV (about 6e-47 cm^2) supports a margin of 1.8 orders or more.

The visible part of Table VII supports only BP1 elastic NLO = 1.028 events, which is consistent with 'at most about 1.03'. The other quantities are not in the shown excerpts: the splitting range 8.9-36.4 keV, the exposures of 9.4-65.5 t-y, the inelastic NLO range, and the BP2 statement. The visible LO numbers for BP2 (inelastic 0.0247, elastic 0.0436) show inelastic below elastic. The 'twice the LO elastic' claim therefore needs the NLO inelastic value quoted explicitly.

issues.text: The core quantity is still unmet. There is no published Omega h^2(m) curve at multiple masses and no second, independent determination of the thermal mass. The m^2 rescaling in f-009 depends on an inferred mass of 1172.31 GeV. If that inference is wrong, every rescaled value and the 1.14 TeV thermal mass shift with it.

The Planck 2018 value of 0.120 +/- 0.001 is used throughout but has never been quoted from 1807.06209.txt, although the file is already downloaded. 1411.6930 normalised to Planck 2013 (0.1187), so the f-009 rescaling should state which target it uses.

The arithmetic checks out: 0.126 x (m/1172.31)^2 gives 0.074, 0.092, 0.111, 0.132 and 0.155, and the thermal masses of 1144 and 1139 GeV are correct. However, the hep-ph/0610249 '10 percent' statement is not visible in the tc-...-68 excerpt.
The excerpt confirms only the 4.2 t-y exposure. The 2.2e-48 / 5.1e-48 cm^2 values at 40 GeV match the published LZ abstract but are not visible in the quoted chunk.

The excerpts support the structure of the cancellation (the Fig. 6 contribution panels), but not the numeric range O(1e-46 to 1e-48) cm^2. This is a 2011 result computed against a scan over the Higgs mass, so it should be quoted at mh = 125 GeV.

The headline answer to 'where the higgsino sits relative to limits' still rests on a linear extrapolation from 40 GeV. None of the following has been read: the LZ or XENONnT limit at 1 TeV, a numeric neutrino-fog value, or projected sensitivities (LZ full exposure, XLZD). The final answer needs these numbers, each with a stated reading uncertainty.

2606.31013 and 2609.09830 have not been checked with get_arxiv_metadata (q-02). The delta_m0 tree-level formula behind the 1.4e7 GeV estimate is unsourced (q-05). The 356 versus 340 MeV correction to the brief depends on f-003, which is contested.

Survey recent arXiv work on the higgsino thermal relic target (1.0-1.2 TeV). Use the inelastic-DM tools to compute the relic density at several masses; compare with LZ/XENONnT sensitivities and the Planck abundance. Where does the higgsino sit relative to current limits?

**Survey** — 30 tools on 3 servers, 5 read-only probes, 3 papers found.

Pure higgsino thermal freeze-out with Sommerfeld and coannihilation corrections predicts Omega h^2 = 0.12 at m_chi ~1.0-1.2 TeV, canonically 1.1 TeV, with theoretical uncertainty from non-perturbative electroweak effects. Direct detection is dominated by Z-mediated inelastic scattering between nearly degenerate neutralinos with splitting delta ~ 100-400 keV, while Higgs-mediated elastic scattering is suppressed by high purity required by LZ 2024 and XENONnT limits. Recent work explores light-slepton coannihilation lowering the thermal mass to ~0.4-0.6 TeV and low-reheating cosmologies raising it, plus CTAO and Fermi-LAT line searches approaching the thermal annihilation cross section. The 2026 LZ 248 keV high-recoil event has renewed interest in inelastic higgsino benchmarks at 1.1 TeV and delta ~ 300-350 keV as a testable recoil-spectrum signature.

Quantities worth checking: Thermal relic density Omega h^2 vs Planck 0.120 +/- 0.001 at m_chi = 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 TeV; Mass splitting delta = m_chi2 - m_chi1 in 100-400 keV range and kinematic threshold for inelastic scattering on xenon; Spin-independent nucleon cross section vs LZ 2024 and XENONnT limits and neutrino fog floor; Differential recoil spectrum dR/dE_R on xenon at 1.1 TeV and delta ~200-350 keV; Annual modulation amplitude and phase at fixed recoil energy for inelastic higgsino; Annihilation cross section <sigma v> vs Fermi-LAT dwarf and Galactic Center line limits and CTAO-North sensitivity.
